(15 pages, 6 figures)"}],"control_number":767281,"earliest_date":"2007-11","document_type":["conference paper"],"texkeys":["Shapiro:2007me"],"abstracts":[{"source":"arXiv","value":"Black holes are popping up all over the place: in compact binary X-ray sources and GRBs, in quasars, AGNs and the cores of all bulge galaxies, in binary black holes and binary black hole-neutron stars, and maybe even in the LHC! Black holes are strong-field objects governed by Einstein's equations of general relativity. Hence general relativistic, numerical simulations of dynamical phenomena involving black holes may help reveal ways in which black holes can form, grow and be detected in the universe. To convey the state-of-the art, we summarize several representative simulations here, including the collapse of a hypermassive neutron star to a black hole following the merger of a binary neutron star, the magnetorotational collapse of a massive star to a black hole, and the formation and growth of supermassive black hole seeds by relativistic MHD accretion in the early universe.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"arXiv"}}],"primary_arxiv_category":["astro-ph"],"titles":[{"title":"Black Hole Formation and Growth: Simulations in General Relativity"},{"source":"arXiv","title":"Black Hole Formation and Growth: Simulations in General Relativity"}],"external_system_identifiers":[{"schema":"SPIRES","value":"SPIRES-7507976"}],"facet_author_name":["989138_Stuart L. Area – PhD course in Astroparticle Physics\n\nDoctoral Thesis\n\nBeyond General Relativity:\n\nModified Theories and Non-Singular Black Holes\n\nCandidate:\n\nFrancesco Di Filippo\n\nAdvisor:\n\nProf. Stefano Liberati\n\nAcademic Year 2019 – 2020\n\n\n\nii\n\n\n\niii\n\nAbstract\n\nEinstein’s general relativity is an extremely elegant and successful theory. Recent obser-\nvations coming from the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration as well as from the Event Horizon\nTelescope give us the possibility to perform precision test of general relativity in regimes\nnever tested before. Even though all the current observations are in perfect agreement\nwith the predictions of general relativity, there are several reasons to study extensions\nof the theory.\n\nFrom the experimental point of view, we are forced to include a dark sector for the\nmatter and energy content of the universe to explain the cosmological data. Whereas\nfrom a conceptual point of view, the theory is not perturbatively renormalizable, and\nit predicts the formation of spacetime singularities.\n\nThis thesis studies possible modifications of general relativity both considering spe-\ncific theories of modified gravity and implementing a model independent approach.\n\nIn the first part of the thesis, we study a specific class of modified theory of gravity\nwhich has the peculiarity of propagating the same number of degrees of freedom of\ngeneral relativity. The existence of these theories apparently challenges the distinctive\nrole of general relativity as the unique non-linear theory of massless spin-2 particles.\nHowever, we provide strong evidence that these theory are actually equivalent to general\nrelativity in vacuum.\n\nIn the second part of the thesis, we focus on the problem of black hole singularities\nwhich are unavoidably present in general relativity. However, it is reasonable to assume\nthat there will be a mechanism preventing their formation in a full theory of quantum\ngravity. Without specifying any theory of quantum gravity or the nature of such mech-\nanism, simply assuming a minimal set of kinematical constraints, we classify and study\nthe properties of non-singular spacetime with a trapping horizon. Contrary to what one\nmight expect, the set of regular geometries that arises is remarkably limited. Further-\nmore we show that it is very difficult to construct a self consistent geometry without\nany long range effect. This give us further motivation to study the phenomenology of\nnon-singular black holes. To this end, we provide a set of parameters describing the\ndeviations from classical black holes, and we review the possible observational channels\nthat can measure or constrain Visser.\nCausal hierarchy in modified gravity.\nPreprint, arXiv:2005.08533.\n\nvii\n\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1802.02537\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02675\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1809.08238\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08192\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1908.03261\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11200\nhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08533\n\n\nviii\n\n\n\nIntroduction\n\nGeneral relativity represents a very elegant theory from a conceptual point of view and\na very successful one from the experimental side. Thanks to the recent observations\ncoming from the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] as well as from the Event\nHorizon Telescope [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], we have the possibility to perform precision test\nof general relativity in regimes never tested before. Remarkably, the outcomes of all\nthese observations are in perfect agreement with the prediction of general relativity.\n\nRegardless of the phenomenological success, there are good reasons to study modi-\nfications of the theory. From an experimental point of view, cosmological data cannot\nbe explained within general relativity only with the matter and the energy that we\nobserve. The most simple explanation is given by the ΛCDM model where one adds\ntwo addiional “dark” cosmological fluids: a pressurless dust and a cosmological con-\nstant, avoiding any modification of the gravitational interaction. Nonetheless, it is also\npossible to explain the cosmological data without introducing dark matter and dark\nenergy, but by modifying general relativity. This possibility is reinforced by the fact\nthe ΛCDM is not free from problems. For instance, there is a naturalness problem for\nthe value of the cosmological constant which is very different from the one which can be\nnaively estimated [13] and different measurements of the Hubble constant at different\nredshifts lead to values in tension with each other [14].\n\nEven stronger reasons to modify general relativity come from theoretical arguments.\nGeneral relativity predicts the formations of spacetime singularities. In 1939 Oppen-\nheimer and Snyder studied the gravitational collapse of a spherically symmetric ball of\npressureless dust [15], obtaining that the endpoint of the collapse is a singular black\nhole. However, it was widely believed that the formation of the singularity was simply\ndue to the highly idealized scenario and that a realistic collapse would not end up with\nthe formation of a black hole. In fact, something similar happens in Newtonian gravity,\nwhere a spherically symmetric collapse produces a region of infinite density , but an ar-\nbitrary small amount of angular momentum will prevent the formation of such a region.\nWhile preliminary results appeared to confirm this possible resolution of singularities\n[16], Penrose’s 1965 singularity theorem [17] proved them as the natural end points of\ngeneral relativity. This theorem states that if a trapped region is formed, the spacetime\ncannot be geodesically complete, implying that there must exist at least one geodesic\nending in a Cauchy horizon or in a singularity. If we assume that the spacetime is\nglobally hyperbolic, there cannot be any Cauchy horizon, and thus a singularity has\n\n1\n\n\n\n2\n\nto form. Subsequent results extended the theorem to cosmological scenarios [18] and\ngot rid of the global hyperbolicity assumption [19] showing that in general relativity\nsingularities are going to be unavoidably present both as an endpoint in gravitational\ncollapse and in cosmology.\n\nA possible approach to accept the presence of singularities in general relativity, is\nto assume that while the theory will unavoidably produce them, it will also always\nhide them as well. The precise mathematical formulation of this concept is given by\nthe cosmic censorship conjecture [20]. There are two main non equivalent formulations\nof the conjecture that go by the names of the weak and strong cosmic censorship\nconjecture1.\n\nThe weak cosmic conjecture states that all singularities are shielded behind an event\nhorizon. This condition ensures that observers far from the black hole have a well defined\nevolution within general relativity, and they are not influenced by singularities.\n\nThe strong cosmic censorship conjecture states that the maximally Cauchy develop-\nment of the initial data is inextendible, meaning that if there are incomplete geodesics,\nthey have to end up in a singularity and they cannot be extended beyond it.\n\nIt is easy to consider exact solutions in general relativity that are counterexamples\nto both the weak and the strong versions of the cosmic censorship, so the correct way\nto formulate these conjectures is to state that under generic initial conditions it is\nimpossible to end up with any of the aforementioned solutions and spacetime evolves\nin a way to satisfy the conjectures.\n\nBoth versions of the censorship conjecture aim to ensure that the black hole singu-\nlarities do not spoil the well-posedness of the initial value problem for observers that\ndo not fall into the black hole. However, it is undeniable that the presence itself of a\nsingularity is abhorrent from a physical point of view as we expect that the ultimate\ntheory has to remain predictive for every observer, not just those outside a black hole.\nTherefore, it seems that some extension of general relativity is required for predicting\nthe fate of observers that within black holes.\n\nFinally, the last reasons we want to mention that tells us that general relativity\ncannot be the ultimate theory of gravity comes from the fact that when we express the\ngeneral relativity in the standard quantum field theory formalism, the resulting quan-\ntum gravity theory is not perturbatively renormalizable [21, 22, 23]. It is often stated\nthat this implies that the theory cannot be predictive in the UV as loops correction\nwill introduce an infinite number of divergences that require an infinite number of free\nparameters to be tamed. This conclusion is a bit rushed, as it is, in principle, still pos-\nsible to have a predictive theory in UV if all the coupling constants flow in a fixed point\nmaking the theory asymptotically safe and non-perturbatively renormalizable [24] (see\nalso [25] for a recent overview). However, there is still no evidence that this is the case,\nand at the very least, we can conclude that a lot of work has to be done to understand\nthe behavior of gravity at high energy.\n\nAll these problems may have a common solution. A full theory of quantum gravity\nwill definitely become relevant in the final stages of gravitational collapse, and it is\nstandard lore to believe that quantum gravity effects will prevent the formation of the\nsingularity. Furthermore, it is possible that the quantum gravity theory will have an\n\n1Note that, despite the name, the strong cosmic conjecture is not mathematically stronger as it\ndoes not imply the weak cosmic conjecture.\n\n\n\n3\n\neffective field theory description in the low energy limit that can have some difference\nfrom general relativity in cosmological scenario and that could, hopefully, explain the\ncosmological data without the introduction of the dark sector, hence resolving the issues\nassociated with it.\n\nHaving established that there are good reasons to modify general relativity, we need\nto understand how to do that. The conceptually simplest way to proceed would be to\npick a candidate for a quantum theory of gravity and study its predictions to understand\nif it is able to address the problems of general relativity. However, such an approach\ncan be very difficult in practice.\n\nIn this thesis we are going to focus on two complementary approaches to look for\ndeviation from general relativity. We are first going to consider a specific class of\nmodified theory of gravity, and, after that, the thesis will focus on an agnostic approach\ndirectly tackling one of the open problems of general relativity, i.e., the singularity\nproblem.\n\nSpecific modified theory approach\n\nIn order to consider a modified theory of gravity, we face the problem that there are\nmany different ways to modify general relativity and we need a guiding principle to\nchoose which type of modification we want to consider. General relativity possesses\na number of properties that make it unique, and we need to decide which of these\nproperties we want to relax and which ones we want to keep. In four dimensions,\nLovelock’s theorem [26] singles out general relativity as the only diffeomorfism invariant\ntheory that propagates only two degrees of freedom. Recent attempts to evade the\nconclusions of the theorem [27] turned out to be unsuccessful (see, e.g. [28]).\n\nIn chapter 1, we are going to study a class of theories that relax the assumption\nof invariance under the diffeomrfism group, but that keeps unchanged the number of\ndegrees of freedom. We will provide strong evidence that, in vacuum, these theories are\nactually general relativity written terms of non standard variables. However, coupling\nwith matter can break the equivalence.\n\nAgnostic approach\n\nThe rest of the thesis focuses on the problem of black hole singularities. It would be an\ninteresting line of investigation to understand whether the minimally modified theories\nthat we have studied could resolve some of the issues with the black hole singularities.\nIn fact, the equivalence of the theories in vacuum tells us that the singular black solution\nof general relativity will also be present in the minimally modified theory. However,\nthe difference in the matter sector may change the dynamics of a gravitational collapse\nand could, in principle, avoid the consequences of Penrose’s theorem and avoid the\nformation of the singularities.\n\nWhile this analysis would definitely be very interesting, the results would be specific\nto a given theory and a given matter coupling. Therefore without a strong motivation to\nsingle out one specif modified gravity theory, in the rest of the thesis, we have addressed\nthe problem of hole singularities in a model independent way, which allows us to obtain\nless stringent but much more generic results. To set the stage, in chapter 2, we study\n\n\n\n4\n\nwhat type of requirement we have to impose to the spacetime in order to have a well\ndefined notion of causality in a generic modified theory of gravity.\n\nWith the knowledge we have acquired, simply giving a minimal set of assumptions\nwithout specifying any particular theory, in chapter 3, we provide a classification of\nnon-singular spacetime with a trapping horizon. To this end, we study the properties\nof four classes of geometry and, using Penrose singularity theorem as a guidance, we\nprove that the most generic non-singular spacetime is given by a combination of these\nfour classes. The analysis is carried in spherical symmetry, but the language we use is\nwell suited to address less symmetric configuration. In fact, most of the results can be\ntrivially extended to a more realistic scenario.\n\nThe classification is performed on purely geometrical grounds. While from the\nmathematical point of view all the geometries are perfectly fine, in chapter 4, we study\nthe viability of these geometries as solutions to the singularity problem once that some\nphysically motivated ingredients are added. Such ingredients include the presence of\nperturbations and the compatibility with semiclassical physics. We show that there is\nno safe option, meaning that the classes of geometries that can very closely mimic a\nblack hole are plagued by self consistency issues, and it is not easy to make them viable.\n\nThis gives us a strong motivation to study the possible phenomenological signature.\nIn chapter 5, we discuss the possible phenomenological channels to detect or constrain\ndeviations from classical black holes. We also provide a set of phenomenological pa-\nrameters to systematically parametrize the room that is still available for black holes\nalternatives.\n\nAppendices\n\nThe appendices contain information that is propaedeutic for the discussion in the var-\nious chapters of the thesis. App. A contains the proof that the minimally modified\ntheory of gravity discussed in chapter 1 recover the Poincaré group in the linear limit of\nthe theory. App. B contains a brief review of the most important aspects of the spinor\nhelicity formalism. App. C contains the proof of some conditions for the absence of\ncurvature singularity that have been used in chapter 3. Finally, App. D contains some\ninteresting properties of the regular black hole geometries that we have considered in\ndifferent stages throughout the thesis.\n\n\n\nChapter 1\n\nMinimally modified theories of gravity\n\nGeneral relativity posses a number of properties that make it a very simple and elegant\ntheory. To study a specific modification of general relativity, we have to decide which\nproperties of the theory we want to keep and which ones we want to relax. In this\nchapter, we are going to study a class of theories introduced in [29] where the guiding\nprinciple is to keep unchanged the number of degrees of freedom propagating in the\ngravitational sector.\n\nThis is not a trivial task as, in four dimensions, Lovelock theorem singles out general\nrelativity as the only diffeomorphism invariant gravitational theory that propagates only\ntwo degrees of freedom.\n\nThese theories avoid the conclusion of Lovelock theorem by relaxing the assumption\nof invariance under the full diffeomorphism group. The basic fields that are used in\norder to construct these theories are the 3-dimensional metric hij, the lapse N and\nthe shift N i. While this corresponds to the familiar ADM decomposition in general\nrelativity, in which the spacetime metric reads\n\nds2 = −N2dt2 + hij(dx\ni +N idt)(dxj +N jdt), (1.1)\n\nin [29] the action is modified and it is given by\n\nS =\n\n∫\ndt d3x\n\n√\nhNF (Kij, Rij,∇i, hij, t) (1.2)\n\nwhere Kij = (∂thij −∇iNj −∇jNi) /(2N) and Rij are the extrinsic curvature and the\nRicci tensor of the constant-t hypersurfaces, respectively, and∇i is the covariant deriva-\ntive compatible with the induced metric hij. In this class of theories the authors study\nwhich conditions have to be satisfied by the function F for the theory to propagates\nonly two degrees of freedom.\n\nA central question is whether or not these theories are equivalent to general rel-\nativity. It is possible that, in spite of being apparently different, these are however,\nphysically equivalent (but are expressed in terms of a non-standard choice of variables).\nAs we will see, clarifying this point has its subtleties due to the non-linear nature\nof general relativity. Before starting our analysis, let us explain what we mean with\nequivalence of theories and why we believe that it is worth analyzing this problem. In\n\n5\n\n\n\n6 CHAPTER 1. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\norder to do so, the starting point is the action of general relativity written in the ADM\ndecomposition\n\nS =\n\n∫\ndt d3x\n\n√\nhN\n\n(\nR +KijK\n\nij −K2\n)\n. (1.3)\n\nNow we can perform a field redefinition to obtain a theory which is off-shell different\nfrom general relativity as the action, and the guage groups are different, but which is\ncompletely equivalent to general relativity on-shell. Provided that the field redefinition\nis linear in the lapse, we would obtain an action of the form of Eq. (1.2) which will,\ntherefore, belong to the class of theories with two degrees of freedom identified in [29].\nIt is therefore crucial to understand if some of the theories found are genuinely new\ntheories.\n\nOf course, one possible way to establish the equivalence of these theories would be\nto find a field redefinition that maps them back to general relativity. In practice, this\nis a very difficult task, so we are going to follow a different approach. We are going\nto compare on-shell tree level scattering amplitudes of graviton with the value they\nassume in general relativity. The chapter is mainly based on reference P1, and it is\norganized as follows. In Sec. 1.1, starting directly with the Hamiltonian picture, we\nwill discuss the non-linear algebra of constraints as well as their linearization (focusing\non the recovery of the Poincaré group in the linear limit) of a certain set of theories\nthat includes some of the particular examples given in [29]. Then, in Sec. 1.2, we will\nconnect the results obtained in the Hamiltonian perspective with the analysis of the\nLagrangian formulation of a broad set of theories, illustrating that theories that recover\nthe Poincaré group in the linear limit describe gravitons (massless spin-2 particles) in\nthis limit. This observation, and the fact that the 3-point amplitudes of gravitons in\nthese examples are the same as in general relativity (as shown in detail), represent\na strong hint that these theories are classically equivalent to general relativity. This\nconclusion is strengthened with the analysis of n-point amplitudes for n ≥ 4, using on-\nshell techniques. In Sec. 1.4 we consider, as a counterpoint, two examples of theories\nthat are not equivalent to general relativity: in one of them the algebra of constraints\ndoes not reproduce the Poincaré algebra in the linear limit and, in the other one,\ngravitons display modified dispersion relations (and additional degrees of freedom can\narise due to radiative corrections). The last part of this chapter, Sec. 1.5, deals with\nadditional issues that come up when couplings to matter are introduced.\n\n1.1 A class of Hamiltonian theories\n\nAs a way to illustrate in a simpler way the main result in [29], and make the present\ndiscussion self-consistent, let us consider a class of Hamiltonian theories that are in\nprinciple structurally different from general relativity, but that still contain two local\ndegrees of freedom. While not encompassing all the possible theories found in [29], this\nis however a large enough set to represent a convenient framework for our discussion\n(let us note that, in particular, it includes general relativity as a particular case).\n\nThe class of theories we introduce in this section are constructed from the vari-\nables {N,N i, hij} and their conjugated momenta {πN , πi, πij}, and are defined by the\n\n\n\n1.1. A CLASS OF HAMILTONIAN THEORIES 7\n\nHamiltonian\n\nH =\n\n∫\nd3x\n\n(\nNH +N iDi + λNπN + λiπi\n\n)\n, (1.4)\n\nwhere\nH =\n\n√\nhF (R + λΠ/h) , Di = −2∇jπ\n\nj\ni. For general relativity, we can easily identify the familiar\n\nexpressions that appear in the so-called Hamiltonian and diffeomorphism constraints.\nIn all these theories, λN and λi are Lagrange multipliers that enforce the primary\n\nconstraints\nπN = 0, πi = 0, (1.6)\n\nwhich in turn induce the secondary constraints\n\nH = 0, Di = 0. We will keep using this nomenclature for\nany theory with total Hamiltonian given by Eq. (1.9)\n\nNote that F ′(x) denotes the derivative of F (x) with respect to its single argument x.\nSeveral observations can be made:\n\n• The algebra is closed and all the constraints are first class, which leaves (20 −\n2 × 8)/2 = 2 degrees of freedom. In other words, all these theories satisfy the\nconditions discussed in [29].\n\n• The algebra obtained is a slight modification of the usual Dirac algebra of gen-\neral relativity [30]. In particular, the only difference appears in the bracket be-\ntween Hamiltonian constraints, where the structure function inside the Hamil-\ntonian constraint is different; let us recall that for general relativity one has\nλF ′(R + λΠ/h)2 = 1. Let us mention that similar modifications have been ob-\nserved to occur in loop quantum gravity [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36], which makes\npart of our discussion below of possible interest for these studies (note that, how-\never, signature change [37, 38] is not structurally allowed in the theories we are\nconsidering in this section).\n\n\n\n8 CHAPTER 1. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\nIn summary, we have a large class of theories that contain two degrees of freedom, the\nsame as general relativity, but which seem to be structurally different from the latter\ntheory. In particular, the off-shell algebra is different from the usual Dirac algebra. One\nmay jump to the conclusion that these theories are different from general relativity. But\nis this true?\n\nBefore diving into this question, let us make a remark that will be important later:\nthe value of λ can be changed arbitrarily by a positive multiplicative factor. This can\nbe noticed by considering the field redefinition\n\nπij → κπij, N i → N i/κ, (1.10)\n\nwith κ ∈ R a constant. It is straightforward to check that the combination N iDi is\ninvariant under this rescaling, so that diffeomorphism constrain is unchanged, but that\nthe Hamiltonian constraint becomes\n\nH =\n√\nhF\n\n(\nR + λk2Π/h\n\n)\n=\n√\nhF (R + λ′Π/h) , (1.11)\n\nwith λ′ = λκ2. Hence, it is possible to change the absolute value of |λ| arbitrarily; note\nhowever that its sign cannot be modified by this redefinition. So, being always possible\nto set λ = ±1, it is F (x) 6= x the real difference with general relativity.\n\n1.1.1 Poincaré algebra\n\nAs a first partial answer to the question asked at the end of the previous section, we\nnow show that in the flat spacetime limit, the Poincaré algebra is recovered in all these\ntheories. As it is mentioned, for instance, in [33, 34, 39], the Poincaré algebra can\nbe obtained as a subalgebra of the off-shell algebra of constraints (1.9) by considering\nthe Minkowski spacetime (i.e., N = 1, N i = 0 and hij = δij) and looking to the\ntransformations generated by the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints associated\nwith the linear functions\n\nα = δµ0 + xiδω\ni0, αi = δµi + xjδω\n\nji. The value θ = 1 corresponds to general relativity, while θ = −1 to\nEuclidean general relativity (see, e.g., [40] and references therein). These expression\n\n\n\n1.2. A CLASS OF LAGRANGIAN THEORIES 9\n\nof the algebra reduces to the Poincaré algebra once we restrict the functions α, αi, β\nand βi to be of the form of Eq. (1.12) (for completeness, this is shown in App. A).\nThis implies that all these theories contain either the Poincaré algebra or its Euclidean\ncounterpart.\n\n1.2 A class of Lagrangian theories\n\nIn the previous sections we have worked with a class of Hamiltonian theories that\ndisplay an arbitrary function F (x) of a particular combination of the variables in the\nphase space, but that still contain the same number of degrees of freedom as general\nrelativity. We have illustrated that for all these theories [satisfying a non-degeneracy\ncondition F ′(0) 6= 0], the Poincaré algebra is recovered in a suitable (standard) limit of\nthe non-linear algebra of constraints. This is a first indication that even if these theories\nmay seem different from general relativity, this may be an artifact of the way in which\nthese are constructed, and at the end of the day these may turn out to be physically\nequivalent to the latter.\n\nA clear possibility is that these theories could be obtained from the usual Hamilto-\nnian formulation of general relativity by means of a non-linear field redefinition. How-\never, this is fairly difficult to show in general, unless one is able to find by inspection\nthe particular field redefinition that does the job (which, in any case, would not be\na systematic approach). Hence, a different strategy is needed in order to learn more\nabout these theories and their relation to general relativity. In particular, in this section\nwe pick up a specific theory among the Hamiltonian theories previously studied, and\nswitch to its Lagrangian formulation in order to illustrate a number of important fea-\ntures. The subsequent discussion is not limited to this particular theory but applies to\na large class of Lagrangian theories, as detailed in Sec. 1.2.4. However, we will use this\nparticular example in order to motivate the different steps in the analysis. This class\nof Lagrangian theories is not necessarily in one-to-one correspondence with the class of\nHamiltonian theories discussed in Sec. 1.1, although we expect that the results below\nwill be shared by all these Hamiltonian theories, as we have shown that the Poincaré\nalgebra is recovered in all of them.\n\nFor a generic function F (x), it is not easy to find the corresponding Lagrangian.\nHowever, one of the Lagrangian examples given in [29] leads precisely to a Hamiltonian\nof the form given in Eq. (1.4). These authors call this theory “square root gravity”,\nwhich is defined by the Lagrangian density\n\nL =\n√\nhN\n\n(\nM4\n√\n\n(c1 + c2K) (c3 + c4R)− c5\n\n)\n. (1.45)\n\nUnless ∂L/∂R|R=K=0 = 0 or ∂L/∂K|R=K=0 = 0, it is always possible to perform field\nredefinitions (constant rescalings) as we have done previously in order to reconstruct\nthe 4-dimensional Ricci scalar up to an irrelevant boundary term. We have then an\nexpansion in K and R that is precisely of the form that has been used in Secs. 1.2.1,\n1.2.2 and 1.2.3, so that the results of these sections equally apply to all the theories\nwith Lagrangian (1.44) (implying, in particular, the equivalence of the linearized field\nequations and 3-point amplitudes with that of general relativity). Let us note that\n∂L/∂K|R=K=0 must be non-zero in order to have a kinetic term for the field hµν , so\nthe only possibility to avoid this general result within this family is considering theories\nin which ∂L/∂R|R=K=0 = 0. We analyze this case separately in Sec. 1.4.1, showing\nthat this kind of theory does not even contain gravitons at the linearized level, which\nraises doubts about whether or not these describe gravitational theories (and is also\ndisastrous from an observational perspective).\n\n1.3 Higher orders in the perturbative expansion\n\nUp to now, we have shown that the theory defined by the Lagrangian density in Eq.\n(1.15) is equivalent to general relativity for its two lowest orders: at the linear level\nthe field equations are equivalent to that of Fierz-Pauli theory, and at first order in the\ninteractions, the 3-point amplitudes are the same as in general relativity. Moreover, we\nhave discussed that the latter property is an unavoidable consequence of the former in\nall theories of the fairly general form (1.44). Armed with this knowledge, we can use now\na battery of results from on-shell scattering amplitudes in order to obtain non-trivial\ninformation about the higher orders in the perturbative expansion. The goal of this\nsection is simple: we know that theories of the form (1.44) that satisfy ∂L/∂R|R=K=0 6=\n0 and ∂L/∂K|R=K=0 6= 0 have the same polarizations of the gravitational field at the\nlinear level and the same 3-point amplitudes as general relativity; in this section we\nstudy whether or not this equivalence holds for n-point amplitudes with n ≥ 4.\n\nIn order to achive our goal, we will have to take a detour from our previous discussion\nin terms of Hamiltonian and Lagrangian mechanics and consider a language which is\nmore powerful in order to deal with the perturbative structure of non-linear theories.\nThis language is that of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theory, in its modern\nincarnation using spinor-helicity variables which are specially suited for the description\nof massless particles. Some of these ingredients are briefly reviewed in App. B in order\nto make the discussion reasonably self-contained.\n\n\n\n16 CHAPTER 1. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\nWe have studied on-shell 3-point amplitudes in Sec. 1.2.3. However, for the purposes\nof this section, we will need to take into account some properties of the off-shell 3-point\nvertices of the actions with Lagrangian density (1.44). The most important observation\nis that, while in general relativity any interaction vertex only contains two powers of\nmomenta, the theories (1.44) do not verify this requirement. In particular, from the last\nline in Eq. (1.42) we can read that off-shell 3-point vertices can have up to 6 powers of\nthe (spatial) momenta. This feature forbids applying previous uniqueness results [52,\n53, 54, 55] that use an extension of the Britto-Cachazo-Feng-Witten (BCFW) relations\n[56, 57] but assume that interaction vertices are at most quadratic in the momenta (that\nhigher-derivative interaction vertices are problematic is well-known [58]). Technically,\nthis follows from the necessity of showing that contributions from Feynman diagrams\nremain bounded for large (complex) momenta; that vertices may contain higher powers\nof momenta spoil the bounds that can be obtained for the quadratic case. The most\nvirulent behavior comes from off-shell 3-point vertices with 6 powers of the momenta,\nnamely the ones in the last line of Eq. (1.42). However, these contributions can only\ncome from internal vertices, as we have shown in Sec. 1.2.3 that these vertices vanish\nwhen at least one of the legs stitched to it is on-shell.\n\nLet us start with the n-point amplitude of n gravitons with the same helicity,\nAn(1+2+... n+), or just with the helicity of one graviton flipped, An(1−2+... n+). In\ngeneral relativity these amplitudes vanish for any value of n. There is a simple argu-\nment to show that this must be the case by counting the powers of momenta in Feynman\ndiagrams (see, e.g., Sec. 2.7 in [48]). The argument boils down to the observation that\nthis amplitude can be non-zero only if vertices contribute at least with 2n powers of the\nmomenta that can be contracted with the 2n polarization vectors (B.13) and (B.14) of\nexternal gravitons [no powers of the momenta can be provided by propagators, which\nis true both in general relativity and in the theories analyzed here; recall Eq. (1.40)].\nIf this is not the case, at least two of these polarization vectors will be contracted with\neach other, and this combination can be shown to be zero up to a gauge transformation,\nimplying that the overall amplitude vanishes. While it is impossible to obtain these 2n\npowers of the momenta in the case of general relativity (and, in general, for any theory\nin which interaction vertices are quadratic in the momenta), here we have to be more\ncareful with the interaction vertices containing higher powers of momenta. However,\nthe potentially most virulent behavior, coming from the [R(1)]3 off-shell 3-point vertex\nin Eq. (1.42), turns out to be innocuous as the corresponding 6 powers of the momenta\ncannot be coupled to the polarization vectors of external particles. Taking a look at\nEq. (1.43), we see that the first part can be gauged away (off-shell), while the second\none contributes with a factor pip\n\ni that has no free indices to be contracted with the\nindices of polarization vectors. Alternatively, in the de Donder gauge, R(1) is simply\nproportional to the scalar p2. The remaining 3-point vertices K(2)R(1) and R(2)R(1) only\nhave 2 powers of the momenta that can be contracted with the εµ+, which leads to the\nsame maximum number of momenta as in general relativity. Let us therefore turn our\nattention to 4-point vertices, from which [K(2)]2 and [R(2)]2 display the worst behavior,\nwith a p4 dependence. However, counting the number of vertices in the corresponding\nFeynman diagrams (see App. B) shows that in this case the maximum possible number\nof momenta is 2n− 4 < 2n. Therefore, we conclude that\n\nAn(1+2+... n+) = An(1−2+... n+) = 0, ∀n ≥ 3. (1.46)\n\n\n\n1.3. HIGHER ORDERS IN THE PERTURBATIVE EXPANSION 17\n\nThis is a quite non-trivial statement that is characteristic of general relativity as well\nas Yang-Mills theories. This implies that, in order to have a non-zero amplitude, we\nneed to flip the helicity of at least two gravitons (which leads to the so-called maximally\nhelicity violating –MHV– amplitudes [59]).\n\nIn order to deal with the MHV amplitudes An(1−2−3+... n+) and other possibly\nnon-vanishing amplitudes, we need to resort to more sophisticated arguments. As re-\nviewed briefly in App. B, the most powerful argument to deal with these amplitudes\ninvolves complexifying the external momenta in order to construc n-point amplitudes\nAn(1−2−3+... n+) from n−1-amplitudes evaluated on complex momenta. This recursive\nprocedure is valid as long as certain technical conditions are satisfied by the complex-\nification of the n-point amplitude An(1−2−3+... n+) [48]. There are different ways in\nwhich the complexification can be done. The one that we want to study was considered\nin the App. A of [53] (see also [54]) in order to obtain what these authors call the “aux-\niliary” recursion relations. This particular complex extension represents the optimal\nchoice in general relativity, and therefore it will be also the optimal choice here, as the\nonly change in the present discussion is the behavior of interaction vertices with the\nmomenta. Note that we cannot apply directly the conclusions of these authors, as the\ntheories we are interested in have interaction vertices which are not quadratic in the\nmomenta.\n\nWithout loss of generality, let us consider an amplitude in which N ≥ n/2 external\nlegs have positive helicity; the case in which there is a larger number of external legs\nwith negative helicity is completely parallel. If s ∈ [1, N ] labels all the external legs\nwith positive helicity, and t marks a single external leg with negative helicity, we define\nthe complex extension\n\np̂s = ps + zqs, p̂t = pt − z\nN∑\ns=1\n\nqs, (1.47)\n\nwhere z ∈ C and {qs}Ns=1 are complex vectors verifying certain requirements [48].\nTo show the validity of the recursion relations, let us exploit the fact that it is a\n\nsufficient condition that all Feynman diagrams contributing to a given amplitude vanish\nasymptotically for large |z|. Taking into account that Feynman diagrams are just the\nmultiplication of diverse elements (external legs, interaction vertices and propagators),\nwe just need to understand how these different elements scale with |z|:\n\n• N+1 external particles are shifted (that is, their momenta are complexified) such\nthat their polarization tensors constructed from Eqs. (B.13) and (B.14) give each\na leading contribution 1/|z|2.\n\n• All propagators in Eq. (1.40) are shifted (this property that depends only on\nthe topology of the relevant Feynman diagrams was shown in [53]) and therefore\ncontribute with a 1/|z| factor each.\n\n• Vertices behave as |z|k. Internal (i.e., off-shell) 3-point vertices display 6 powers\nof the spatial momenta instead of being just quadratic in the covariant momenta,\nwhich suggests a |z|6 dependence. However, a careful inspection shows (as dis-\ncussed in Secs. 1.2.2 and 1.2.3) that these off-shell vertices are proportional in the\n\n\n\n18 CHAPTER 1. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\nde Donder gauge to the covariant combination (p2)3, which means that these also\nscale as |z|3. A similar comment applies to internal vertices that contain R(1).\n\nPutting all these elements together, for Feynman diagrams involving only k-point ver-\ntices the leading z dependence goes like\n\nAn(z) ∝\n(\nz−2\n)N+1 (\n\nz−1\n)p (\n\nzk\n)v\n, (1.48)\n\nwhere the first multiplicative factor is the contribution from the polarization tensors of\nthe shifted external legs, p is the number of propagators and v is the number of vertices.\nFor k-point vertices one has (App. B)\n\np =\nn− k\nk − 2\n\n, v =\nn− 2\n\nk − 2\n. (1.49)\n\nThe recursion relations can be valid only if An(z) ∝ zw with w < 0 (which in general\nrelativity is always satisfied [53]). This leads to the inequality\n\nN >\n(k − 1)n− (3k − 4)\n\n2(k − 2)\n. (1.50)\n\nIt is straightforward to show that the most stringent of these conditions is obtained\nfor k = 3, which implies that interaction vertices with k ≥ 4 only give subleading\ncontributions to the asymptotic behavior on |z| of Feynman diagrams.\n\nOverall, this leads to the main results of this section, together with Eq. (1.46):\n\n• n = 4 and n = 5: all amplitudes An(1h12h2 ... nhn) can be constructed from 3-point\namplitudes and are therefore the same as in general relativity.\n\n• n ≥ 6: the MHV amplitude A6(1−2−3+4+5+6+) is the same as in general rela-\ntivity. This argument does not fix the form of A6(1−2−3−4+5+6+) or any of the\nremaining n-point amplitudes with n > 6 that are not already contained in Eq.\n(1.46).\n\nIn summary, we have applied state-of-the-art techniques of on-shell scattering ampli-\ntudes in order to calculate a sequence of scattering amplitudes which would be other-\nwise extremely difficult (and time-consuming) to calculate. This illustrates that on-shell\ntechniques can be used in order to understand the physical content of modified grav-\nity theories. The information extracted in this way (see Fig. 1.3) is quite interesting,\nas it uncovers unexpected cancellations of the additional (non-relativistic) interaction\nvertices, and strengthens the possibility that these theories are equivalent to general rel-\nativity. In particular, we have determined that differences might arise only for 6-point\namplitudes [in the A6(1−2−3−4+5+6+) amplitude] or higher.\n\nLet us stress that this does not necessarily imply that it is likely that there will be dif-\nferences. It is ubiquitous in the study of on-shell scattering amplitudes that unexpected\ncancelations occur, so that terms that may seemingly give additional contributions leave\nno trace. In fact, we already know that these kinds of cancellations indeed happen for\nthe theories analyzed here. For instance, in the amplitudes A4(1h12h23h34h4) the con-\ntributions coming from the additional (i.e., not present in general relativity) 4-point\n\n\n\n1.3. HIGHER ORDERS IN THE PERTURBATIVE EXPANSION 19\n\nvertices [K(2)]2 and [R(2)]2 cancel identically. A similar observation follows for arbitrary\nAn(1h12h2 ...nhn) for n ≤ 5, and applies to all the possible interaction vertices that are\ninvolved in these amplitudes, including the most virulent [R(1)]3. This even applies to\nAn(1+2+... n+) and An(1−2+... n+) for arbitrary values of n. It is not unreasonable to\nthink that these cancellations will keep taking place for the remaining tree-level ampli-\ntudes, but that the on-shell arguments used here are not powerful enough to show this.\nReaching a definitive conclusion is not possible at the moment; it may be that some\ngeneralization of these arguments will be successful, or additional calculations might\nuncover a counterexample. But we certainly think this is an interesting question that\ndeserves further study.\n\n= + (1.51)\n\nFigure 1.3: One of the results in this section is that the A4(1h12h23h34h4) is constructible\nfrom on-shell 3-point amplitudes of complex momenta using recursion relations, which\nin particular implies equivalence to general relativity at this particular order in the\nperturbative expansion. As in general relativity, this means that 4-point vertices carry\nno physical information, but are present in order to guarantee off-shell gauge invariance.\nThis result is remarkable as it extends this observation from the 4-point vertices K(4)\n\nand R(4) of general relativity, to include also [K(2)]2 and [R(2)]2. Moreover, we have\nshown that perturbative equivalence with general relativity holds for An(1h12h2 ...4h4)\nup to n = 5 no matter the helicity configuration, and for selected configurations when\nn > 5.\n\nBefore finishing this section, let us point out that the BCFW shift is not the only\npossible way to extend the momenta in the complex plane. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\n1.4 Genuinely different theories\n\nIn the previous sections we have used different probes of large classes of theories and\nfound no evidence of differences with respect to general relativity. It would be inter-\nesting to find theories that still satisfy the conditions in [29] ensuring that the number\nof degrees of freedom is the same as general relativity, but that are manifestly different\nfrom general relativity. In this section we analyze two kinds of theories that fall within\nthis category, discussing their main properties and, in particular, their pathologies.\n\n1.4.1 Theories with no gravitons\n\nAs already noticed in [29], theories that do not contain the 3-dimensional Ricci tensor\nRij in the Lagrangian density describe automatically two degrees of freedom . In\nparticular, for theories of the form (1.44) this would imply ∂L/∂R = 0. The simplest\nexample of this kind of theory is given by\n\nL =\n√\nhN K. (1.54)\n\nLet us now show that this theory is clearly inequivalent to general relativity, by looking\nat its Hamiltonian formulation: the momenta are given by\n\nπij = 2\n(\nKij −Khij\n\n) 1\n\n2\n\n√\nh, πN = 0, πi = 0, (1.55)\n\nand the total Hamiltonian takes the usual form\n\nH =\n\n∫\nd3x (NH +N iDi + λNπN + λiπi), (1.56)\n\nbut with\n\nH =\nΠ√\nh\n. (1.57)\n\nThe secondary constraints are again H = 0 and Di = 0. The main difference lies now\nin the algebra of constraints, which takes the form\n\n{H[α],H[β]} = 0,{\nD[αi],H[α]\n\n}\n= H [Lαiα] ,{\n\nD[αi],D[βj]\n}\n\n= D\n[\nLαiβ\n\nj\n]\n. (1.58)\n\nNote the difference with respect to Eq. (1.9): the first bracket is identically vanishing.\nThis has clear physical implications, which can be noticed for instance recalling our\ndiscussion in Sec. 1.1.1 and App. A: even if the theory describes two degrees of freedom,\nat linear level these excitations do not carry a representation of the Poincaré group (not\neven in some kind of low-energy limit). For instance, in the theory analyzed in this\nsection, time translations and boosts commute, as well as two boosts (in the Poincaré\ngroup, these commutators will be proportional to spatial translations and rotations,\nrespectively). Therefore, these theories are escaping equivalence with general relativity,\nbut at the price of modifying drastically even the linear properties of the theory (i.e.,\nnot describing gravitons at the linear level).\n\n\n\n1.4. GENUINELY DIFFERENT THEORIES 21\n\nIn particular, it is not clear if it is legitimate to call these theories “gravitational”\ntheories [29]. The linear excitations in this theory do not satisfy a wave equation,\nwhich would imply that there are no gravitational waves and therefore contradicts\nobservational facts. This is a reasonable outcome, which shows that tampering with\nthe very properties of the carrier of the gravitational force generally has drastic physical\nconsequences.\n\n1.4.2 Theories with a modified dispersion relation for\ngravitons\n\nThe previous example is interesting from a theoretical perspective but is, in some sense,\ntoo trivial. In this section we consider a class of examples that are more interesting\nphysically. In some sense these examples are complementary to the ones in the previous\nsection: instead of considering a Lagrangian density that does not depend on Rij, let us\nconsider Lagrangian densities that are obtained by adding a piece that is independent\nfrom Kij (and also the lapse N). As shown in a brief section at the end of the paper [29],\nadding this term renders the Hamiltonian constraint second class, but it also introduces\na tertiary constraint. Therefore, the number of degrees of freedom does not change even\nif the way the counting is performed is changed. This class of examples was also found\nin [61]. Phenomenological consequences for some of these theories (and extensions)\nare studied in [62]. Here, we focus on the effects that these kind of terms have when\nadded to the Einstein-Hilbert action; our conclusions stated below do not depend on\nthis specific choice of starting point. For concreteness, let us consider\n\nL =\n√\nhN(K +R) + `2\n\n√\nhRijR\n\nij, (1.59)\n\nwhere ` is a constant with dimensions of length.\nLet us now obtain the form of the field equations. The first piece in Eq. (1.59) leads\nto the usual Fierz-Pauli equations, so we will focus on the second piece, for which we\nneed to recall (e.g., [43]) that R\n\n(1)\nij = (∆hij − ∂i∂khkj − ∂j∂khki + ∂i∂jh̃)/2, so that the\n\ncorresponding contribution to the field equations is proportional to\n\n1\n\n2\n\n(\nδki δ\n\nl\nj∆− 2δki ∂j∂\n\nl + δij∂\nk∂l\n) (\n\n∆hkl − ∂k∂mhml − ∂l∂mhmk + ∂k∂lh̃\n)\nδiµδ\n\nj\nν . (1.60)\n\nWe can see that the additional term describe higher-derivative corrections to the purely\nspatial components of the Fierz-Pauli equations, similarly to what happened in the\nsquare root gravity, Eq. (1.24). However, in the square root gravity these contributions\nwere identically vanishing. Here we will see that the same does not apply.\n\nFirst of all, let us recall that, as in the square root gravity, the µ = ν = 0 component\nof the field equations is given by Eq. (1.26). This, in turn, implies that the trace of Eq.\n(1.60) vanishes on-shell: it is given by\n\n1\n\n2\n\n(\nδkl∆ + ∂k∂l\n\n) (\n∆hkl − ∂k∂mhml − ∂l∂mhmk + ∂k∂lh̃\n\n)\n=\n\n3\n\n2\n∆(∆h̃− ∂i∂jhij) = 0. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\n• Impose the de Donder gauge ∂µh̄µν = 0, where h̄µν = hµν − ηµνh/2.\n\n• Exploit the µ = 0, ν = 0 and µ = 0, ν = i components of the field equations to\ngauge away the h̄00 and h̄0i components of the gravitational field.\n\n• Use the trace of the field equations, �h̄ = 0, to fix completely the residual gauge\nfreedom setting h̄ = 0.\n\nThis implies that the field equations can be written simply as\n\n�hij + `2∆2hij = 0. (1.62)\n\nThis is a quite interesting equation that implies that this theory describes gravitons\n(with two degrees of freedom), but with modified dispersion relations. At least at\nlow energies (measured in terms of the scale `), the usual Lorentz-invariant picture\nis recovered. This suggests that these theories are interesting alternatives to general\nrelativity that reduce to the latter at low energies.\n\nHowever, there is a feature of the theories which include “potential” terms in the\n3-dimensional Ricci tensor Rij that must be kept in mind. The inclusion of this kind\nof potential term independent of the lapse N and the extrinsic curvature Kij changes\ndrastically the nature of the constraints of the theory. First of all, the form of the\nHamiltonian and diffeomorphism constraints is unchanged. However, the Hamiltonian\nconstraint is not automatically preserved by evolution, and an additional constraint\nmust be added in order to ensure its preservation. This, in turn, implies that the\nHamiltonian constraint is second class. Hence, the only remaining gauge symmetries\nare spatial diffeomorphisms. But here is where the trouble lies: instead of the very\ncombination\n\nK = KijK\nij −K2, (1.63)\n\nthat appears in the Lagrangian density (1.59) and is characteristic of general relativity,\nspatial diffeomorphisms can only select the combination\n\nKijK\nij − µK2, (1.64)\n\nwith µ an arbitrary constant; this is for instance a well-known observation in the frame-\nwork of Hořava-Lifshitz gravity [63]. Equally well-known in this framework (e.g., [64])\nis the fact that a theory with a Lagrangian density linear in the combination just above\ncan only contain two degrees of freedom if and only if µ = 1; for different values of\nthis parameter, an additional degree of freedom (a scalar graviton) appears. Let us\nstress that the same result follows from our analysis in Sec. 1.1; one of the features that\nguarantees that the theories analyzed in that section (and also the ones in Sec. 1.4.1)\ncontain only two degrees of freedom is that µ = 1 for them [equivalently, the momenta\nπij enter through the combination Π in Eq. (1.5)].\n\nIn summary, including potential terms such as\n√\nhRijR\n\nij in Eq. (1.59) generally\nmakes the Hamiltonian constraint second class and therefore leaves spatial diffeomor-\nphisms as the only gauge symmetries of the theory. As a consequence, it is not possible\nto guarantee that the value of µ is protected against radiative corrections, and there-\nfore that these theories do not acquire additional degrees of freedom in this way [65].\n\n\n\n1.5. COUPLING TO MATTER 23\n\nHence, the theory may describe instead two polarizations of the gravitational field with\nmodified dispersion relation, and an additional scalar graviton.1\n\n1.5 Coupling to matter\n\nOur analyses above have been restricted to theories which only include the gravitational\nfield. In this last section we include matter fields (for simplicity, a scalar field). This is\nmotivated due to two reasons. The first one is that any realistic theory of gravity must\ninclude matter. The second one is that in [29] the authors study Friedmann-Lemâıtre-\nRobertson-Walker solution in the square root gravity studied in Sec. 1.2 and find that\nthe corresponding equations are genuinely different than the ones obtained in general\nrelativity. This may suggest that, even if the square root gravity may be equivalent\nto general relativity in vacuum, differences might be unavoidable when couplings to\nmatter are included. However, we think that one must be careful before jumping into\nthis conclusion, as many subtleties arise in the procedure of coupling matter in these\nalternative theories.\n\n1.5.1 Algebra of constraints for minimal coupling\n\nLet us come back to our starting point, namely the Hamiltonian theories introduced in\nSec. 1.1, and include a scalar field in the system as the simplest possible representation\nof matter fields. (1.79)\n\nThis leads to a quaternary constraint, the smeared version of which reads\n\nC[µ] =\n\n∫\nd3x\n√\nhµ\n\n[\n∂i(N∂\n\niφ)−N ∂V\n\n∂φ\n\n]\n. (1.81)\n\nFrom all the constraints, H + Hφ, πN , P and C are second-class constraints.\nThis implies that the phase space is 5-dimensional, similarly to what happens\nin Hořava-Lifshitz gravity [69, 70]. Therefore φ cannot describe standard matter\ndegrees of freedom.\n\n• φ−f(t) = 0: we impose this form of the constraint (instead of ∂iφ = 0) in order to\nensure a more direct matching between the constraints and the degrees of freedom\nremoved. Again, consistency with the dynamical evolution implies\n\n−ḟ + {φ,HT} = −ḟ +\nNP√\nh\n, (1.82)\n\nwhere ḟ = df/dt. Similarly to the previous situation, these two additional con-\nstraints, together with H+Hφ and πN , are second-class constraints. The counting\nof degrees of freedom is therefore the same as in the example just above.\n\nSummarizing, coupling a scalar field in a minimal way can only be consistent if the scalar\nfield is constrained. Therefore, this scalar field cannot be used to describe standard\nmatter. Introducing an unconstrained scalar field would only be possible at the cost of\nexplicitly breaking the symmetries of the gravitational action, hence exciting additional\ndegrees of freedom (let us note that something similar would happen if a scalar field is\ncoupled to general relativity in a way that diffeomorphism invariance is not preserved.).\n\n\n\n26 CHAPTER 1. MINIMALLY MODIFIED THEORIES OF GRAVITY\n\nThis result would apply to any kind of field that is minimally coupled. Therefore, in\norder to compare these theories with general relativity coupled to matter (or to explore\ntheir possible phenomenological consequences), first of all one must find how to couple\nconsistently matter to these theories in a way that no constraints have to be satisfied by\nthe matter fields. In the two next sections we discuss briefly two attempts at achieving\nthis.\n\n1.6 Conclusions\n\nIn this chapter, we have presented a comprehensive analysis of the class of theories\nfound in [29], which are characterized by the fact that these contain the same number\nof degrees of freedom as general relativity. We have used a battery of techniques in order\nto gain an intuition of the physical meaning of the existence of these theories. First of\nall we need to count the number of degrees of freedom using the Hamiltonian analysis.\nOnce we know that there are only 2 degrees of freedom, we can use the Lagrangian\nformulation of the theory expanding around Minkowskii spacetime to study the linear\npolarization state of the graviton and the three point function. This analysis shows that,\nwhile the theory is apparently Lorentz breaking, the polarization state and the three\npoint function are Lorentz covariant and equal to the general relativity counterpart.\nThis feature allows us to construct the spinor helicity variables in the standard way\nand to use the recursion relation to construct higher order point function. This shows\nhow intertwined the three steps of our analysis are as each step could not be applied\nwithout the previous one.\n\nOur main conclusion is that these results strengthen the view that general relativity\nis a unique theory that is not easily deformed. This claim follows from a combination\nof results:\n\n• There are certainly examples that are manifestly different from general relativity\n(as explained in Sec. 1.4). However, these examples entail profound deviations\nfrom general relativity; either these are too trivial to describe gravity and ex-\nperimentally excluded, or it is not clear if these really have only two degrees of\nfreedom, as it does not seem possible to ensure that the removal of additional\ndegrees of freedom is protected under radiative corrections.\n\n• The most interesting theories would exhibit the same linearized properties of\ngeneral relativity (perhaps at low energy), but would include non-linear deviations\nfrom the latter. The formalism developed in [29] is general enough to encompass\nthese theories, and we have studied in Secs. 1.1 and 1.2 quite general families\nof theories that would seemingly fall into this category. However, every attempt\nto show differences with respect to general relativity has only demonstrated the\nexistence of unexpected cancellations that eventually dissipate the possible sources\nof these differences. This has been shown to occur on-shell, both at the linear and\nnon-linear level.\n\nOur analysis agrees with the one present in [71] where the author from a different\nperspective obtains the same result. These conclusions do not imply that the class of\ntheories found in [29] is not interesting. On the contrary, we think that the results by\n\n\n\n1.6. CONCLUSIONS 27\n\nthese authors provide a convenient framework in which a series of new questions about\nthe possibility of deforming general relativity can be formulated.\n\nFurthermore, the equivalence of the theories only holds in vacuum and matter can\nbreak it. As we have shown, it is not consistent to use minimal coupling, and in\n[71] it has been shown that there are consistent ways to couple matter, which can\nalso break the equivalence with general relativity. While it is not clear if this would\nsimply be equivalent to consider general relativity with non minimally coupled matter,\nworking with a modified theory can provide a guiding principle in the choice of a\nmatter coupling that would otherwise seem unnatural in general relativity. It has been\nshown, for instance, that one example of minimally modified theory has very interesting\ncosmological consequences [72].\n\nThe main focus of this thesis is the study of black holes, specifically we try to get\ninsight toward the resolution of the singularity problem. Given that black holes are\nvacuum solutions of general relativity, we already know that the family of minimally\nmodified theories possess singular solutions. Anyway, it is still an open and interesting\nquestion of whether these solutions will unavoidably be reached in the dynamical evo-\nlution of the theory as it happens in general relativity. It other words, we still do not\nknow is the differences in the matter sector of the theory could prevent the formation of\nsingularities or if there is a singularity theorem also in these theories. This possibility\nwill be addressed in future works.\n\n\n\n28\n\n\n\nChapter 2\n\nCausal hierarchy beyond general relativity.\n\nWorking with a specific theory has many advantages as it allows you to have full control\nover the model. However, in this case, the range of applicability of the results is limited\nto the theory under consideration. In what follows we will try to be as much model\nindependent as possible. In this chapter we are going to study the requirements that\ncausality conditions can impose on the manifold in a generic theory of modified gravity.\n\nIn general relativity there is a is well-established standard causal hierarchy, key\nelements of which are chronology, causality, strong causality, stable causality, and global\nhyperbolicity. Here we investigate how to extend this causal hierarchy depending on the\nextra structure (such as: multiple metrics, aether fields, modified dispersion relations,\nHořava-like gravity, parabolic propagation, etcetera) that the modified theory can have.\nThis chapter contains some of the results of P7.\n\n2.1 The standard general relativity causal\n\nhierarchy\n\nIn general relativity one can invoke a well-established hierarchy of causality conditions\nwhich is explained in detail both at a pedagogical level [73, 19] and at a more formal\nlevel [74].\nLet us briefly review these definitions as our goal is to extend them to a more generic\nframework. The two more basic levels of the causal hierarchy are:\n\n• Chronology condition: There are no closed timelike curves.\n\n• Causality condition: There are no closed non-spacelike curves.\n\nThe absence of closed timelike curves is needed to forbid time travel. Closed null\ncurves are less problematic, but it is usually possible to deform a null closed curve in\norder to construct a timelike closed curve [74] and, even when this is not possible, we\ncan imagine to slightly perturb the manifold to end up with a closed timelike curve.\nFor this reasons, it is desirable to forbid closed null curves as well.\nStrong causality is the next step in the usual hierarchy. There are more than one\nway to characterize strong causality (see P7). The simplest one is the following: For\n\n29\n\n\n\n30 CHAPTER 2. CAUSAL HIERARCHY BEYOND GENERAL RELATIVITY.\n\nany point x there is an open set U such that any causal curve that starts at x and then\nleaves U cannot ever re-enter U . What that means is that not only closed causal curve\nare forbidden, but also that non-spacelike curves cannot return arbitrary close to their\nstarting point.\n\nThe set of causality conditions we have introduced so far ensures the absence of\npathologies in the spacetime we are considering. Given that we are interested in theories\nwhere the spacetime is a dynamical object, we can always perform a small perturbation\nof our spacetime. Therefore we may also want to rule out those spacetimes that are\narbitrary close to violating the hierarchy of causality conditions above. To this end, we\nconstruct a partial ordering on the space of Lorentzian metrics L(M) by saying that\none metric [ĝ]ab is “wider” than another second metric [g]ab, denoted [ĝ]ab > [g]ab, if\nall non-spacelike vectors in the second metric are strictly timelike in the first metric.\nThis partial ordering can be used to define open intervals in the set of all Lorentzian\nmetrics, and these open intervals can be used to define a sub-basis for a topology on\nthe set of Lorentzian metrics one can define on the spacetime manifold — this topology\nis called the interval topology and, for our purposes, it behaves as the typical C0 open\ntopology (different metrics become close to each other when their metric coefficients in\nsome prescribed set of coordinates are close, even if their derivatives are not). For the\ndiscussion in the next section it will be important to keep in mind that, being a partial\norder, not every pair of metrics need to be comparable.\n\nWith this in mind, the next step in the hierarchy, the stable causality condition,\ncan be defined in at least 3 equivalent ways:\n\n• There exists a global time function τ(x) whose gradient is everywhere timelike.\n(So, adopting −+ ++ signature, the vector −gab∇bτ is future-pointing timelike.\nThis definition of stable causality implies that for any future-pointing timelike\nvector V a one has V a∇aτ > 0.)\n\n• There is a metric wider than the physical metric such that the wider metric\nsatisfies the chronology condition.\n\n• There is an open set in the C0 open topology on the set of all Lorentzian metrics\nwhich contains the physical metric and such that all of the metrics in that open\nset satisfy the chronology condition.\n\nThe second and the third statements are clearly equivalent as they are merely different\nways of express the same physical concept. The proof that the first statement is equiv-\nalent to the other two is not trivial. While some discussion can be found in classical\ntextbooks, see e.g. [73] for the equivalence between the first and second statement, or\n[19] for the equivalence between the first and third statement, some technical points are\noverlooked there and a for a complete proof we refer to [75].\n\nFinally, the last step in the standard causal hierarchy, global hyperbolicity, can\nalso be defined in at least 3 equivalent ways:\n\n• (Causality condition) + (causal diamonds are compact).\n\n• Wave equations with suitable initial data have unique solutions.\n\n• The spacetime is foliated by spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces.\n\n\n\n2.2. MULTI-METRIC FRAMEWORKS 31\n\nFor a technical discussion see references [75, 76]. We shall soon see that the last of\nthese conditions, the existence of a foliation by suitably redefined and suitably modified\nCauchy hypersurfaces, is one of the more straightforward causality conditions to work\nwith once one steps far beyond standard general relativity.\n\n2.2 Multi-metric frameworks\n\nPerhaps the most straightforward extensions of the usual causal hierarchy occur in\nmulti-metric frameworks. Multi-metric extensions of general relativity have a long and\nquite complicated history — over the last decade one of the key examples of this type\nof model has been the dRGT “massive gravity” models [77, 78, 79, 80], though ear-\nlier attempts go back several decades [81]. Central to all of these models are multiple\nLorentzian metrics {[gi]ab}Ni=1 (some dynamical, some possibly non-dynamical back-\nground metrics) interacting in various ways.1\n\nTo extend the usual causal hierarchy to such a multi-metric framework at minimum\none would want to apply the usual causal hierarchy to each effective metric separately,\nand to demand that you cannot violate causality by switching metrics [gi]ab part way\nthrough whatever physical process you are interested in. Perhaps the simplest way to\nformulate this is to redefine the notion of chronological/causal curves as follows:\n\n(i) A piecewise chronological curve is one that can be split into connected segments\neach one of which is timelike with respect to at least one of the metrics [gi]ab.\n\n(ii) A piecewise causal curve is one that can be split into connected segments each\none of which is non-spacelike with respect to at least one of the metrics [gi]ab.\n\nWith these definitions in place we can immediately generalize the chronology and\ncausality conditions in multi-metric framework as follows:\n\n• Piecewise chronology condition: There are no closed piecewise chronological\ncurves.\n\n• Piecewise causality condition: There are no closed piecewise causal curves.\n\nWe can similarly modify the definitions of chronological/causal past/future, and the\ndefinitions of chronological/causal diamonds, so as to define strong causality in terms\nof piecewise timelike curves.\n\nIt is useful to break down the piecewise chronology/causality conditions above into\nequivalent conditions that are often simpler to work with:\n\n• The piecewise chronology condition being satisfied by {[gi]ab}Ni=1 is equivalent\nto each of the individual metrics [gi]ab independently satisfying the chronology\ncondition, plus the compatibility condition between all the pairs of metrics that\nI+\ni (p) ∩ I−j (p) = ∅, ∀i, j ∈ [1, ..., N ].\n\n1Instead of thinking of the {[gi]ab}Ni=1 as a set, sometimes it will be useful to think about these\nmetrics as an element ([g1]ab, ..., [gN ]ab) of L(M)N , the Cartesian product of N copies of L(M).\n\n\n\n32 CHAPTER 2. CAUSAL HIERARCHY BEYOND GENERAL RELATIVITY.\n\n• The piecewise causality condition being satisfied by {[gi]ab}Ni=1 is equivalent to each\nof the individual metrics [gi]ab independently satisfying the causality condition,\nplus the compatibility condition between all the pairs of metrics that J+\n\ni (p) ∩\nJ−j (p) = ∅, ∀i, j ∈ [1, ..., N ].\n\nIn the multi-metric framework, there are different possible definitions of piecewise\nstable causality which suitably generalize the usual notion of stable causality. For\ninstance, working in terms of a global time function:\n\nA1 : Each of the individual metrics [gi]ab is stably causal, and in addition there exists a\nglobal time function τ whose gradient is everywhere future-pointing with respect\nto all of the individual metrics [gi]ab. That is, all of the vector fields [Vi]\n\na that\nare future-pointing and timelike with respect to the appropriate individual metric\n[gi]ab must satisfy [Vi]\n\na∇aτ > 0.\n\nThence a piecewise chronological curve, having a tangent vector V a that is timelike\nwith respect to at least one of the individual metrics [gi]ab, must satisfy V a∇aτ > 0,\nand so cannot be closed. Thence, this definition implies that all the future-pointing\npropagation cones must lie on the same side of the constant-τ hypersurfaces.\n\nFurthermore, the two definitions that rely primarily on the existence of the partial\norder > also generalize naturally, as one just needs to replace L(M) by L(M)N , the\nlatter equipped with the product order:\n\nA2 : There is an element in L(M)N wider than the physical metrics ([g1]ab, ..., [gN ]ab)\nsuch that it satisfies the piecewise causal condition.\n\nA3 : There is an open set in the C0 open topology on the set L(M)N which contains\nthe physical metrics ([g1]ab, ..., [gN ]ab) and such that all the elements in that open\nset satisfy the piecewise causal condition.\n\nOne can then show that these definitions are equivalent (see P7 for a proof of this\nstatement).\n\nThere is an alternative way of proceeding in case the set {[gi]ab}Ni=1 satisfies some\nadditional requirements. If there exists a metric in the set {[gi]ab}Ni=1 that is wider\nthan the rest, or if there exists a metric [gwide]ab in L(M) that is wider than all the\nelements {[gi]ab}Ni=1 (that is, the propagation cone of [gwide]ab contains the union of all\nthe propagation cones of the individual [gi]ab), then we can apply the usual definitions\nof general relativity the metric [gwide]ab :\n\nB1 : There exists a global time function whose gradient is everywhere timelike with\nrespect to [gwide]ab.\n\nB2 : There is a metric wider than [gwide]ab such that the wider metric satisfies the\ncausality condition.\n\nB3 : There is an open set in the C0 open topology on the set of all Lorentzian metrics\nwhich contains the metric [gwide]ab and such that all of the metrics in that open\nset satisfy the causality condition.\n\n\n\n2.3. INFINITE SIGNAL VELOCITIES 33\n\nIt is also important to notice that, if [gwide]ab exists, piecewise chronological/causal\ncurves for {[gi]ab}Ni=1 are just ordinary chronological/causal curves of [gwide]ab.\n\nHence, we have two triplets of definitions {Ai}3\ni=1 and {Bi}3\n\ni=1 providing slightly\ndifferent characterizations of stable causality, which are not equivalent in general. It\nis straightforward to realize that the equivalence between these triplets requires (at\na minimum) the existence of [gwide]ab. However, there is a situation which, besides\nfrom making these two characterizations comparable from the perspective of logical\nimplication, is interesting from a physical standpoint, namely when {[gi]ab}Ni=1 is a\ntotally ordered set with respect to >. Under this assumption, the two triplets are\nindeed equivalent, as shown in reference P7. Intuitively, one can see that the necessary\ncondition mentioned above for these being equivalent is satisfied, as {[gi]ab}Ni=1 being\ntotally ordered implies that [gwide]ab can be identified with the maximal element in\n{[gi]ab}Ni=1.\n\nWhen it comes to global hyperbolicity all of the 3 standard versions of this\nnotion can easily be adapted to the multi-metric framework, although again there are\ntwo possible versions which are not fully equivalent in general:\n\nC1 : Causality condition + causal diamonds are compact; (use piecewise causal curves).\n\nC2 : For each individual metric [gi]ab wave equations with suitable initial data have\nunique solutions.\n\nC3 : The spacetime is foliated by spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces; where Cauchy now\nmeans spacelike with respect to each individual metric [gi]ab, and for each metric\n[gi]ab the causal curves of that metric intersect the Cauchy surface once and once\nonly.\n\nAlternatively:\n\nD1 : Causality condition + causal diamonds are compact (use [gwide]ab).\n\nD2 : For the metric [gwide]ab wave equations with suitable initial data have unique\nsolutions.\n\nD3 : The spacetime is foliated by spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces; where Cauchy now\nmeans spacelike with respect to the metric [gwide]ab, and the causal curves of that\nmetric intersect the Cauchy surface once and once only.\n\nThese are the minimum requirements for reformulating the causal hierarchy in a multi-\nmetric framework.\n\n2.3 Infinite signal velocities\n\nIn some frameworks (for instance in Hořava gravity) we have that some of the modes\npropagates at infinite speed with respect to some aether covector field ua (not at this\nstage necessarily hypersurface orthogonal). (No metric is required to establish\nthis.)\n\nWe shall first show that for infinite signal speeds sensible causal behaviour implies that\nthe aether field has to be hypersurface orthogonal. INFINITE SIGNAL VELOCITIES 35\n\n2.3.2 Uniqueness of the aether field\n\nSuppose now that we have two propagating modes, both with infinite signal speeds, but\ndefined with respect to two distinct hypersurface orthogonal aether fields ua1 and ua2.\nWe want to show that ua1 = ua2 if any sensible notion of causality is to survive. For the\ncurrent argument it is good enough to work in flat Minkowski space. Pick any point\np in spacetime and go to coordinates where 1\n\n2\n(ua1 + ua2) is pointing in the t direction,\n\n(1, 0, 0, 0), and the spatial 3-vectors (u1)i and (u2)i are pointing in the ±x directions,\n(±1, 0, 0). Then for some −1 < v < 1 we have\n\ngab = ηab; (u1,2)a = γ(−1;±v, 0, 0), (2.7)\n\nwhere γ = (1− v2)1/2 so that |u1,2|2 = −1.\n\nConsider the closed circular curve\n\nC : xa(λ) =\n(\n\n0, r∗ cos(θ(λ)), r∗ sin(θ(λ)), 0\n)\n\n(2.8)\n\nwith tangent vector\n\nta(λ) =\ndxa(λ)\n\ndλ\n\n=\n(\n\n0,−r∗ sin(θ(λ)), r∗ cos(θ(λ)), 0\n) dθ\n\ndλ\n\n= r∗\n\n(\n0,− sin(θ(λ)), cos(θ(λ)), 0\n\n) dθ\n\ndλ\n.
