(2.10)\n\nOn each of the two half-circles θ ∈ (0, π) and θ ∈ (π, 2π) the curve will be chronological,\n(taua < 0), with respect to either one or the other aether fields. At θ = 0 and θ = π the\ncurve is still causal (taua ≤ 0, in fact taua = 0). But this means one has a closed causal\ncurve with two chronological sections — so you can send messages into your own past.\nThe only way to avoid this serious violation of the causality condition is to set v = 0,\nthat is, for the two aether fields to coincide.\n\nCausal structure\n\nHence in the presence of infinite signal velocities the preservation of even the most basic\nnotions of causality implies that there is a global time function τ(x) whose normalized\ngradient (2.6) is unique and causally well-behaved in the sense described below:\n\n• Define the analogue of chronological curves in terms of the tangent being future-\npointing with respect to the global time function, ta∇aτ > 0.\n\n• Define the analogue of causal curves in terms of the tangent being non-past-\npointing with respect to the global time function, ta∇aτ ≥ 0.\n\n\n\n36 CHAPTER 2. CAUSAL HIERARCHY BEYOND GENERAL RELATIVITY.\n\nWith these definitions there automatically are no closed chronological curves — thence\na variant of the chronology condition is built into this formalism.\n\nThere are closed causal curves (infinite speed communication) but this is not a\nproblem since by assumption there is a unique global time function to keep things\nunder control. The presence of closed causal curves also implies that strong causality is\nviolated.For infinite signal velocities stable causality needs significant revision. In fact\nthere is certainly by construction no “wider” metric to deal with.)\nFinally,the concept of global hyperbolicity needs significant revision and it needs to be\nreplaced by some stronger requirement.\n\nIn fact we need to introduce the new concept of global parabolicity, which is now de-\nfined as demanding a foliation by (parabolic) Cauchy hypersurfaces (crossed by chrono-\nlogical curves once and once only). This implies in particular that for any point x we\ndemand that I+(x)∪ I−(x)∪ τ−1(x) is the entire spacetime, so that diffusion equations\nwith suitable initial data (on any fixed but arbitrary slice of the preferred foliation)\nhave unique solutions.\n\n2.3.3 Universal horizons\n\nWorking in Hořava-like models (the key ingredients being the existence of a preferred\nfoliation and infinite signal velocity) leads to a new concept — that of a universal\nhorizon [82, 83, 84]; see also references [85, 86].\n\nFigure 2.1: Carter–Penrose diagram describing a universal horizon. The diagram shows\nseveral constant-chronon hyper-surfaces, (leaves of the preferred foliation), with the red\nline depicting the universal horizon.\n\nThe most basic form of universal horizon arises in static and spherically symmetric\nsituations iff the gradient of the chronon is anti-parallel to the gradient of the radial\ncoordinate, ∇aτ = −χ2 ∇ar. They also appear in slowly rotating black hole solutions in\nHořava gravity [87]. If this happens, then for any chronological curve the tangent vector,\nby definition satisfying ta∇aτ > 0, also satisfies ta∇ar < 0. Thus all chronological\ncurves are trapped and forced to move “inwards”. Thence the universal horizon is a\nconstant chronon hypersurface, (a leaf of the preferred foliation), that is simultaneously\na constant r hypersurface. See figure 2.1.\n\n\n\n2.3. INFINITE SIGNAL VELOCITIES 37\n\nTo properly define “static” one also needs to have a metric gab available, in order\nto map the Killing vector into a covector, Ka = gabK\n\nb, to which one can apply the\nhypersurface orthogonality constraint. One also needs the metric to define the notion\nof the Killing vector being timelike (sufficiently far away from the black hole region).\nUnder these conditions the static Killing vector is 4-orthogonal to ∇r, and so the\nuniversal horizon can equally well be defined by Ka∇aτ = 0, see [85]. Moreover since\nthe static Killing vector is hypersurface orthogonal it induces a natural “Killing time”\ncoordinate, t, in terms of which we have Ka ∝ ∇at. So at the universal horizon one\nhas gab∇aτ ∇bt = 0; that is, gradients of the “chronon time” and “Killing time” are\n4-orthogonal (note however that ∇at is spacelike inside the Killing horizon).\n\nBecause one has a Lorentzian metric gab available, one can introduce the usual\nnotions of i−, i0, and i+, and also J ±. Asymptotically, as one moves “outwards”\non the constant chronon hypersurface corresponding to the universal horizon one must\napproach i+. (This is not what one would naively expect in “normal” situations, an\nasymptotic approach to i0. See figure 2.1. This observation can be modified to develop\na general definition of universal horizon.)\n\nA generic condition for defining a universal horizon is that it is a constant-chronon\nleaf of the preferred spacetime foliation that contains i+. So a universal horizon would\nnot be a Cauchy hypersurface, since causal curves that intersect J + would not neces-\nsarily intersect the universal horizon. In contrast, under “normal” conditions constant-\nchronon leaves of the preferred spacetime foliation asymptote to i0; so they would be\nCauchy hypersurfaces. This compatible with the constructions developed in [85].\n\nNow is the universal horizon a Cauchy horizon? This depends, very delicately, on\nprecise technical definitions. The key thing about Cauchy horizons is that something\nodd is happening to the “initial data” needed to define time-evolution into the future.\nIs there something odd with universal horizons? One issue is this: Since i+ lies on\nthe universal horizon, then anything outside the universal horizon can influence physics\nat i+. But then given the assumed infinite signal speeds used to define the universal\nhorizon, anything anywhere in the domain of outer communication can influence physics\nanywhere on the universal horizon. This is certainly odd behaviour.\n\nMore precisely — the leaves of the preferred foliation before formation of the uni-\nversal horizon all asymptote to i0, and so to get a well-defined Cauchy problem at worst\none needs to impose some regularity condition at spacelike infinity i0. In contrast, af-\nter the universal horizon forms one needs new extra “initial data” (corresponding to\nsome regularity condition at future timelike infinity i+) in order to set up a well-defined\nCauchy problem. It is in this precise technical sense that the universal horizon can be\nconsidered to be a Cauchy horizon.\n\nThere are various ways of rephrasing this in a more formal manner. For instance:\nIf x lies on a universal horizon then J−(x) = J−(i+). Furthermore, if the event x\nprecedes formation of the universal horizon, then x ∈ I−(i+) and J + ⊂ I+(x). The\noverall message is clear: Preferred foliations combined with infinite signal speeds lead\nto unusual but internally consistent notions of causal hierarchy.\n\n\n\n38 CHAPTER 2. CAUSAL HIERARCHY BEYOND GENERAL RELATIVITY.\n\n2.4 Conclusions\n\nThe framework we have developed above allows one to mathematically extend the\nusual Lorentzian causal hierarchy to multi-metric spacetimes, Einstein-aether models,\nHořava-like spacetimes, modified dispersion relations, and parabolic PDEs. The key\ndividing point in the analysis is whether the signal velocity is finite or infinite. When\nthe signal speed is finite, a variant of the usual general relativistic causal hierarchy\ncan be formulated. When the signal speed is infinite, a significantly modified causal\nhierarchy must be formulated in terms of a global time function (chronon). Preserving\neven minimal notions of causality in the presence of infinite signal velocity requires the\naether field to be both unique and hypersurface orthogonal, leading us to introduce the\nnotion of global parabolicity. Either case provides a logically coherent framework for\ndealing with “superluminal” signalling while still maintaining a consistent approach to\ncausality.\n\nFor every scenario that we have considered, global hyperbolicity is a necessary con-\ndition for a well defined notion of causality, even if in some cases it is not a sufficient\nconditions and stronger constraints have to be imposed. For this reason, in the next\nchapter, where we are going to study the singularity problem with the minimum possible\nnumber of assumption, we will assume that the manifold is globally hyperbolic.\n\n\n\nChapter 3\n\nGeodesically complete black holes\n\nIn this chapter we will adopt an agnostic approach and look directly where the de-\nviations from general relativity may arise. This means that instead of focusing on a\nparticular modified theory, we are going to directly look at the problem of the black\nhole singularities, which is expected to be resolved once that quantum gravity effects\nare taken into account. This will allow us to obtain less stringent but more general re-\nsults. We will not impose any particular quantization scheme of the gravitational field\nand, using Penrose’s singularity theorem as guidance, which tells us that singularities\nare inevitable in general relativity under specific conditions imposed on matter fields,\nwe will perform a systematic analysis of the possible non-singular spacetimes with a\ntrapping horizon. Such analysis will be blind to the dynamics (classical, semi-classical,\nor quantum) of a specific theory and will only assume a minimal set of kinematical\nrequirements. This feature makes our analysis quite general and applicable to any the-\nory of quantum gravity that satisfies the aforementioned kinematical requirements in a\ncertain regime, and virtually to any theory of modified gravity. It is possible to schemat-\nically divide Penrose’s theorem into two part: In the first part of the theorem, the weak\nenergy condition and the Einstein fields equations together with geodesic completeness\nare used in order to prove the existence of a focusing point (see Fig. 3.1), then, consid-\nerations of a purely geometrical nature are used in order to prove that the existence of\na focusing point is actually incompatible with the topology of spacetime [17]. Hence,\nin order to understand the possible geometries that follow from the violation of either\nthe weak energy condition or the Einstein fields equations, we just need to categorize\nin geometric terms the possible ways in which the focusing point can be avoided. This\nchapter is based on reference P6, and it is organized as follows. In Sec. 3.1 we briefly\nreview the original Penrose singularity theorem and explain in depth the rationale of our\nanalysis. In Sec. 3.2, we explain the geometrical setting that we will be using and prove\nsome results that will be important for the subsequent discussion. Our main results are\nformalized in Sec. 3.3, where we categorize and discuss the possible geometries. Finally\nSec. 3.4 contains a brief discussion of our main conclusions.\n\n39\n\n\n\n40 CHAPTER 3. GEODESICALLY COMPLETE BLACK HOLES\n\nFigure 3.1: Pictorial representation of the formation of a focusing point. Such a focusing\npoint is not compatible with the topology of spacetime.\n\n3.1 Avoiding singularities: Beyond Penrose’s\n\ntheorem\n\nPenrose’s singularity theorem [17], and its modern variants and extensions (see for\ninstance [88]), demonstrates that once a trapped surface S 2 is formed, then in some\nregion of spacetime contained in the causal future J(S 2) of S 2, one of the following\nmust hold in order to avoid a spacetime singularity (more precisely, to avoid that the\nspacetime is geodesically incomplete.):\n\n(a) The weak energy condition is violated.\n\n(b) The Einstein field equations do not hold.\n\n(c) Pseudo-Riemannian geometry does not provide an adequate description of space-\ntime.\n\n(d) Global hyperbolicity breaks down.\n\nThese options span a huge space of possibilities that are very difficult (if not impossible)\nto describe exhaustively. Our goal is to gain a complete understanding of the infor-\nmation that pseudo-Riemannian geometry may contain about theories that go beyond\ngeneral relativity, and regularize the singularities of the latter. Accordingly, we will\nwork in a framework where we ab initio impose the minimal conditions that:\n\n(1) Pseudo-Riemannian geometry provides an effective description of spacetime;\n\n(2) The spacetime is globally hyperbolic.1\n\n1Note that Penrose’s theorem also assumes that the Cauchy surface is non-compact. As explained\nin [89] the non-compact assumption can be relaxed by assuming the existence of at least one future\ninextendible curve from the Cauchy surface C 3 which does not intersect the causal future of the\ntrapping surface. We implicitly assume that this is realized, as it corresponds to the very physically\nreasonable assumption that there exists at least one observer which does not fall into the collapsing\nstar;\n\n\n\n3.1. AVOIDING SINGULARITIES: BEYOND PENROSE’S THEOREM 41\n\n(3) The spacetime is geodesically complete;\n\n(4) There are no curvature singularities.2\n\nOn the other hand, we will accept that both (a) and (b) in Penrose’s list of possibili-\nties can take place, perhaps simultaneously. We will see that the geometric structure\nassumed in (1), (2), (3) and (4) above is tight enough to leave only a handful of possi-\nbilities.\n\nAmong this assumptions, the first one is arguably the most controversial one. It is\nreasonable to think that in a theory of quantum gravity spacetime may lose its smooth-\nness in certain situations, so that a description in terms of differentiable manifolds\nbreaks down. Anyway, if this happens in a bounded region, it seems always possible to\ndevise a classical geometry that matches the physical one at the boundary of this non-\nclassical region; while one does not expect this effective classical description to provide\na precise description of the non-classical regime, it may capture some of the relevant\nphysics of the transition through this region.\n\nEven more importantly, advances in frameworks such as loop quantum gravity, loop\nquantum cosmology and asymptotic safety show that a description in terms of an effec-\ntive metric provides a good approximation in many situations [94, 95, 96, 97, 98, 99],\nso that, for a large sector of initial conditions for the quantum state of the system,\nthe description in terms of differentiable manifolds remains meaningful throughout dy-\nnamical evolution. Whether these initial conditions are relevant to describe physical\nsituations of interest in black holes (where several technical issues remain to be solved\n[100, 101, 102]) is unclear at the moment but, regardless of this issue, we think that\nthere is no question that effective descriptions in terms of differentiable manifolds can\nprovide useful illustrations of the physics at play.\nFinally, it might be useful to study the difficulties that arise trying the regularize\nthe spacetime while maintaining pseudo Riemannian geometry even if this description\nbreaks down in some region of spacetime, as the analysis can provide insight on where\nthis description has to break down.\nThe other assumptions on our list are less debatable. Once that we have accepted that\npseudo-Riemannian geometry provides a good description of the spacetime, we need to\nimpose some causality requirements on the manifold. As discussed in chapter 2, global\nhyperbolicity might not be enough to guarantee a regular causal structure beyond gen-\neral relativity, but it is definitely a necessary condition.\nFinally, conditions (3) and (4) are simply two different (and non equivalent) ways to\nimpose the absence of singularities.\nLet us note that some of these assumptions have been widely used in previous explo-\nrations of singularity regularization in black holes [103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109,\n110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115]; however, it is worth remarking that global hyperbolicity\nis violated in static regular black holes (we will discuss this explicitly in due course).\nWhat makes our approach novel, and more powerful, is that all these works assume\nadditional postulates in order to select specific realizations of non-singular spacetimes,\nwhile here we want to provide a complete catalogue of possibilities based only on ge-\nometric notions. Our study can be understood as a supplement to Penrose’s theorem\n\n2It is worth mentioning the existence of works in the literature in which assumption (2) holds but\nthis one is dropped, such as [90, 91, 92, 93].\n\n\n\n42 CHAPTER 3. GEODESICALLY COMPLETE BLACK HOLES\n\nthat goes a step beyond and characterizes all the spherically symmetric geometries that\navoid the formation of focusing points while satisfying (1–4) above.\n\n3.2 Geometric setting\n\nLet us start with some geometric preliminaries. We will be dealing with a 4-dimensional\nand globally hyperbolic spacetime M , with t : M → R a global time function and C 3\n\na Cauchy surface. Additionally, our spacetimes of interest describe the collapse of a\nregular distribution of matter from a given initial Cauchy surface with topology R3. It is\nimportant to note that this fixes the topology of all the Cauchy hypersufaces of entire\nmanifold as our assumptions are incompatible with topology change [116, 117, 118].\nIt is also useful to restrict the initial discussion to spherically symmetric spacetimes,\npostponing for future works the discussion of the more general setting in which this\nassumption is dropped. Let us recall the standard property that the isometry group\nof a spherically symmetric spacetime permits to identify a foliation in 2-spheres S2.\nFurthermore, spherical symmetry allows us to prove the following auxiliary result:\n\nProposition 1: Under the assumptions (1–4) above, the entire manifold M can be cov-\nered with a single coordinate chart in which all points p ∈M are labelled using double\nnull coordinates (associated with radial null geodesics) and two angular coordinates.\n\nProof: Due to the existence of a local light-cone structure and the dimensionality\nof M , through every point p in the manifold there are exactly two future-directed\nradial null geodesics (which we will call in the following left-going and right-going) and\ntwo past-directed radial null geodesics (their continuation to the past of p). Global\nhyperbolicity implies that either the two future-directed or the two past-directed causal\ncurves through p must intersect C 3. As there are only two such geodesics for each p, we\ncan use these (together with the two angular coordinates on the unit 2-sphere) in order\nto label all points in spacetime, as long as these labels are unique. In order to show that\nthese labels are unique, let us demonstrate that any situation in which these are not\nunique is inconsistent with our assumptions. For two points p, q ∈M , with p < q, let\nus define their causal diamond D(q, p) as the intersection between the causal future of p\nand the causal past of q, namely D(q, p) = J−(q)∩J+(p) (for fixed values of the angular\ncoordinates). If the two radial null geodesics crossing at p and intersecting C 3 also cross\nat q, the boundary of D(q, p) is smooth except at the points p and q; in other words,\nthe sides of the diamond are smoothed, as each of them are identified with segments of\na left-going and right-going radial null geodesic, respectively. This smoothing implies\nthe existence of at least two points in the boundary of D(q, p) in which the light cones\nin the corresponding tangent spaces are degenerate, as Σ2 is simply connected. Let us\nconsider for instance the side of the diamond generated by the left-going radial null\ngeodesic; it is clear that there exist right-going null geodesics that cross the former\nat two points, but also other right-going null geodesics without crossing points (this\nis also true for smaller segments of the left-going radial null geodesic). Smoothness\nimplies the existence of an intermediate right-going radial null geodesic that is tangent\nto the segment of the corresponding left-going radial null geodesic at one point at least;\nthe light cone at this point would be then degenerate. �\n\nThe areas of the 2-spheres preserved by rotations are geometric invariants which, in\n\n\n\n3.2. In the\nfollowing, T 3 will denote the set of marginally trapped spheres (so that θ(l) = 0):\n\nProposition 6: T 3 is a smooth compact submanifold only if the function v(R0) is not\nbijective, so that its domain contains at least two open subsets where the inverse R0(v)\nexists.\n\nProof: Let us assume that v(R0) is bijective in all its domain of definition, so that its\ninverse R0(v) is strictly increasing and defines the (evolving) position of a future inner\ntrapping horizon, as a consequence of propositions 4 and 5. These outgoing radial null geodesics, being\ninside the trapped region, have crossed before the future outer trapping horizon. Hence,\nall such geodesics must intersect T 3 twice. If T 3 is compact, there will always exist a\n“tangent” outgoing radial null geodesic intersecting T 3 only once (this is the limiting\ncase in between the geodesics with two crossings and the geodesics with no crossings).\n\n\n\n50 CHAPTER 3. GEODESICALLY COMPLETE BLACK HOLES\n\nThe alternative is that T 3 is not compact, so that there is no outgoing radial null\ngeodesic that intersects it only once (alternatively, one can take the limit in which this\nsingle intersection point is reached in infinite affine distance). In the compact case,\nboth trapping horizons (inner and outer) will merge at the point where the “tangent”\noutgoing radial geodesic meets T 3. Given that the position of the future inner trapping\nhorizon is a strictly increasing function of the radial coordinate, T 3 cannot be smooth\nat this point, displaying a cusp instead. �\n\nThe simplest situation compatible with the proposition above leads to the Penrose\ndiagram depicted in Fig. 3.5 (more complicated situations just contain more outer and\ninner horizons). The topology of T 3 is S1 × S2, and the domain of the function v(R0)\nhas two subsets where an inverse exists. In one of these subsets (associated with the top\nquadrant on the left diagram in Fig. 3.6), the function R0(v) is strictly increasing, so\nthat this portion of T 3 is identified with the expanding future inner trapping horizon.\nOn the other hand, the right quadrant on the left diagram in Fig. 3.6 indicates the\nregion in T 3 in whichR0(v) is decreasing, which is then identified as the shrinking future\nouter trapping horizon. Thus, the Penrose diagram depicted in Fig. 3.5 describes the\nformation and disappearance of a black hole that remains non-singular throughout its\ndynamical evolution, as forced by our assumptions.\n\nFigure 3.5: Penrose diagram of the formation and dissapearance of a geodesically-\ncomplete black hole. The submanifold T 3 is the boundary of the shaded region. The\ndashed line is an outgoing radial null geodesic, while the remaining curved lines mark\nthe hypersurfaces of constant radius r.\n\nOur discussion does not assume any specific dynamical laws for either gravity or\nmatter sectors which, in particular, implies that the disappearance of the black hole\n\n\n\n3.3. On the left: the\nboundary of the top quadrant (red line) corresponds to the strictly increasing branch\nof R0(v), while the boundary of the right quadrant (yellow line) corresponds to the\nstrictly decreasing branch of R0(v). In other words,\nblack hole evaporation would correspond to selecting specific geometries, with certain\nfeatures and time scales, within the class that we have obtained as the result of our\npurely geometric analysis (moreover, it is important to keep in mind that we are not\ntracing explicitly the evolution of matter). For instance, an alternative to black hole\nevaporation that shares the same Penrose diagram was given in [134]. It is also possible\nthat T 3 is not simply connected, but is composed of disconnected regions. Also, if one\ndemands time-reversal symmetry, there must be a region of anti-trapped surfaces, and\nthe corresponding spacetime describes the transition between a black hole and a white\nhole [135, 136, 137, 138] (see Fig. 3.8).\n\nFigure 3.7: Different coordinate patches that are relevant for our discussion on the\navoidance of crossing points between outgoing radial null geodesics (the red dot in this\nfigure). The straight lines at 45 degrees represent ingoing radial null geodesics.\n\n\n\n52 CHAPTER 3. GEODESICALLY COMPLETE BLACK HOLES\n\nLet us now show that the explicit assumption in the above discussion that there\ncannot be crossing points between two outgoing radial null geodesics is, in fact, a\nconsequence of global hyperbolicity, starting with a detailed discussion of the case in\nwhich R0(v) is a constant function:\n\nProposition 7: A spacetime in which R0(v) is a constant function cannot be globally\nhyperbolic.\n\nProof: That there cannot be crossing points between two outgoing radial null geodesics\nhaving θ(l)\n\n∣∣\nr=R0\n\n= 0 does not imply that these geodesics cannot have the same value\nof the radial coordinate for the corresponding values of their affine parameters. The\n(weaker) consequence that follows is that the one-to-one correspondence between the\nvalue of the radial coordinate and spheres in spacetime must break down, such that a\ngiven value of the radial coordinate does not uniquely identify a single sphere. We can\ntry, of course, to use the set of null coordinates (u, v) (in order to construct a complete\nset of coordinates we have to consider the angular coordinates as well, but it is not\nnecessary to consider them explicitly). However, we shall now show that the geodesics\nreaching r = R0 exit the spacetime region that can be covered with the (u, v) coordinate\npatch. Indeed, let us assume that both spheres (located at the red dot in Fig. 3.7) can\nbe covered with the (u, v) patch. Then, one sphere will be labeled by the specific values\n(u1, v1), while the other sphere will be associated with (u2, v1). This would imply that\nthe u = u1 and u = u2 geodesics must intersect v = v1 at points that are identified with\ndifferent values of the affine parameter along the latter ingoing radial null geodesic.\nHowever, this is in contradiction with Fig. (3.7), as one can consider an open subset\nof the manifold around the red dot and follow the evolution of the affine parameter\nalong the ingoing radial null geodesic in this subset (so that it must be the same for\nthe two points labelled with different values of u). Given that null coordinates always\nexist locally, the second sphere must be labelled by a radial ingoing null geodesic that\ncannot cross the Cauchy surface C 3. Hence, the spacetime is not globally hyperbolic.\n�\n\nEven if the proposition above is valid for R0(v) being a constant function, it is\nstraightforward to see that a similar comment regarding the lack of global hyperbolicity\nin the presence of would-be intersection points applies to generic functions R0(v), as\nthe argument above does not depend on the form of R0(v), but only on the interplay\nbetween different coordinate patches at the would-be intersection points. It is also worth\nstressing that the local behavior around these points may seem odd, but it is in fact\nubiquitous in attempts of constructing non-singular black holes (we will discuss this in\nmore detail in the corresponding cases below). The only difference is that our discussion\nis general enough to accommodate generic dynamical situations, while the well-known\ncases in the literature with Cauchy horizons are typically eternal black holes.\nWhile we have so far focused on the minimal setting that just requires the existence of\na single trapped region, as depicted in figure 3.5, note that there are models proposed\nin the literature that present additional features while still belonging in this class.\nFor instance, see Fig. 3.8 for a sketch of a situation in which there is a bounce and\nsubsequent formation of an additional anti-trapped region [135, 136, 137].\n\n\n\n3.3. TAXONOMY OF NON-SINGULAR GEOMETRIES 53\n\nFigure 3.8: After the disappearance of the trapped region, an anti-trapped region is\nformed. This situation describes a bounce from a black hole like geometry to a white\nhole like geometry. Situations in which a recollapse takes place [135, 136] can be de-\nscribed by a sequence of trapped and anti-trapped regions.\n\nCase A.II: One-way hidden wormholes (λ0, R0, θ̄ ≥ 0)\n\nCharacterizing this class is simpler than for the previous one. We just need to take\ninto account that there exists an ingoing radial null geodesic that starts with a negative\nvalue of the expansion, that eventually vanishes and becomes positive. That both\nexpansions (outgoing and ingoing) vanish, although in different regions in spacetime,\nis characteristic of dynamical wormhole throats [139, 140]. In fact, we can show the\nfollowing proposition:\n\nProposition 8: There exists a hypersurface r(u, v) = R0 where the radial coordinate\nhas a local minimum.\n\nProof: The value of the radial coordinate along the outgoing radial null geodesic\nstemming from S 2 (see the right panel in Fig. 3.9) must reach a minimum at r = R0.\nLet us now study the intersections between outgoing and ingoing radial null geodesics,\nin similar terms as we did before the intersection of two outgoing radial null geodesics.\nInstead of dealing with a single intersection between outgoing radial null geodesics, in\nthis case we deal with double intersections between outgoing and ingoing radial null\ngeodesics (Fig. 3.9). This is also forbidden in spherical symmetry, as it would imply\nthat two different points would be associated with the same values of (null) coordinates.\nIn fact, as in the previous case, both coordinate sets (u, r) and (v, r) cannot be used\nto go through the points in which the expansion of ongoing and ingoing null geodesics,\nrespectively, vanishes. However, the main difference with respect to the previous case\nis that the splitting of the second intersection point can be well described in the (u, v)\ncoordinates, as illustrated graphically in Fig. 3.9, but at the price of creating two\ndifferent hypersurfaces in spacetime corresponding to the same value of the radius\n\n\n\n54 CHAPTER 3. Two radial null geodesics, ingoing and outgoing, depart from the crossing point\n1. The ingoing geodesic crosses the point 2 with a value of the radius corresponding to\nthe would-be crossing point 3, reaches r = R0 (which is the same for both ingoing and\noutgoing geodesics due to the wormhole being static), and bounces back until reaching\nwhat looks like a second crossing point 3. Dotted lines are lines of constant radius. The corresponding\nblack hole is always growing and never disappears; any process that describes the partial\nevaporation or total disappearance of the black hole must involve some outgoing radial\nnull geodesics satisfying the conditions characteristic of the case (λ0, R0, θ̄ < 0) studied\nabove.\n\nAnother issue that is worth clarifying is the asymptotic (λ → ∞) behavior of the\nlines of constant radial coordinate in the trapped region which, as depicted in Fig. 3.11,\n\n\n\n56 CHAPTER 3. (3.2) vanishes as\nwell (see App. C for explicit expressions), and so does the line element on the lines of\nconstant radial coordinate,\n\nds2\n∣∣\nr=r0\n\n= −e−2φ(v,r)F (v, r)dv2. (3.8)\n\nCase B.II: Asymptotic hidden wormholes (∞, R∞, θ̄ ≥ 0)\n\nSimilarly as the case just above, this situation can be understood as the λ0 →∞ limit\nof a previously discussed case, namely (λ0, R0, θ̄ ≥ 0), which described a wormhole.\nHence, this kind of geometry corresponds to an asymptotically cylinder-like geometry.\nThis is easiest to realize for the static case limλ→∞ θ\n\n(k) = 0, in which the radius of the\ncylinder is given by the size of the corresponding surface B2 (which is at infinite affine\ndistance). The Penrose diagram would be given by Fig. 3.10 but removing the shaded\nregions. In the dynamical situation, we would have a “half-wormhole” where the second\nuniverse has been discarded and the throat pushed out to infinite affine distance along\noutgoing radial null geodesics.\n\nCases B.III, B.IV, C.I and C.II: Curvature singularities,\n(∞, 0, θ̄ < 0), (∅, 0, θ̄ < 0), (∞, 0, θ̄ ≥ 0) and (∅, 0, θ̄ ≥ 0)\n\nThese four situations are sufficiently similar that we can analyze them simultaneously,\nwith only slight differences due to the different behavior of the expansion of ingoing\nradial null geodesics. In fact, their main feature is that outgoing radial null geodesics\nreach r = 0. It is straightforward to show that this is not compatible with the regularity\nof curvature invariants, provided we maintain all our assumptions (such as geodesic\ncompleteness). Outgoing radial null geodesics reach r = 0 in an infinite affine distance\nbut, generally, ingoing null geodesics will reach r = 0 (as there is no wormhole throat in\n\n\n\n3.3. TAXONOMY OF NON-SINGULAR GEOMETRIES 57\n\nthis case) in finite affine distance. At the same time, there is no future inner trapping\nhorizon (in other words, a second point in which θ(l) vanishes) which, following the\ndiscussion in Sec. C, is a necessary condition to ensure regularity at r = 0. Hence,\nthese cases lead to a curvature singularity at infinite affine distance along outgoing null\ngeodesics, but generally finite affine distance along ingoing null geodesics for instance.\nIn other words, we have seen in the discussion of the cases above that, in order to avoid\na curvature singularity at r = 0, one needs either a wormhole structure (a minimum\nvalue of the radial coordinate that prevents reaching r = 0) or a future inner trapping\nhorizon. As the geometries studied in this item contain by construction none of these,\nthese must be singular (if global hyperbolicity is maintained).\n\nFigure 3.12: Static regular black holes evade Penrose’s theorem due to the introduction\nof a Cauchy horizon (here represented as the horizontal plane) before the focusing point\nis reached, which allows the focusing point to be regular in these geometries.\n\nIt is always possible to violate the assumption of global hyperbolicity in Penrose’s\ntheorem (which is also one of the four conditions behind our analysis) in order to avoid\nbeing singular. Interestingly, geometries that appear often in the literature belong to\nthis case. Even if the focusing point in these situations is reached generically in finite\naffine distance, this point in the discussion is a natural placement of these well-known\ngeometries describing static regular black holes [103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110,\n111, 112, 113, 114, 115]. As shown graphically in Fig. 3.12 , these geometries do\nnot evade Penrose’s theorem by avoiding the formation of focusing points, but rather\nby introducing a Cauchy horizon before this focusing point is reached by outgoing\ngeodesics. For completeness, we also provide in Fig. 3.13 the Penrose diagram of the\ncorresponding eternal geometries. Static regular black holes correspond to the limiting\nsituation in which the expansion θ(k) associated with the ingoing radial null geodesics\ncrossing C 3 vanishes along the Cauchy horizon (in these spacetimes, there are ingoing\nradial null geodesics that intersect the trapped outgoing radial null geodesics while\nhaving θ(k), but only in the region beyond the Cauchy horizon). One may think that\nit should be possible to devise situations in which θ(k) actually changes sign without\nviolating global hyperbolicity. However, these situations would always involve two\nintersections between outgoing and ingoing radial null geodesics which, due to the lack\nof wormhole throats in this situation (r = 0 is reached by outgoing radial null geodesics\n\n\n\n58 CHAPTER 3. GEODESICALLY COMPLETE BLACK HOLES\n\nby construction), implies the lack of global hyperbolicity.\n\nFigure 3.13: Penrose diagram that can represent different kinds of (eternal) black holes,\nfrom charged to rotating black holes, but also regular black holes in which the central\nsingularity has been removed. The colored quadrants on the left and on the right\nrepresent respectively the regions which are covered by the (v, r) patch but not with the\n(u, r) patch, and by the (u, r) patch but not with the (v, r) patch. These are particular\nexamples of spacetimes that are not globally hyperbolic, following our general discussion\nin this section. The complete Penrose diagram is obtained by stacking indefinitely the\nsection represented here. Our discussion in this chapter is more general, as it does not\nrequire that the diagram is not symmetric as this one (this symmetry is a consequence\nof the eternal nature of the black holes represented in this diagram).\n\n3.4 Conclusions\n\nWe have studied in completely general terms the possible spherically symmetric geome-\ntries describing geodesically-complete black holes. Beside geodesic completeness, we\nhave also demanded global hyperbolicity (so that it is reasonable to think that these\ngeometries can be obtained through dynamical evolution) and the absence of curvature\nsingularities.\n\nRemarkably, we have found that purely geometric considerations are enough to\nstrongly constrain the allowed class of spacetimes. Using our classification, we were\nable to identify four classes of geometries, that can either be taken as they are or be\ncombined, in order to yield the most general spherically symmetric spacetime satisfying\nour requirements (1–4). Figure 3.14 summarizes the classification that we have provided\nand the different viable classes of geometries.\n\n\n\n3.4. CONCLUSIONS 59\n\nFigure 3.14: The table summarizes the classes of the allowed geometries. The most\ngeneral geometry is given by a combination of the geometries in the table.\n\nThe first class corresponds to geometries in which the defocusing of outgoing null\ngeodesics is placed at a finite value of the affine parameter and for a finite value of the\nradial coordinate, whereas ingoing null geodesics do not have a defocusing point. This\nclass of geometries is associated with a geodesically-complete black hole that disappears\nin finite time, which we call an “evanescent regular black hole”. Note that we are\ncarefully avoiding the use of “evaporation”; our geometric analysis does not provide\nany hint about the dynamical process behind the disappearance of the black hole. Such\nprocess could either be Hawking radiation or some other process taking place in shorter\ntime scales, for instance the proposed transition to a white hole;\n\nThe second class differs from the first one due to the value of the expansion parame-\nter of ingoing null geodesics, which is non-negative at the point in which the defocusing\npoint for the outgoing geodesics. We have discussed that this implies the existence of\nsomething closely resembling a wormhole throat. We refer to these geometries as “one-\nway hidden wormholes” to stress the fact that the throat is inside a trapped region.\n\nThe last two classes can be understood as the limit of λdefocus →∞ of the previous\ntwo cases. The difference between these two classes is once again the value of the\nexpansion parameter of ingoing null geodesics. If the expansion is negative, then we\nhave an “everlasting regular black hole”. If the expansion parameter is asymptotically\nzero or positive, we would get an “asymptotic hidden wormhole” which would again be\nnon-traversable and now involve a one-way trip to the edge of spacetime.\n\nWe can see that the set of possibility is quite limited. In the next chapter we are\ngoing to constrain it even more as we will discuss some self consistency requirement that\nwill allow us to question the viability of specific realizations of some of the geometries\ndiscussed in this chapter.\n\n\n\n60\n\n\n\nChapter 4\n\nOn the viability of non-singular black holes\n\nIn the previous chapter we have discussed a geometrical classification of non-singular\nspacetimes with a trapping horizon. We have obtained the very interesting result that\nthe most general spacetime can be classified within one of the four classes we have\nstudied or it is a combination of them. In other words, there are very few possible\nnon-singular configuration.\n\nThese families of spacetimes can be understood as effective descriptions of the evolu-\ntion of non-singular black holes, sharing some qualitative properties but still displaying\nquantitative differences that can be described in terms of parametric and functional\ndegrees of freedom. In this chapter, we want to highlight that the effective descrip-\ntion in terms of these spacetimes would only be meaningful if displaying a satisfactory\nlevel of selfconsistency. Of course, the lack of knowledge of the specific dynamics that\nmay yield these spacetimes implies a degree of uncertainty about some fine details of\nthese models. However, this does not prevent extracting certain conclusions that, if\nformulated carefully enough, would remain robust regardless of this uncertainty.\n\nIn particular, we will see in Sec. 4.1 that it is very difficult to have a consistent\nmodel of evanescent or everlasting horizon geometry unless the lifetime of the object is\nvery short. In Sec. 4.2 we will study the self consistency issues that affects the one way\nand the asymptotic hidden wormholes geometries. Finally, in Sec. 4.3 we will discuss\nthe implications of our conclusions. The content of this chapter is based on P2, P5\nand P6.\n\n4.1 Evanescent horizons and everlasting horizons\n\nIn the previous chapter, we have seen that one of the most conservative possibilities\nto regularize the singularity consist in changing the geometry close to the would be\nsingularity introducing an inner horizon.\n\nThe non-singular core in these geometries replaces a region in which the spacetime\ncurvature takes Planckian values or larger, and therefore in which the classical dynamics\nis modified [104, 105], by a region in which curvature is bounded.\n\nWhen doing so, it is possible to leave the geometry outside the outer horizon un-\nchanged, obtaining an object completely indistinguishable from a black hole. The ge-\nometry will certainly deviate from the one corresponding to a black hole when the outer\n\n61\n\n\n\n62 CHAPTER 4. ON THE VIABILITY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nand inner horizon merge, but this could happen after a very long time1. Given the pos-\nsible absence of phenomenological signatures, it is impossible to device any experiment\nable to rule out this possibility from a observational point of view and it is crucial\nto address the self consistency of the model. We will see that the inner horizon has\nan unstable nature which casts serious concerns regarding the self consistency of the\nmodel.\n\n4.1.1 Time independent geometry\n\nThe geometries in the classes of evanescent horizons or everlasting horizons are charac-\nterized by the formation and eventual disappearance of an outer and an inner horizon.\nTherefore, the geometry has to be time dependent. In fact, as already discussed is\nSec. 3.3, by explicitly looking at the Penrose diagram of a static regular black hole\nreported in Fig. 4.1 (see also [112]), it is immediate to see that a static regular black\nhole do not belong to any of the classes discussed in the previous chapter and the con-\nclusion of the Penrose theorem are avoided by violating global hyperbolicity. This class\nof geometry are therefore actually outside our classification as one of the hypothesis\nis not satisfied. Anyway, it is convenient to start the analysis by considering a static\nconfiguration which will approximate the time dependent geometry if the evolution is\nslow enough. We will explicitly introduce the time dependence in Sec. 4.1.3.\n\nWithout loss of generality, the geometry of a static and spherically symmetric regular\nblack hole can be written as\n\nds2 = −e−2φ(r)F (r)dt2 +\ndr2\n\nF (r)\n+ r2(dθ2 + sin2 θ dφ2). (4.12)\n\n4.1.2 Instability of the inner horizon\n\nFrom the analysis of the previous section it seems that it is possible to replace the\nsingularity with an inner horizon without changing the exterior geometry. This would\nimply that any quantum gravity effect will be confined within the trapping horizon and\ninvisible to an external observer. Anyway we will now show that this picture is too\nsimplistic due to the unstable nature of the inner horizon.\n\nSuch unstable nature is due to the exponential focusing of null rays and it was\npreviously noticed, and thoroughly studied, in the different but related context of\ncharged and rotating black holes. The main aspects were settled more than two decades\nago [144, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149], though formal proofs of a number of technical aspects\nwere only available later [150] (see also [151] for a review). In brief terms, the central\nconclusion of these works is that the inner horizon is unstable in the presence of both\ningoing and outgoing perturbations, which are expected to exist in realistic collapse\nscenarios. While this is a classical instability, it is natural to expect the existence of\nsemiclassical instabilities as well [152].\n\nLet us start by explaining why it is natural to expect the existence of outgoing\nand ingoing perturbations in realistic scenarios. A regular black hole, being just a\nregularization of an ordinary black hole, would form after the gravitational collapse\nof a massive star. The star would emit radiation even after crossing the outer horizon\n(after this, the initially outgoing radiation is strongly lensed back to the collapsing star).\nOn the other hand, there will be ingoing perturbations that come, for instance, from the\nbackscattering of gravitational radiation. The process can be modelled following [148],\nwhere outgoing and ingoing perturbations are described in terms of null shells. This\nsimplification allows to perform all necessary calculations analytically, and exploits the\nDray–’t Hooft–Redmount (DTR) relation [153, 154]. Furthermore, despite its simplicity,\nthis type of perturbation represent a good approximation of a real perturbation. In fact,\nwe are exclusively interested in the geometry close to the inner horizon where, due to\nthe intensive blueshift, the infalling waves are well described by the geometrical optic\napproximation.\n\n\n\n4.1.
