(4.30)\n\nThis timescale is so huge that for generic initial condition the instability will be triggered\nwell before the beginning of the exponential decay regime, showing that the cosmological\nconstant in completely negligible for our discussion.\n\n4.2 One way hidden wormholes and asymptotic\n\nhidden wormholes\n\nThe geometries belonging to the class of one way hidden wormhole do not have an\ninner horizon and, therefore, they are not plagued by the mass inflation instability.\nAnyway, the presence of a minimum radius poses problem concerning the topology of\nthe spacetime. We will divide the discussion in two parts as the picture is similar but\ndifferent for the one way hidden wormhole case and the asymptotic hidden wormhole\ncase.\n\n4.2.1 One way hidden wormhole\n\nThis class of geometry is characterized by a minimum radius throat. If the minimum\nof the radius is a global minimum than the topology of the Cauchy surfaces is R× S2.\nAnyway, we want the spacetime to describe a gravitational collapse. This means that\nin a given initial Cauchy surface there is a regular distribution of matter implying that\nthe topology of that surface is simply the topology of R3. As discussed in Sec. 3.2,\ntopology change is not compatible with our assumption of global hyperbolicity which\nimplies that all the Cauchy surfaces are homeomorphic with each other. Therefore, the\n\n\n\n72 CHAPTER 4. ON THE VIABILITY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nonly possibility is that in any Cauchy surface the value of the radius r = R0 is only a\nlocal minimum.\n\nTherefore, the r = R0 line, besides having a portion which is a minimum radius\nhypersurface (that is, the radius would be greater at both sides of the hypersurface),\nwould have to reach both i− and i+. If we trace this r = R0 line back to i−, one\ngoes continuously from a situation in which the radius is greater at both sides of this\nhypersurface to a situation in which the radius is greater on one side and smaller on the\nother one. Let us focus our attention on the side in which there is a transition from the\nradius being greater than its value on this hypersurface to becoming smaller, and take\ntwo points in these two regions. Along an arbitrary line connecting these two points, it\nis clear that, due to continuity, there is a point in which r = R0 as well (which is not\ncontained in the previous hypersurface). This argument can be repeated for all points\non this side of the original r = R0 hypersurface and arbitrarily close to the latter, which\nimplies the existence of two r = R0 that merge at some point. The metric cannot be\nanalytical at this point. Also, the single r = R0 line that remains after the merger\nmust disappear (if we assume that it does not end up in i0), which implies the existence\nof another point in which the metric is non analytic (see Fig. 4.5 for a sketch of the\nPenrose diagram in this situation).\n\nFinally let us note that there is one last possibility that have been considered to\nmake this class of geometries viable. It is simply possible that the geometry is not\ndefined in the regions where it cannot analytic. This is exactly what happen in [167,\n168, 169] where the authors provide a metric which locally describes an element of this\nclass of geometries but which is not globally defined, i.e., there are regions where an\neffective spacetime is not defined. This possibility lies outside our classification as we\nare assuming an everywhere defined metric, but it is a clear example of the fact that\nour analysis can provide useful insights also when this is not the case.\n\n4.2.2 Asymptotic hidden wormhole\n\nIn the case of asymptotic hidden wormhole there is an extra consistency issue which\nis not easy to solve. This issue concern the consistency with semiclassical physics.\nOur analysis has a purely geometrical nature but we expect that the resulting geom-\netry agrees with semiclassical physics and in particular with Hawking radiation. The\nasymptotic hidden wormhole class can be compatible with the existence of Hawking ra-\ndiation if and only if the latter eventually switches off due to some unknown quantum\ngravity effect. Anyway, the switching off of Hawking radiation cannot be described us-\ning quantum field theory on the geometric backgrounds leading to remnants that have\nbeen discussed in complete generality in this thesis; this description must break down\nat some point, meaning that the effective description in terms of differentiable mani-\nfolds is no longer meaningful below a certain length scale. On the other hand, for these\ngeometries there is an extra possibility to avoid the topology change. This possibility\nconsist in the fact that the throat represent a spacelike boundary of the spacetime. This\nsolution is only viable in the asymptotic hidden wormhole case as the boundary has to\nbe reached only asymptotically for infinite value of the affine parameter in order to be\nconsistent with geodesic completeness. The fact that the boundary is spacelike allows\nall the Cauchy hypersurfaces reach r = 0. Anyway, in practice, it is difficult to devise\n\n\n\n4.3. CONCLUSIONS 73\n\nFigure 4.5: One-way hidden wormhole with some lines of constant r depicted. In order\nto avoid issues with topology change the metric must fail to be analytic in at least two\npoints. Such points are encircled for clarity.\n\na geometry that realizes this configuration.\n\n4.3 Conclusions\n\nIn this chapter we have studied the viability of the non-singular black hole solutions\nwe have introduced in the previous chapter. In Fig. 4.6 we consider again the table\npresent in Fig. 3.14 adding an extra line containing the information regarding the issues\nassociated with each class of solution. The most immediate consequence of our analy-\nsis is that one cannot just naively assert that singularity regularization will solve the\noutstanding issues of black hole physics without introducing additional aspects that,\nafter a thorough analysis, may lead to radical surprises for our theoretical and obser-\nvational understanding of black holes. In fact, the remarkable result is that there is\nno fully “safe” option: all classes of geometries display internal inconsistencies (insta-\nbilities, topology change or incompatibilities with semiclassical physics), except for the\nparticular case of evanescent black holes in short timescales. However, the timescales in\nthe latter case are so short (of the order of the light-crossing time) that this possibility\nentails a complete rethinking of the concept of black hole. Indeed, a fast bounce would\nnot be obviously at odds with observations only if the matter remains close enough to\nthe would-be-horizon, or if this process constitutes a transient phase after which the\nobject relaxes to a stable state (maybe horizonless to avoid the self-consistency issues\nof the other classes of geometries).\n\nLet us stress that, although we have assumed an everywhere well defined geometry,\nour analysis is valuable also when this is not the case and it allows us to understand how\nto construct singularity regularization scenario that solves the self consistency issues\nraised in this chapter by allowing for region where an effective geometry cannot be\n\n\n\n74 CHAPTER 4. ON THE VIABILITY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nFigure 4.6: The table summarizes the classes of the allowed geometries and the issues\nassociated with them.\n\ndefined. Interesting examples are constituted by the pictures studied in [167, 168, 169]\nwhere the geometry is defined almost everywhere but in a small region, a feature that\nallows these models to escape some of the self consistency issues raised here.\n\nFinally, it is important to stress that, while the analysis was performed in spherical\nsymmetry, the language we have used is well adapted to deal with the more realistic\nsituation in which this simplifying assumption is lost. In fact, the only place in which\nspherical symmetry was explicitly used was to derive the conditions in Eq. C.2 which\nwere necessary to prove the existence of an inner horizon for the classes of evanescent\nor everlasting horizon. A generalization of this result to the non spherically symmetric\ncase would be enough to generalize the whole analysis.\n\n\n\nChapter 5\n\nPhenomenology of non-singular black holes\n\nAfter having discussed a geometrical classification of non-singular spacetimes in chapter\n3 we have studied in detail their internal consistency in chapter 4. We have seen\nthat the regularization schemes without possible phenomenological observation are very\ndifficult to make self consistent. This gives us motivation to look into the possible\nobservational windows that could discriminate between singular black holes and non-\nsingular alternatives.\n\nThe discussion in this chapter is mainly based on P4 and it is divided in two main\nparts. The first part consists of a brief review of the different scenarios that have\nbeen proposed in the literature in order to avoid theoretical problems that are inher-\nent to classical and semiclassical black holes (e.g., the singularity or information loss\nproblems), including a discussion about their collocation into the classes of geometries\nprovided in chapter 3. The second part of the chapter focuses on the observational tests\nthat are available to probe the structure of astrophysical black holes, with the goal of\nemphasizing how close we are to testing the existence of all the relevant mathematical\nelements of these objects as described by general relativity, and parametrizing the room\nthat is still available for alternatives in terms of a set of phenomenological parameters.\nThe meaning of these phenomenological parameters is illustrated by comparison with\nthe scenarios described in Sec. 5.1.\n\n5.1 A taxonomy of proposals\n\n5.1.1 Regular black holes\n\nThe first class that we need to introduce is the one of regular black holes which has been\ndiscussed in detail in the previous chapter. As we have discussed, the main property\nof this type of geometry is that the singular core of a classical black hole spacetime\nis replaced by a smooth spacetime region. In order to make the curvature invariants\nfinite everywhere, we are forced to introduce a inner horizon that pose stability issues.\nTherefore, the situation for this class of geometry can be summarized as follow:\n\n• There might be small correction to the classical geometries in regions which are\nobservationally available. However the existence of such deviation is not necessary\n\n75\n\n\n\n76 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\n• The inner horizon is generically unstable and small perturbations can have large\neffect on the geometry.\n\nTherefore, while we have discussed that it is difficult to make this geometry self con-\nsistent, we will see in the rest of the chapter that this model is very poor from a\nphenomenological point of view.\n\n5.1.2 Bouncing geometries\n\nInstead of focusing on the description of the regular geometries that may describe black\nholes once formed, let us now analyze in more detail the fate of one of the main actors in\nthe formation process: matter. Black holes are formed from collapsing lumps of matter.\nIt is therefore of utmost importance to understand the physical mechanisms that may\nprevent these lumps of matter from collapsing completely, resulting in a singularity,\nand the implications that follow.\n\nIn practical terms, we can divide the spacetime of a collapsing (spherically symmet-\nric) distribution of matter in two regions: the external one, which is idealized as being\nvacuum, and the internal one which describes the interior of the collapsing matter. In\nthe previous section we have been dealing mainly with the external geometry. However,\nthe physics of the internal geometry is important as well, and in fact it might be the\nmost important one regarding the regularization of the singularity [170].\n\nThe non-singular core of the regular black holes discussed above can be understood\nas the result of the tendency of matter towards collapsing, together with the existence\nof repulsive forces of quantum-mechanical nature that are triggered when Planckian\ncurvatures are reached. However, from this perspective it seems unnatural that these\ntwo tendencies cancel exactly in order to stabilize the collapsing distribution of matter\nat a fixed radius no matter what the initial conditions are. Dynamically, it seems more\nnatural to expect that the existence of a repulsive core would lead generally to bouncing\ngeometries (while asymptotically stationary solutions with a small core may be reached\nfor very particular values of the initial conditions).\n\nThis kind of bouncing behavior was first studied in [104, 105, 171, 172], but has been\nindependently proposed more recently in scenarios inspired by emergent gravity [173,\n135, 136] and loop quantum gravity [134, 137]. Regardless of the special details of\neach particular implementation of this idea, there are two aspects that are robust (see\nhowever [174, 175, 176, 177, 178, 179] and [180, 181] for alternative bouncing scenarios):\n\n• Timescale [182]: concerning the timescale of a bounce of matter we need to\nseparate the discussion in two cases. In the first case the timescale for the bounce\n(suitably defined in terms of the proper time of the relevant observers) is shorter\nthan the (naive) evaporation time of the black hole,\n\nτB < τ (3) ∼ tP(M/mP)3 (5.1)\n\nPlausible values for this timescale are\n\nτB = τ (j) ∼ tP(M/mP)j, j = 1, 2. (5.2)\n\nThese two values verify τ (j) � τ (3). Let us note that these timescales are generally\nmultiplied by logarithmic factors that have not been written explicitly but become\n\n\n\n5.1. A TAXONOMY OF PROPOSALS 77\n\nrelevant for certain values of the parameters involved.\nThe second possibility is that the timescale scale of the bounce, in absence of\nHawking radiation, would be larger than the timescale of the evaporation time of\nthe black hole [169]. In this case the time evolution matches the one of a black\nhole evaporating in semiclassical gravity until it reaches Plankian size. Only at\nthat point the physics responsible for the bounce becomes relevant and we have a\nbounce of a Plankian size blak hole into a white hole. We are not going to focus\nmuch on this possibility in the following as it is very poor from a phenomenological\npoint of view due to the huge timescale of the process.\n\n• Modifications of the near-horizon geometry [135, 137]: the external geometry of\nthe spacetimes in which the bounce of the distribution of matter can be observed\nby external observers in the original asymptotic region must include modifications\nof the near-horizon geometry, even if the bounce of matter takes place much\ndeeper inside the gravitational potential well (roughly, when the density of the\nradius of the collapsing structure is Planckian). The ultimate reason is that\nthese geometries must interpolate between a black-hole-like geometry and a white-\nhole-like geometry. The only continuous way to define this interpolation involves\nmodifications of the geometry up to a certain radius r? > rs, the value of which\nis typically constrained by (r? − rs) . rs. This point can be illustrated using\nPainlevé-Gullstrand coordinates:\n\nds2 = −dt2 + [dr − fv(r)dt]2 + r2dΩ2, (5.3)\n\nwhere f = ∓1 correspond to a black hole or a white hole in these coordinates,\nrespectively, and v(r) =\n\n√\nrs/r. In order to modify the geometry continuously\n\nfrom one case to the other, a function f(t, r) that interpolates between these\nvalues and which is nonzero at r = rs, is needed.\n\nThe shortest possible time for the bounce to take place is τB = τ (1), as proposed\noriginally in [173, 135, 136]. Another possibility, conjectured in [137, 183], has τB = τ (2).\nThe second timescale is small if compared with τ (3), but is still quite large so that, for\na black hole to be exploding today, it must be a primordial black hole (though with\ndifferent mass than in the case of regular black holes for which the relevant timescale is\nassumed to be τ (3)). So far it does not seem possible to justify the timescale τB = τ (2)\n\nthrough specific calculations such as the one in [183], while the timescale τB = τ (1)\n\narises in two independent calculations [172, 184].\nRegarding possible observational channels, the second feature above (the modifi-\n\ncations of the near-horizon geometry) might seem the most promising one at a first\nglance. Note that, in contraposition to regular black holes, these modifications are now\na must. However, let us note that in the most natural scenarios, the modifications in\nthese geometries are by construction O(1) only after the time τB.\n\nThis implies that, if we are probing the geometry with physical processes during an\ninterval of time ∆t (which could be, for instance, the time that an observed photon\ntook to go through this region of the geometry), any cumulative effects due to these\ndeviations from the classical geometries would be suppressed by the dimensionless quo-\ntient ∆t/τB. For τB = τ (2) this dimensionless number will be generally small. Hence,\nit is reasonable to think that, unless we are considering physical processes with typical\n\n\n\n78 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\ntimescales comparable to the timescale of the bounce τB, it would be difficult to use\nthese processes in order to learn about the geometry. It might be possible however\nthat there exist non-trivial mechanisms that act to amplify the value of the number\n∆t/τB when the latter is small, though at the moment this is just a conjecture. On the\nother hand, if one was able to perform experiments which monitor the evolution of the\nblack hole during a time interval ∆t ∼ τB, the very end of the bounce process would\nbe observable, which would certainly be more dramatic.\n\nIn consequence, in the absence of mechanisms that can compensate the small quo-\ntient ∆t/τB, (looking for these amplification mechanisms would be an interesting ex-\nercise), the most promising observable feature of models with τB = τ (2) is, again, the\none associated with the end of the dynamical process; for regular black holes this was\nthe evaporation process, but here is the very bounce of matter. The associated physics\nresides simply in the timescale τB, which for instance controls the typical size of the\nblack holes for which these effects would be observable today.\n\nLet us anyway assume that bounces with a timescale τB take place in nature. One\nis then forced to answer the question: what happens after the bounce? There are\nessentially two possibilities. One possibility is that the bounce releases all the available\nenergy and matter such that the black hole dissipates completely. This would imply that\nblack holes disappear in a timescale τB, which can be compatible with observations only\nif τB is large enough. This possibility is the one considered for instance in [185, 186]\nand, as we have discussed, from a phenomenological perspective the most promising\nobservational opportunity is the detection of this cataclysmic event (see Sec. 5.3.5 for\na more detailed discussion).\n\nA second (and, arguably, more natural) possibility is that part of the energy con-\ntent is released after the bounce, leaving a remnant that may again undergo renewed\ngravitational collapse [136, 184]. In this scenario, it may be possible that a different\nkind of horizonless equilibrium configuration is reached, so that the bounce itself (which\nmay occur several times) would be just a transient. This second possibility is arguably\nmore rich observationally, as both the transient phase with timescale roughly τB and\nthe horizonless stable phase would have distinctive observational signatures which we\nshall now explore in the next section.\n\n5.1.3 Quasi-black holes\n\nIn order to encompass different alternatives in the literature, let us define a static\nand spherically symmetric quasi-black hole in a rough way as a spacetime satisfying\nthe following conditions: (i) the geometry is Schwarzschild above a given radius R\nthat is defined to be the radius of the object, (ii) the geometry for r ≤ R is not\nSchwarzschild, and (iii) there are no event or trapping horizons. In other words, this\nkind of geometry is qualitatively similar to that of a relativistic star, but with a typical\nradius of the structure R that can be arbitrarily close to rs, hence violating the isotropic-\npressure Buchdahl-Bondi bound [187, 188] (let us note in passing that including pressure\nanisotropy permits one to attain more compact configurations that are not limited\nby the isotropic Buchdahl-Bondi bound [189].) In fact, in this section we consider\nobjects that can be characterized as having a surface. Configurations that fall within\nthe definition above but do not have a surface (wormholes) are described in the next\n\n\n\n5.1. A TAXONOMY OF PROPOSALS 79\n\nsection.\nThere are several proposals in the literature for this kind of geometry (including\n\ngravastars [190, 191, 192], fuzzballs [193, 194], and black stars [195, 196]), but all of\nthem present severe restrictions. In general terms, it is possible to prescribe (or derive\nfrom first principles [197]) this kind of geometry only when the outer geometry is that\nof non-rotating or slowly rotating black holes. Most importantly, there is virtually no\nknowledge about the dynamics of these objects; not only there are large gaps in the\nunderstanding of their possible formation mechanisms, but also of their behavior under\nother dynamical processes that they may undergo after formation. For instance, it is\ngenerally not clear how these objects interact with regular matter. There have been\nstudies proposing Hawking radiation as the main ingredient to form these objects [198,\n199, 200, 201, 202, 203], but these proposals share a number of problems (e.g., [204,\n205, 206]) that raise substantial doubts about their validity. It is also worth stressing\nthat quasi-black holes violate the assumptions of no-hair theorems (e.g., [207]), so that\nit is in principle possible that the external geometry is different than the Schwarzschild\ngeometry in static (but not spherically symmetric) situations or the Kerr geometry in\nthe rotating case. In particular, while in the static case such deviations are very strongly\nsuppressed [208], this is no longer true for the rotating case [209].\n\nIf quasi-black holes are formed, this would require the existence of a transient before\nthe system can settle down in this kind of configuration. The details of this transient\nare still largely unknown and would probably be rather complex, but in a first approach\nwe can parametrize our ignorance in terms of another timescale, namely a relaxation\ntimescale (in the bouncing scenario discussed above, this scale would be controlled by\nτ (1), with logarithmic corrections depending on the values of certain parameters [182]).\nThis timescale could also show up in other events such as, for instance, the merger\nof two of these objects. As emphasized above, it is not known whether or not it is\npossible that the result of the merger of two quasi-black holes is still a quasi-black hole.\nHowever, if this is the case, it is reasonable to assume that the final quasi-black hole\nstate is reached after this relaxation timescale.\n\nAside from these transients, these objects are expected to lead to distinctive phe-\nnomenological signatures arising from interaction with light, matter and gravitational\nwaves — due to the large modifications of the geometry starting at r = R. In par-\nticular, while black holes are perfectly absorptive, quasi-black holes do not necessarily\nsatisfy this property (although there are again many uncertainties in this regard). Note,\nhowever, that any physical observable (i.e., a quantity that can be measured in an ex-\nperiment) is expected to go back continuously to its value for a black hole in the limit\nin which µ→ 0, where\n\nµ = 1− rs\n\nR\n. (5.4)\n\nThis observation would seem to imply that, for extremely small µ, all observables should\ndiffer by very small amounts from the values they would take for a classical black hole\n(we can think about performing a Taylor expansion on the parameter µ). This depends,\nhowever, on the functional dependence of observables on µ. We will see that different\nobservables display different behaviors (e.g., polynomial or logarithmic) with respect to\nµ.\n\nIn order to develop some intuition on the typical values of µ, let us make explicit\nthe relation between µ and the distance between the surface and the would-be horizon.\n\n\n\n80 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nFor µ� 1, and if the surface is at a proper radial distance `� rs from rs, one has\n\nµ ' 1\n\n4\n\n(\n`\n\nrs\n\n)2\n\n' 7× 10−78\n\n(\nM�\nM\n\n)2(\n`\n\n`P\n\n)2\n\n. (5.5)\n\nIt is illustrative to consider for instance ` ∼ `P and the mass corresponding to Sgr A*,\nM = 4× 106 M�, which yields µ ∼ 10−91.\n\n5.1.4 Wormholes\n\nWormholes are tunnels connecting different regions of spacetime and supported by large\namounts of exotic matter or energy [210, 211, 212, 213, 191, 214]. The most interesting\nclass of wormholes are the so-called traversable wormholes, that can be maintained open\nfor enough time to allow geodesics to travel through them. Let us focus for simplicity on\nMorris-Thorne wormholes [215, 216]: time independent, non-rotating and spherically\nsymmetric solutions of general relativity (with a suitable matter content) describing\na bridge/passage between two asymptotically flat regions, not necessarily in the same\nuniverse. These objects are described by the metric\n\nds2 = −e−2φ(x)dt2 + dx2 + r2(x)dΩ2, (5.6)\n\nwhere x ∈ (−∞,+∞) and one requires the absence of event horizons and metric com-\nponents that are at least C2 in x. Asymptotic flatness for x→ ±∞ requires\n\nlim\nx→±∞\n\nr(x)\n\n|x|\n= 1 (5.7)\n\nand\nlim\n\nx→±∞\nφ(x) = Φ± ∈ R. (5.8)\n\nOn the other hand, the radius at the wormhole throat is r0 = min {r(x)}, which can\nalways be chosen to be at x = 0. The geometry (5.6) corresponds to flat spacetime,\nup to small corrections, far away from the throat. It is nevertheless possible to modify\nthe external geometry so that it describes the gravitational field of a massive source, as\nin the Schwarzschild geometry [217, 218], or also to include rotation (e.g., [219]) which\nwould be eventually necessary in order to describe realistic astrophysical black holes.\nMoreover, as in the case of quasi-black holes, the no-hair theorems do not directly\napply to these objects, so that even in static situations it may be possible that higher\nmultipoles take nonzero values.\n\nThis metric is a solution of the (non-vacuum) Einstein equations that requires a\nstress-energy tensor that violates the null energy condition, which states the positivity\nof the product Tµνk\n\nµkν for any null-like vector kµ (this implies that the weak, strong\nand dominant energy conditions are violated as well [210, 220]). Hence, the matter\nand energy content that keeps the throat open cannot have standard properties. These\nexotic properties may find a justification in the quantum properties of matter, when the\nlatter is described in terms of quantum fields. Quantum effects in curved backgrounds\nand, in particular, the polarization of the quantum vacuum, may provide the necessary\nstress-energy tensor to support wormholes [221, 222].\n\n\n\n5.1. A TAXONOMY OF PROPOSALS 81\n\nIt is generally accepted that standard particles of matter and waves can cross\ntraversable wormholes without experiencing appreciable interactions with the exotic\nmatter opening the throat, although there is virtually no knowledge about the possible\ninteractions between standard matter and the source of the wormhole geometry. Hence,\nhere we will consider that the interior of wormholes is essentially transparent, but keep-\ning in mind that a deeper analysis of this issue would be desirable. This assumption\nwould be certainly more reasonable if the exotic matter inside the wormhole comes en-\ntirely from the polarization of the quantum vacuum. This traversability property (or,\nin other words, the lack of a physical surface) represents the main difference between\nwormholes and quasi-black holes as defined in the previous section. Aside from this\ndifference, these two kinds of objects share several properties. In particular, most of (if\nnot all) the uncertainties regarding the understanding of the dynamics of quasi-black\nholes and their formation mechanisms equally apply to wormholes.\n\n5.1.5 From local to global classification on geometries.\n\nAt this point we have provided two different classification of non-singular geometries,\none introduced in chapter 3 and the one introduced just now. We now want to provide\na link between the two classifications and we are going to do so by analyzing one by one\nthe geometries in chapter 3 and checking where they are placed in the classification just\nintroduced. As we will see, there is no one to one link between the classes of geometry\nof the two classifications. This is not surprising as the classifications are based on very\ndifferent aspects of the spacetime. The classification provided in chapter 3 is based on\nlocal properties of the geometry close to the trapping region. On the other side the\nclassification just introduced is based on global properties of the geometries as seen\nfrom a asymptotic observer. Although the discussion of this section might be extracted\nfrom chapter 3, we include some key point here for convenience.\n\nEvanescent horizon and everlasting horizon\n\nLet us start from the class of evanescent horizons and everlasting horizon. These classes\nare characterized by the presence of an inner and a trapping horizon that merge at some\npoint in the case of evanescent horizon or that reaches S + in the case of everlasting\nhorizon. The first possible global geometry associated to these classes is the one cor-\nresponding to a regular black hole which eventually evaporates leading to a spacetime\nwithout trapping horizon or which never disappears and either grows or stays stationary.\n\nIn the case of evanescent horizon there is another possibility which corresponds to\na bouncing geometry. In this case the outer and the inner horizon are formed during\nthe gravitational collapse and they disappear during the bounce. In this case, after the\ndisappearance of the trapping region, an antitrapping region is formed (this possibility\nis depicted in Fig. 3.8) where the geometry is locally the one of a white hole. This is\na clear example of how the same local properties at the trapping region correspond to\ntwo very different global geometries.\n\n\n\n82 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nOne-way hidden wormhole and asymptotic hidden wormhole\n\nAs the names suggest, one-way hidden wormholes and asymptotic hidden wormholes\nmay correspond to a global geometry of a wormhole which can be traversed only in one\ndirection as the throat is hidden beyond a trapping horizon1. Anyway, in this chapter\nwe are mainly focused on traversable wormholes as they have a richer phenomenology.\nFrom the phenomenological point of view, this classes of geometries are more similar\nto regular black holes than to traversable wormholes.\n\nAs before, the one-way hidden wormhole can correspond to a bouncing geometry. In\nthis case, matter bounces in the throat of the “wormhole” directly into an antitrapping\nregion. As explained in Sec. 3.3 and depicted in Fig. 4.5, to realize this possibility the\ngeometry cannot be defined everywhere.\n\nOther geometries\n\nLet us finally stress that the quasi-black hole and the traversable wormhole classes do\nnot have any corresponding geometry in the classification of chapter 3 for the very\nsimple reason that these classes do not posses a trapping region.\n\n5.2 Phenomenological parametrization of\n\ndeviations from general relativity\n\nFrom the perspective of astrophysical observations using electromagnetic waves, black\nholes are regions in spacetime that can be detected only indirectly through their gravi-\ntational effects on matter surrounding them. This has changed with gravitational wave\nastronomy. However, observationally is not clear that these regions of spacetime corre-\nspond strictly to black holes in the sense of general relativity. This is a fundamental\nquestion regardless of the stance taken with respect to the different alternatives in\nSec. 5.1. Only a detailed analysis of this question would make possible separating what\nis really known from the aspects that can be only inferred from (most of the time,\npartial) theoretical arguments.\n\nIn order to illustrate this point and make quantitative statements, let us introduce\na set of phenomenological parameters encapsulating deviations from the behavior ex-\npected in general relativity. We will compare the physics associated with each of these\nparameters with the theoretical models reviewed in Sec. 5.1, and then consider how\nthese parameters can be constrained observationally. These parameters are functions\nof the physical quantities characterizing the most general black hole geometry that is\nexpected to be relevant for astrophysical scenarios, namely the Kerr geometry [223]:\nthe mass M and the angular momentum J (that we do not deal explicitly with for\nsimplicity). Let us start with two timescales:\n\n1. Lifetime, τ+: The timescale in which a black hole with mass M , in vacuum,\ndisappears completely (due either to Hawking radiation, or some other effect).\n\n1Note that in the case of asymptotic hidden wormholes case the throat is only reached asymptotically\n\n\n\n5.2. PHENOMENOLOGICAL PARAMETRIZATION 83\n\n2. Relaxation, τ−: is the amount of time in which O(1) transient effects taking place\nafter violent dynamical processes dissipate (formation of the black hole, merger,\netc.). Typically this can be identified with the imaginary part of the lowest quasi-\nnormal mode of the final-state system (e.g., [224]).\n\nThese two timescales describe the interval of time t ∈ [τ−, τ+] in which the system is\nexpected to be evolving slowly enough that it can maintain stable structural properties.\nWithin this time interval, it is meaningful to define the following parameters:\n\n3. Size, R = rs(1 + ∆): Value of the radius below which the modifications to the\nclassical geometry are O(1). We will use the more convenient parameter ∆ ≥ 0.\nNote that this parameter is related to µ in Eq. (5.4) as µ = ∆/(1+∆). For ∆� 1\nit follows that µ ' ∆, so that these two parameters can be used interchangeably.\n\n4. Absorption coefficient, κ: Measures the fraction of the energy that is semi-permanently\nlost inside the region r ≤ R. This can be due to the inelastic interaction with\nthe horizonless object, when exciting internal degrees of freedom in the bulk, or\nsimply due to its propagation into some other spacetime region (consider, for\ninstance, a wormhole).\n\n5. Elastic reflection coefficient, Γ: If there is a certain amount of energy falling\nonto the object and reaching r = R, this coefficient measures the portion that is\nreflected at r ≥ R due to elastic interactions (i.e., energy which is not absorbed\nand bounces back).\n\n6. Inelastic reflection coefficient, Γ̃: Measures the portion of energy that is temporar-\nily absorbed by the object and then re-emitted. That is, it measures the amount\nof energy that is inelastically reflected. It is related to κ and Γ by Γ̃ = 1− κ− Γ.\n\n7. Tails, ε(t, r)� 1: Modifications of the geometry that decay with radial distance,\ntypically polynomial but possibly modulated by functions of compact support.\nHence, there might be a maximum radius such that ε(t, r ≥ r?) = 0. In principle\none would need to introduce a series of functions εJ(t, r) to describe different\ndecaying tails for different coefficients of the metric [225]. For r? =∞ these tails\nwould produce nonzero values of higher-order multipole moments (e.g., [207]).\n\nThese phenomenological parameters (and function) allow us to characterize our igno-\nrance about the actual properties of astrophysical black holes: for a black hole in general\nrelativity,\n\nτ+ =∞, τ− ∼ 10M, µ = 0,\nκ = 1, Γ = 0, ε(t, r) = 0.\n\n(5.9)\n\nRegarding the first parameter τ+, we expect it to be at most τ+ = τ (3) as defined in\nEq. (5.1) due to Hawking radiation. But this is still infinite for any practical purposes\nfor astrophysical black holes. The estimate for τ− is obtained taking the inverse of the\nimaginary part of the lowest quasi-normal mode which governs the damping rate of\nperturbations [226, 227]. The rest of the parameters are unchanged in the semiclassical\napproximation. Hence testing the (semiclassical) black hole picture essentially means\nconstraining the value of these parameters. The closer these parameters are to their\n\n\n\n84 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nvalues in Eq. (5.9), the more confident we will be that astrophysical black holes are\nclassical black holes (especially if we are able to discard some regions containing values\nassociated with known theoretical models). The corresponding values for the various\nclasses introduced in Sec. 5.1 are given in Table 5.1. In the rest of the chapter, we\ndiscuss the most stringent bounds that can be currently placed on these parameters.\n\nIt is always possible to introduce even more additional parameters or functional\nrelations, such as frequency-dependent values of µ(ω) and Γ(ω). However, in practical\nterms this just implies that we are including additional parameters that would provide\nmore freedom to play with the observational data. The set we introduced above is\nminimal, but still interesting enough to give a detailed picture of the observational\nstatus of black holes. In practice, the only additional freedom that we will consider\nis the possibility that some of these coefficients are different for electromagnetic and\ngravitational waves.\n\nModel τ− τ+ ∆ κ Γ Γ̃ ε(t, r)\n\nClassical black hole ∼ 10M ∞ 0 1 0 0 0\nRegular black hole ∼ 10M U 0 1 0 0 MD\n\nBouncing geometries MD MD 0 1 0 0 r? = O(rs)\nQuasi-black hole MD/U ∞ > 0 MD/U MD/U 1− κ− Γ U\n\nWormhole U ∞ > 0 MD 1− κ 0 U\n\nTable 5.1: Values of the phenomenological parameters for the different classes of black\nhole mimickers. MD stands for Model Dependent and U for Unknown, whereas MD/U\nemphasizes that the quantity is model dependent but at the moment there is no partic-\nular model within the class that is able to predict specific values for the corresponding\nparameters.\n\n5.3 Electromagnetic waves\n\nThe presence of dark distributions of mass that do not themselves emit electromagnetic\nradiation can be indirectly detected by their gravitational effects on the surrounding\nluminous matter. This has been traditionally the strategy followed in order to hunt for\nblack holes in astronomical data. This electromagnetic radiation can also be used to\nprobe the gravitational field around these dark distributions of mass and even constrain\nsome of their surface properties. In this section we review the most powerful observa-\ntions and reevaluate their strength on the basis of the parametrization introduced in\nSec. 5.2 above.\n\n5.3.1 Orbiting stars\n\nThe first kind of situation we shall consider can be idealized as a many-body system\nof compact distributions of matter that are interacting gravitationally, with at least\none element that is not (appreciably) emitting electromagnetic radiation. The simplest\npossible configuration would be a binary system composed of a regular star and a dark\n\n\n\n5.3. ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES 85\n\ncompanion, an example of which is A0620-00 [228] (which is also the closest system of\nthis kind to the solar system). The electromagnetic radiation coming from the luminous\nstar can be used in order to deduce the mass of its companion through the so-called mass\nfunction [229, 230], which in the case of A0620-00 yields 6.60±0.25 M� [231]. This value\nis well above the maximum theoretically allowed mass for neutron stars [15, 232, 233].\nWhile the mass parameter can be extracted, all the phenomenological parameters in-\ntroduced in Sec. 5.2 remain virtually unconstrained (or weakly constrained if compared\nwith other observations detailed below). Hence, observations of these binary systems of\nstellar-mass objects justify the existence of dark and compact distributions of matter\nthat are not neutron stars, but not much more information about the intrinsic properties\nof these structures can be extracted.\n\nThe situation may improve if the mass of the dark object increases by several orders\nof magnitude, which would typically imply moving from a binary system to a many-\nbody system. The larger number of luminous stars improves the statistics and therefore\nallows placing stronger constraints. On the one hand, there is only a single system\nof this kind that is accessible to current technology: the center of our own galaxy.\nSagittarius A* (Sgr A*) is an astronomical radio source at the center of the Milky Way,\nwhich has long been considered to be the location of an astrophysical black hole [234].\nOn the other hand, this region has been extensively studied during more than two\ndecades [235, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240], with the result that the trajectories of a large\nnumber of orbiting stars are known with excellent precision [241, 242]. A sizable portion\nof the claim that Sgr A* is a black hole comes in fact from these observations.\n\nThe main parameters which are fixed by these observations are the mass of Sgr A*\nand our distance from it. Precise values and errors can be found in the above references,\nbut roughly these are given by M = 4×106 M� and d = 8 kpc, with errors of the order\nof 1%. The measure of the distance obtained from tracking these stars, which is based\non the geometric method proposed in [243], is in good agreement with the results of\nother methods (e.g., [244]).\n\nMore interesting for the present discussion is the remark that these observations\nalso constrain the size of Sgr A*, on the basis that these stars have been observed\nto travel freely without colliding with the central ultracompact object (UCO in the\nfollowing). The values of the periastron in these orbits provide upper bounds to the\nvalue of R (equivalently, ∆). For the purposes of estimating the order of magnitude of\nthis quantity, it is enough to consider the star S2 (also known as S0-2) [236, 237] which\nis one of the most precisely tracked. The periastron of S2 is 17 light hours, while the\nSchwarzschild radius of Sgr A* is 40 light seconds. Therefore,\n\n∆ ≤ O(103). (5.10)\n\nThis first bound is a very crude bound which will be considerably tightened using other\nobservational channels. Given that this kind of observation is essentially geometric in\nnature, the remaining phenomenological parameters that describe the physical intrinsic\nproperties of the dark object remain unconstrained in practice. This continues to be\ntrue for more refined observations of the galactic center [245] that allow one to improve\nthe constraint (5.10) by about three orders of magnitude. In the future it may however\nbe possible to constrain the tails ε(t, r), though this would require gathering data for\nseveral stars with much shorter orbital periods [246], and which remain close enough\n\n\n\n86 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nto Sgr A* [247, 248]. For instance, measurements of the redshift of S2, and their\nincompatibility with Newtonian mechanics, have been recently reported [249]. Moreover, the distances involved in the orbits of the\nstars discussed in the previous section are large in comparison with the gravitational\nradius of the Sgr A*. However, another source of information comes from matter\ninfalling on the UCO. Moreover, for M & 108M� (this value for the order of magnitude\ntakes into account the relevant relativistic features), tidal forces are not strong enough,\nso that main-sequence stars are able to reach the Schwarzschild radius while keeping\ntheir integrity [256, 257].\n\nThat tidal disruption events (TDEs) have been observed for UCOs ofM ∼ 106M� [258]\nleads to a first upper bound rs(1 + ∆) ≤ rT for these UCOs [253]. (5.21).\n\n5.3.3 Accretion disks around supermassive black holes\n\nThe most stringent constraints on some of the phenomenological parameters come from\nthe information about the average amount of infalling matter per unit of time onto\nUCOs. The value of this accretion rate Ṁ is generally more stable than the (much\nhigher, but also more variable) accretion rate associated by the direct capture of an\nindividual star, which are also much more sparse events. Estimations of the accretion\nrate for these objects depend on the physics of accretion disks [261, 262, 263], as the\naccretion rate is typically estimated from the luminosity of the disk. As we have done\nin the previous section, we will not discuss the model-dependent features behind these\nestimations. We will just assume that it is possible to obtain a measure of the order\nof magnitude of Ṁ , focusing our discussion on the (already rich) physics that can be\ndescribed in terms of Ṁ and our phenomenological parameters introduced previously.\nMore accurate estimations of Ṁ would just permit to refine the observational bounds\ngiven below.\n\nLet us start summarizing the main argument that has been invoked several times in\nthe literature [264, 265, 266, 267, 268]. We can reduce this argument to its essentials\nby considering the system composed by the UCO and the accretion disk as a composite\nsystem in which energy is exchanged between its two components. The accretion rate\nṀ measures the energy that the accretion disk is pumping into the UCO. On the other\nhand, the quantity that is interesting in order to test the nature of the UCO is the\nenergy that the UCO emits by itself, as this measures the reaction of the UCO to its\ninteraction with the accretion disk. Ideally, one would like to disentangle the two fluxes\nof energy and measure independently the radiation emitted by the UCO. However, this\nis not yet observationally possible (and, as we discuss below, might be even impossible\nin practice due to its extreme faintness). Therefore, it is necessary to make additional\nassumptions in order to determine the properties of this outgoing energy flux:\n\n1. Thermality: It was pointed out in [264, 265, 266] that the strong lensing of out-\ngoing geodesics emitted at different points in the surface r = R (a phenomenon\nthat we have discussed in Sec. 5.3.2) implies that the surface reaches thermal\nequilibrium on a short timescale. This follows from the fact that different points\nof the surface are strongly coupled. Therefore, we can safely assume that the\nemitted radiation is thermal. This is correct for ∆ ' µ � 1, which means that\nthe arguments in this section hold only in these situations.\n\n2. Steady state: The only parameter to be fixed after accepting the assumption\nabove is the temperature T∞ of the emitted radiation. The only possible model-\nindependent argument to fix the power of the outgoing radiation is invoking con-\nservation of energy and assuming that a steady state between the two components\n(UCO and accretion disk) has been reached, so that the two fluxes of energy carry\nthe same amount of energy. This is a strong assumption that must be appropri-\nately justified and that, as we see below, fails due to several competing effects.\n\nIf these two assumptions hold, then the emission of the UCO can be calculated:\nIt is given by a thermal distribution with a temperature determined by the accretion\n\n\n\n5.3. ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES 91\n\nrate Ṁ . For Sgr A*, this radiation should be bright in the infrared, but it has been\nshown [264, 265, 266, 267] that the emission of Sgr A* in the infrared is about 10−2\n\ntimes this theoretical estimate (see [268] for the same argument applied to M87). The\nconclusions by these authors is that it is not possible that Sgr A* has a surface, and\ntherefore that it must have a horizon. This is a very strong claim, as it would discard\nevery possible value of ∆, except for ∆ = 0 which corresponds to a black hole. Even\nsub-Planckian values of ∆ would be discarded. Let us now analyze in careful detail\nhow this conclusion comes about — so to dispel any possible doubt concerning its\nrobustness.\n\nAn obvious starting point for this revision are the two assumptions mentioned above.\nIndeed, as we show below, the Achilles’ heel of this argument is the steady state as-\nsumption. This assumption is not valid for sufficiently compact UCOs; which leads\nto constraints on the maximum compactness of the object. This observation has been\nmade only recently [253, 269]. It is worth mentioning that even recent reviews on this\ntopic such as [234] still quote [264, 265, 266, 267, 268] as definitive evidence for the\nexistence of event horizons, thus ignoring this loophole.2 Our novel contribution to this\ndiscussion is the introduction (in terms of the phenomenological parameters defined in\nSec. 5.2) of additional physical features that are expected to be relevant in realistic\nscenarios. As we discuss below, the introduction of these additional physical aspects\nmake these constraints remarkably weaker.\n\nLet us consider a simple calculation of the time at which steady state is reached (see\nfigure 5.2). The initial configuration is given by an accretion disk that starts pumping\nenergy into the UCO, the energy emission of the latter being negligible before accretion\nbegins. We will start considering the most favorable case in which the UCO returns all\nthe accreted energy as thermal radiation, and evaluate the timescale at which steady\nstate can be achieved. Hence, the accretion rate onto the UCO is zero for t < 0 (this\nis just an irrelevant choice of the origin of time) and Ṁ ∈ R for t ∈ [0, T ], where the\ntimescale T is short enough so that the approximation of constant Ṁ is reasonable\n(more details below). For simplicity, we assume that all propagating energy is carried\nalong null geodesics, and also restrict the discussion to spherically symmetric situations.\nThe amount of energy emitted per unit time by the UCO, Ė, is measured at the location\nof the accretion disk r = Rdisk. Our goal is describing its evolution for t ≥ 0. There are\ntwo effects to keep into account. First of all, the energy emitted Ė remains negligible\nuntil the first ingoing radial null geodesics can bounce back at the surface r = R and\nreturn to the accretion disk. This time can be directly evaluated using the Schwarzschild\nmetric as\n\nTbounce = 2\n\n[\nRdisk −R + rs ln\n\n(\nRdisk − rs\n\nR− rs\n\n)]\n. (5.22)\n\nThis timescale is divergent in the limit R → rs, or equivalently ∆ → 0. However, the\nlogarithmic behavior implies that even for extremely small, but strictly non-vanishing\n∆, Eq. (5.22) would be at most O(10) × rs. Hence, this timescale is essentially the\nlight-crossing time of the UCO.\n\n2It is perhaps worth stressing again that no local observation in space and time will be ever able\nto observe an event horizon, which is intrinsically a teleological notion. At most, observations will be\nable to confirm or exclude the existence of trapping horizons or other local definitions of the boundary\nof black holes. On the right: steady state in which the energy emitted\nfrom the UCO and reaching the accretion disk is Ė = Ṁ .\n\nThis effect alone would delay the moment in which the steady state would be\nreached, but, given the logarithmic dependence, even sub-Planckian values for R − rs\n\nwould be ruled out. However, there is a second effect to keep into account. Outgo-\ning null geodesics are strongly lensed, which implies that a fraction of them do not\nescape and fall again onto the surface of the UCO. This effect is unavoidable due to the\ninherently inelastic nature of the process that is necessary for thermalization to take\nplace: the energy falling from the accretion disk is absorbed by the UCO in the first\nplace, and then emitted. Even assuming spherical symmetry for the infalling energy,\nparticles would not hit the surface and bounce back radially. On the contrary, this\nemission would be almost isotropic in a local frame at rest in the surface, thus implying\nthat only a very small fraction of the initially absorbed energy contributes to Ė. The\nremaining energy follows highly curved trajectories and is reabsorbed by the UCO in\na timescale that can be calculated and is also controlled by its Schwarzschild radius,\nbeing O(10)×rs at most. As\nstressed in Sec. 5.1, most alternative geometries such as the ones of quasi-black holes\nand wormholes are prescribed in static situations. The lack of a framework in which\nto deal with dynamical processes is highly unsatisfactory, and is arguably the main\ncriticism that can be raised against these models on purely theoretical grounds.\n\nOne may expect that it would be difficult to reach model-independent conclusions,\ngiven that different models could display very different dynamical behavior. However,\nit has been shown recently [115] that certain model-independent dynamical considera-\ntions are restrictive enough to lead to a consistency relation that takes the form of a\nlower bound on µ. These model-independent considerations reduce essentially to the\nobservation that the boundary (i.e., surface) of standard celestial objects evolves follow-\ning causal trajectories in spacetime. Note that these trajectories need not correspond\nto actual moving particles, as this growth will be generally caused by the stacking or\npiling up of different particles of matter. But this growth is nevertheless driven by\nphysical interactions, which must propagate in a causal manner. On the other hand,\ntrapping horizons are known to be spacelike for standard accreting matter [120, 130].\nThere is a clear tension between these two different behaviors. This tension results into\ntwo possibilities: (i) the UCO is less compact than a given threshold, so that its surface\ncan grow in a timelike (or at most, null) manner without forming trapping horizons, or\n(ii) the UCO is more compact than this threshold, hence developing trapping horizons\nin a given interval of time that can be calculated.\n\nOption (i) translates into a consistency constraint that depends on the parameter\nµ and the particular model of accreting matter. In spherical symmetry and using the\n\n\n\n98 CHAPTER 5. Let us stress that models for the forma-\ntion of quasi-black holes through short-lived bouncing geometries involve the formation\nof trapping horizons for finite periods of time, that can be as short as τ ∼ τ (1).\n\nContrary to the upper bounds analyzed above, Eq. (5.44) is not affected by the phe-\nnomenological parameters κ and Γ. Since it boils down to a statement about causality,\nthe argument behind Eq.
