The constraint 5.45 has a different nature\nrespect to the other constraints presented in this chapter as there are a couple of\nassumption beyond it. First of all the analysis relies on the assumption that the in-\nteractions involved are local and causal in nature. This might not be the case if large\nquantum effects are involved in the stability of quasi-black holes given that, e.g., all of\nthe energy conditions (including the dominant one) could be violated in these scenarios.\nFurthermore, even if the infalling matter causes the formation of a trapping horizon,\nnothing forbid the trapping horizon to disappear again after the flux of energy has been\nabsorbed.\n\n5.3.4 UCOs shadows\n\nAny discussion regarding the observation of black holes via the EM channel would\nnot be complete without mentioning the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration\nwhich was able to directly detect the light coming from the black hole at the center\nof the M87 galaxy with an angular resolution of the order of the microarcsecond (µas)\n\n\n\n5.3. ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES 99\n\nthus being able to take an image of a black hole for the very first time [7, 8, 9, 10, 11,\n12]. The image revealed the shadow of the UCO3 that is associated with the photon\nsphere [274, 275, 276, 277, 278, 279] (although its size does not directly corresponds\nto the size of the latter due to lensing effects, and is weakly sensitive on its relative\ndistance from the horizon).\n\nThis particular observation has received widespread attention in the astrophysics\ncommunity, and it is often described as “imaging the event horizon of black holes” [280].\nHowever, despite the fact that detecting the shadow is a truly remarkable achievement,\nthe length scale that controls this phenomenon is not the Schwarzschild radius rs, but\nrather the much larger rph = 3rs/2. The gap between these two distances is macroscopic,\nrph − rs = rs/2. In other words, the observation was able to constrain an hypothetical\nboundary of the UCO within its photonsphere and to rule out some specific model which\npresent O(1) modification of the geometry at photonsphere [12], but any object that is\ncompact enough to have a photon sphere (R < rph) should display the necessary physical\ncharacteristics to lead to a similar (and in most cases, indistinguishable) shadow. This\nhas been recently stressed by several authors [281, 207, 282, 283, 284]. Furthermore, let\nus stress that the observation cannot improve on the constrain coming from Eq. 5.43 as\nEHT is blind to the frequency at which an hypothetical surface in thermal equilibrium\nshould emit [12]. Overall, we can conclude that the existence of horizons cannot be\ndecided only on the basis of the observations of the shadows of astrophysical black\nholes.\n\n5.3.5 Bursts\n\nThe search for EM bursts has been claimed in the past as a possible strategy for de-\ntecting the outcome of bouncing geometries. Of course, if the previously discussed\ninstability of regular black holes implies their conversion into bouncing solutions, the\nsame observations will be relevant for constraining them. It is less clear if the possi-\nble conversion of regular black holes or short-lived bounces into quasi-black holes and\nwormholes would imply any transient burst and what it might depend on. It is natural\nto conjecture that, if these objects are the outcomes of a series of rapid bounces with\nshort timescale τ (1), high-energy quasi-periodic bursts with typical frequency 1/τ (1)\n\nshould be expected [136]. However, without detailed models that describe, for instance,\nthe damping of these oscillations, not much more can be said at the moment.\n\nWhile what we said above holds in the case of short-lived bounces of typical timescale\nτ (1), more complex is the case of long-lived bounces with τ = τ (2), for which several phe-\nnomenological studies have been performed in the literature [185, 186, 285, 286]. In this\ncase no relevant signal is expected up to this timescale while two distinct components\nare predicted as being associated to the typical size of the exploding object (infrared\ncomponent) and to the typical energy of the universe at the moment of its formation\n(ultraviolet component). If τ = τ (2), it is reasonably arguable that only primordial\nblack holes, which formed in the early universe, would have the size and the lifetime\nfor exploding soon enough so that we could observe the corresponding signals.\n\nFor primordial black holes whose lifetime is of the order of the Hubble time, it was\n\n3It would probably be more appropriate to call it “silhouette” given that there is no physical surface\non which the shadow is cast\n\n\n\n100 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nshown that the infrared component of the signal could get up to the GeV scale and\nbe peaked in the MeV, while the ultraviolet part of the burst is expected to be in the\nTeV range [285, 286]. If confirmed by more accurate modelling, this would place the\nsearch for the bursts associated to bouncing geometries within the realm of current\nhigh energy astrophysics experiments (provided that a sufficient number of primordial\nblack holes is created in the early universe). Furthermore, the fact that bursts further\naway in redshift would correspond to less massive and more primordial objects implies\nthat their higher peak frequency would partially compensate their higher cosmological\nredshift [286]. This is a peculiar behaviour that might be used a a signature for this kind\nof signals and might help distinguish them from other, more standard, astrophysical\nemissions.\n\nWith regards to our parameterization, it is clear that the detection of one of these\nbursts could be used to cast constraints on both τ± (depending on the particular sce-\nnario), but would not tell us much about tails, ε(t, r).\n\n5.4 Gravitational waves\n\nThe detection of gravitational waves in LIGO and VIRGO [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] opens up\nadditional possibilities for testing the properties of astrophysical black holes. One of the\nbest sources of gravitational waves are mergers of compact objects: astrophysical black\nholes [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] or neutron stars [6]. The merger of compact objects releases abun-\ndant information about their nature, although part of it is difficult to extract due to\nthe intrinsically nonlinear nature of the process. It is also interesting that, as discussed\nbelow, observations using electromagnetic and gravitational wave observations are com-\nplementary, in the sense that the different nature of the physical processes involving\nthese forms of radiation makes the corresponding observational channels more sensible\nto (and therefore more suitable to measure) different phenomenological parameters. We\nwill illustrate this point using the parametrization introduced in Sec. 5.2.\n\n5.4.1 Coalescence of compact objects\n\nThe waveform produced in a merger can be roughly divided into three main parts: (i)\nthe inspiral phase in which the two objects are far apart, (ii) the merging phase in which\nthe two objects enter in direct contact, and (iii) the ringdown phase that describes the\nrelaxation of the outcome of the merging phase. These three phases are defined by\nthe different physical processes taking place; from a mathematical perspective, these\nphases are also characterized by the different techniques that are most appropriate for\nextracting the corresponding gravitational wave signatures.\n\n• Inspiral phase:\n\nIn the inspiral phase the two objects are far apart, so that Newtonian gravity can\nbe used in order to describe this phase to a good approximation. Hence, as in the\ndiscussion of orbiting stars in Sec. 5.3.1, the details of the near-horizon geometry\nwill not appreciably affect the evolution of the system in this phase. However,\nwhile in this phase, binary systems could still possibly display detectable differ-\nences with respect to a binary of black holes if the two objects have surfaces\n\n\n\n5.4. GRAVITATIONAL WAVES 101\n\ninstead of horizons (i.e., if ∆ > 0), due to the effects that the gravitational field\nof each of the two objects can have on the internal structure of its companion\nthrough the induced tidal forces. All known results regarding classical general\nrelativity black holes are consistent with these objects having identically zero\ntidal deformability [287, 288, 289]. However, ultracompact configurations with-\nout horizons can be tidally deformed [290]. Moreover, if Γ 6= 0 the object would\ndecrease its tidal heating (measured in terms of the amount of gravitational radi-\nation that the object absorbs [291, 292]). It has been argued [293] (see also [294])\nthat both effects could be used in order to place upper bounds on the values of\nthese two parameters ∆ and Γ using data from the Laser Interferometer Space\nAntenna (LISA), with constraints on the value of Γ being the most promising\nones. Soft fluctuations of the near-horizon geometry, given by tails ε(t, r) with\ncompact support, can be also constrained using this part of the waveform [295].\n\n• Merger:\n\nThe dynamics in the merger phase is highly nonlinear, which renders most of the\nparameters in our phenomenological parametrization in Sec. 5.2 useless. In fact,\nvirtually nothing is known about this nonlinear regime in theories beyond general\nrelativity. It seems that this problem has to be addressed numerically and on\na case-by-case basis. However, some of the models discussed in Sec. 5.1 could\nleave an imprint during this phase. In particular, short-lived bouncing geometries\nwould disrupt the merger on timescales of the order of τ−, perhaps leading to\nthe formation of quasi-black holes as proposed in [136, 184]. This would create a\ndistinctive periodic pattern [136, 170] that is similar to the (linear) phenomenon of\ngravitational wave echoes discussed in the next section, sharing the typical values\nof the timescale between subsequent echoes but being inherently nonlinear. For\ncompleteness, we also mention that horizonless configurations may also lead to\nelectromagnetic afterglows in this phase [296, 297]. However, the strength of this\nemission is largely unknown, and also it is not clear how such a phenomenon\nwould avoid being suppressed by the lensing discussed in Sec. 5.3.2.\n\n• Ringdown:\n\nThe ringdown part of the signal can again be described making used of a linear\nanalysis, in terms of the so-called quasinormal modes [224]. The corresponding\nwaveform is typically given by a linear combination of damped sinusoids. Shortly\nafter the first detection of gravitational waves, a theoretical analysis [218] demon-\nstrated explicitly that the form of this part of the signal is associated with the\nphoton sphere at rph = 3rs/2, and not the horizon. Hence, a similar comment as\nin Sec. 5.3.4 applies: testing the damping of the waveform does not allow drawing\nconclusions about the near-horizon geometry. However, if the object is not to\ncompact, the presence of the surface can modify the ringdown (see, e.g. [298])\nand, as discussed in the next section, for an UCO modifications of the near-horizon\ngeometry may trigger new characteristic effects in the late-time ringdown.\n\n\n\n102 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\n5.4.2 Echoes in the late-time ringdown\n\nAfter the relaxation of the object produced in the merger through the emission of grav-\nitational waves, its properties could still leave imprints in the late-time gravitational-\nwave signal. These imprints would be the result of the interaction of the gravitational\nradiation, emitted previously, with the central object. As discussed in detail below,\nfor sufficiently compact situations a significant fraction of this gravitational radiation\nis backscattered by the gravitational field of the central object, traveling back to and\ninteracting with the latter. The phenomenological parameter that control this late-time\nbehavior is the reflection coefficient Γ. For a black hole, Γ = 0, which means that all\nbackscattered radiation will disappear down its gravitational well. If Γ 6= 0, some of\nthis radiation would bounce back from the object and could be measured by distant\ndetectors.\n\nLet us start with the simplest possible description of the main physics involved,\nadding additional details progressively. The first element that must be discussed is the\nmechanism that leads to the backscattering of the initially outgoing radiation [299].\nThis can be introduced by considering the propagation of test particles or waves in the\nSchwarzschild geometry. For instance, the modes of a scalar field Φ(t, r, θ, ϕ), in the\nusual decomposition in spherical harmonics\n\nΦ(t, r, θ, ϕ) =\n∞∑\nl=0\n\nl∑\nm=−l\n\nφlm(t, r)\n\nr\nYlm(θ, ϕ), (5.47)\n\nsatisfy the wave equation (\n− ∂2\n\n∂t2\n+\n\n∂\n\n∂r2\n∗\n− Vl\n\n)\nφlm(t, r) = 0, (5.48)\n\nwhere r∗ is the standard tortoise coordinate and\n\nVl =\n\n(\n1− 2M\n\nr\n\n)(\nl(l + 1)\n\nr2\n+\n\n2M\n\nr3\n\n)\n(5.49)\n\nis the Regge–Wheeler potential. This potential has a maximum in the vicinity of\nrph = 3M , with the deviation from this value controlled by 1/l, and smaller the larger\nthe value of l. The radius rph = 3M marks also the location of the photon sphere (or\nlight ring), namely the innermost circular null geodesic that is stable (as discussed in\nSec. 5.3.2). Due to the existence of this maximum in the potential, outgoing waves\noriginated at r < rph will be backscattered. The fraction of backscattered radiation\ncan be calculated explicitly [300, 301, 302, 303]. Only objects that are compact enough\nto have a photon sphere will display this phenomenon, and therefore we focus in the\nfollowing on these objects.\n\nIn the case of a black hole, the backscattered waves will be lost into the horizon.\nHowever, for objects in which Γ 6= 0 and ∆ 6= 0, part of the incoming radiation will be\nbe reflected outwards. When crossing the photon sphere at rph, part of this radiation\nwill escape and part will be backscattered. This leads to a periodic phenomenon that\nwould produce a series of “echoes” of the first event. Slightly modifying Eq. (5.22), the\ncharacteristic timescale of this phenomenon is given by\n\nTecho = 2M − 4M ln(2∆) + Tint, (5.50)\n\n\n\n5.4. GRAVITATIONAL WAVES 103\n\nwhere the first two terms on the right-hand side measure the time that a pointlike\nparticle following a radial null geodesic takes to travel from rph = 3M and R = rs(1+∆)\nand then from R = rs(1+∆) to rph = 3M , and Tint provides a measure of the time that\nthe gravitational wave spends inside the central object (that is, in the region r ≤ R).\n\nThe precise value of Tint depends on the particular model being used but, if one\nignores the interaction between gravitational waves and the central object (which, as\nexplained below, is most likely not consistent), this quantity is expected to be of the\norder of the light-crossing time or, equivalently, proportional to M (an explicit calcula-\ntion is provided for instance in [304]). Then, for ∆� 1 the leading order in Eq. (5.50)\nwould be\n\nTecho ' −4M ln(∆). (5.51)\n\nThis logarithmic behavior has been already discussed in Sec. 5.3.3. The amplitude\nof these echoes is proportional to the reflection coefficient Γ and also depends on the\ndetails of the barrier peaked around the photon sphere. Of course, the amplitude of\nsubsequent echoes decreases monotonically, and a power-law for this decay has been\nfound [301, 305].\n\nThe reader may have noticed that there seems to be an inconsistency between our\ntreatment of electromagnetic waves in Sec. 5.3.2, and the treatment of gravitational\nwaves in this section. More specifically, we are not bringing up the lensing that had to\nbe taken into account in order to describe the behavior of electromagnetic waves. In\nother words, we are implying that gravitational waves are not affected by this lensing.\n\nThere are several aspects behind this assumption. The first one is that the processes\ninvolving electromagnetic waves have been assumed to be deeply inelastic, following our\nintuition about the interaction of light and matter in other systems. However, in the\nlinear approximation used to describe gravitational wave echoes, it is assumed that\ngravitational waves interact elastically with the central object (we critically revise this\nassumption at the end of this section). If we accept this main difference it follows then,\nas long as we are analyzing waves with angular momentum below the critical value\nL? derived in Sec. 5.3.2, that electromagnetic waves experience lensing effects while\ngravitational waves are unaffected.\n\nMoreover, it is worth stressing that these two kinds of radiation have different wave-\nlength, which determines whether or not the geometric optics approximation is reason-\nable. The gravitational waves produced in the merger of two compact objects into a\ncentral object of mass M have wavelengths that are comparable to the Schwarzschild\nradius of the central object [306] (of course, there is a distribution in wavelengths, or\nfrequencies, around this typical scale). On the other hand, the electromagnetic waves\nrelevant for our discussion in Sec. 5.3.2 have much shorter wavelengths. Hence, it is\nreasonable to describe the behavior of electromagnetic waves in these spacetimes within\nthe geometric optics approximation, in which the strong lensing of lightlike geodesics by\nthe gravitational field of the central object is unavoidable. As the gravitational waves\nof the wavelengths involved in the merger cannot be described in this approximation,\nthey may circumvent the attraction of the central object and escape outwards even if\nhaving an angular momentum greater than L?, depending on the value of l (something\nthat would lead to a grey-body feature of the gravitational wave spectrum). We think\nthat this aspect is worth studying in detail.\n\nPrevious works (including [299, 301, 302, 307, 305]) have not analyzed this issue\n\n\n\n104 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nexplicitly, perhaps due to particular choices of initial conditions for gravitational ra-\ndiation. In fact, it may be the case that phenomenologically reasonable values of L\nare below L?, hence preventing lensing to play any role in realistic scenarios. However,\nin order to deal with realistic situations one would also need to include the angular\nmomentum of the central object, which would certainly change the value of L?.\n\nOn the other hand, let us recall that Eqs. (5.50) and (5.51) are strictly valid for\nnull geodesics. Hence, it is assumed in the literature that the geometric optics approx-\nimation is indeed reasonable at least for the analysis of certain aspects of the problem,\nnamely the evaluation of the characteristic timescale (5.51). The critical wavelength\nbelow which the geometric optics approximation can be used in order to describe the\nbehavior of waves in the potential (5.49) is substantially larger than M for ∆� 1 small\nenough; in fact, this critical wavelength is roughly given by Eq. (5.51). This restricts\nthe wavelengths for which the discussion of the echoes provided above is consistent:\n\nλ� | ln ∆| × O(M). (5.52)\n\nIt is important to analyze the physics associated with this upper bound in more detail, in\norder to understand for instance how sharp it is. This is moreover relevant for modeling\npurposes, as Eq. (5.52) points out that the frequency content of the originally outgoing\ngravitational radiation will effectively experience a band-pass filter that selects the\nfrequencies that would appear in the subsequent echoes. Moreover, waves with L > L?\nmay also experience a lower bound given by M . λ, although this is far from clear.\n\nIt is illustrative to use our parametrization in Sec. 5.2 in order to understand the\nkind of information that can be extracted from the search of echoes in gravitational wave\nevents. The amplitude of gravitational wave echoes would be, following the discussion\nabove, proportional to Γ. Hence, both the observation and non-observation of echoes\ncan put constraints on the value of this parameter (this is, for instance, the main result\nin [308, 309]). The non-observation of echoes can only constrain this parameter and\ncannot say anything about the radius R or, alternatively, ∆. Of course, a positive\ndetection of echoes could be used in order to determine the size of the central object,\nthrough the use of Eq. (5.51). The other two parameters which are relevant for the\nprocess are τ+, which has to be greater than the characteristic timescale of echoes (this\nwould place a very uninteresting lower bound on this quantity), and τ− which has to\nbe smaller (the consequences of this for theoretical models were analyzed in [310]).\n\nThe interest in this phenomenon has grown after tentative evidence for their ex-\nistence in LIGO data was claimed [311, 312]. These works assume crude templates\nthat are missing some of the details in the discussion above and in later works such\nas [301, 305], the importance of which for data analysis is not yet clear. Moreover,\nthese claims are still controversial, although parts of the initial results have been cor-\nroborated by other groups [313, 314, 315, 316]. For completeness, let us also mention\nthat qualitatively similar claims have been made about the binary neutron star merger\nGW170817 [317]. However, the latter analysis does not make any specific assump-\ntions about the waveform of the echoes and just looks for periodicities. This opens\nthe possibility of alternative explanations for these periodicities, as mentioned in the\nconclusions of [317] but also explored for instance in [318] and in Sec. 5.4.1 above in\nwhich it was stressed that short-lived bouncing geometries are also expected to lead to\nperiodic patterns in the late-time part of gravitational wave signals.\n\n\n\n5.4. GRAVITATIONAL WAVES 105\n\nBefore ending this section, we want to stress that the discussion above neglects the\n(generally nonlinear) interaction between gravitational waves and the central object. In\npractical terms, the echo timescale is calculated in an approximation in which gravita-\ntional waves propagate in a fixed background, and the amplitude of the echoes is just\nproportional to the reflection coefficient Γ. This issue has been ignored in the literature,\nbut here we want to highlight that this does not seem consistent and that this feature\nhas fundamental implications for the existence (or not) of echoes.\n\nLet us start by considering a toy model in the purely classical framework of general\nrelativity, consisting of a perfectly reflecting (Γ = 1) and spherically symmetric mirror\nwith radius R = rs(1+∆) enclosing a mass M , so that the geometry outside the mirror\nis Schwarzschild. We now consider an ingoing spherical shell of gravitational radiation,\nof which we just need to monitor the energy density; so that we will describe it in terms\nof pressureless null dust with uniform energy density. This ingoing radiation will be\nreflected by the mirror and will therefore travel outwards after interacting with the lat-\nter. However, the peeling of outgoing null geodesics leads to an accumulation of energy\naround the gravitational radius (see Fig. 5.4) For ∆ � 1 this accumulation of energy\nleads to the formation of trapping (and, in this classical setting, event) horizons even for\nan extremely modest amount of energy being received and reflected at the mirror [115].\nAbove a certain threshold in the power stored in the gravitational radiation, a black\nhole will form around the mirror and no radiation will escape to infinity.\n\nFigure 5.4: Exponential peeling of outgoing geodesics reflected at r = R. Even if the\ningoing distribution of energy has low density (light gray region), the accumulation of\ngeodesics around the gravitational radius produces high densities (dark gray region)\nthat result in large backreaction effects on the background geometry.\n\nThe formation of a black hole in this toy model is intimately associated with the\nbreakdown of the linear approximation for the gravitational waves propagating in the\nbackground geometry produced by the mirror, given that in the linear approximation\nthese waves will always escape to infinity. Hence, this shows that one has to be careful\nwhen using the linear approximation to extract the features of echoes. The formation\nof a trapping horizon might be avoided if the nonlinear interactions between the ingo-\ning gravitational waves and the central objects are considered. A model-independent\noutcome of these interactions has to be the expansion of the central object in order to\navoid the formation of trapping horizons. This expansion of the object needs energy,\n\n\n\n106 CHAPTER 5. PHENOMENOLOGY OF NON-SINGULAR BLACK HOLES\n\nwhich can only be taken from the gravitational radiation. A straightforward application\nof the argument in [115] shows that the more compact the central object is, the larger\nis the fraction of the energy stored in the gravitational waves that has to be trans-\nferred through nonlinear interactions.4 If most of the ingoing gravitational waves must\ninteract and transfer their energy to the central object, it is likely that the reflection\ncoefficient Γ will be extremely small, and therefore that there would be no echoes.\n\nA similar argument for the importance of the non linear effects can be obtained by\nlooking at the quasinormal modes of an ultracompact object. As seen in [320, 321] the\nimaginary part of the quasinormal modes goes to zero when the compactness approaches\nthe black hole value. This implies that the linear perturbation are long lived and\nare likely to trigger non liner instabilities. This type of instability has been observed\nstudying the perturbation of a quasi extremal Kerr black hole [322].\n\nOf course, it is possible that the timescale of the instability is very long or that\nthe nonlinear interactions with the central object are elastic and that the energy inside\nthe central object is transferred back to the outgoing gravitational waves after their\ntravel through its interior. In any case, these arguments show that previous theoretical\nanalysis of this phenomenon are missing important details of the physics involved, which\nmust be incorporated in order to arrive to a consistent picture. Therefore, we believe\nthat a more detailed analysis is needed in order to determine whether the existence of\nechoes really is a robust theoretical prediction. Progresses along this line of research\nwill be reported in future investigations.\n\nModel Stars Accretion Shadows Bursts Coalescence Echoes\n(EM) (EM) (EM) (EM) (GW) (GW)\n\nRegular black hole ε(t, r) 7 7 7 7 7\n\nBouncing geometries ε(t, r) 7 7 3 τ− (short-lived)\nQuasi-black hole ε(t, r) µ,Γ, κ 7 7 τ−, µ,Γ Γ, [µ]\n\nWormhole ε(t, r) 7 (Γ + κ = 1) 7 7 τ−,Γ Γ, [µ]\n\nTable 5.2: Parameters that can be possibly constrained or measured for the different\nclasses of quantum-modified black holes and different observational channels. Square\nbrackets are used in order to stress that µ can be measured using gravitational wave\nechoes only in the event of a positive detection (in other words, the non-observation of\nechoes places constraints on Γ only).\n\n5.5 Conclusions\n\nIn this chapter we have studied and parametrized the possible theoretical alternatives\nto classical black holes and we have discussed the current status of the relevant ob-\nservational constraints. We have classified the different alternatives into four classes:\n\n4It is important to stress that it is clear that these interactions must be sufficiently exotic (see,\ne.g., [319] for a particular discussion) to avoid the formation of trapping horizons (in particular, it\nseems that these interactions must involve some kind of non-locality), although we will not insist on\nthis point.\n\n\n\n5.5. CONCLUSIONS 107\n\nregular black holes, bouncing geometries, quasi-black holes and wormholes, and we have\nprovided a set of phenomenological parameters that identify the key properties of each\nclass. Both electromagnetic and gravitational wave observations can be used in order to\nconstrain these parameters. Table 5.2 summarizes the parameters that can be measured\nor constrained with each of the different observational channels we have discussed.\n\nThe most promising observational channel using electromagnetic waves can only\nprobe quasi-black holes. Eq. (5.39) represents the most stringent bound that electro-\nmagnetic observations can put on a combination of the parameters κ and µ (a similar\nrelation including Γ can be derived). This provides an upper bound on the allowed\nvalues of µ that is generally weaker than the upper bound Eq. (5.31) that does not take\ninto account the parameter κ (as in previous works in the subject). These constraints\ncan become very weak for reasonable values of the parameters involved. We have also\nreviewed in Sec. 5.3.3 the existence of lower bounds on the parameter µ that can also\nbe inferred from the observation of accretion disks around supermassive black holes.\nThese lower bounds provide the most restrictive constraints on quasi-black holes and\nare insensitive to the parameters κ and Γ (albeit they do rely on the assumption of\nstandard local interactions).\n\nAs with wormholes, testing regular black holes or long-lived bouncing geometries\nwith electromagnetic observations seems hopeless during most of their extended life-\ntimes. The final stages in the evolution of these objects may be typically violent, which\ncould lead to prompt emissions of electromagnetic radiation. Hence, quasi-black holes\nare arguably the most interesting scenarios from the perspective of electromagnetic ob-\nservations, as they offer a number of phenomenological opportunities during all stages\nof their life cycle (that may involve transients characterized by short-lived bounces).\n\nRegarding gravitational waves, we can conclude that the most promising theoretical\nscenarios from an observational perspective are quasi-black holes, wormholes, and short-\nlived bouncing geometries. The remaining theoretical scenarios, such as regular black\nholes, will be very difficult (if not impossible) to probe observationally in the near\nfuture, except perhaps for cataclysmic events that may lead to bursts of gravitational\nradiation (that can be associated, for instance, with long-lived bouncing geometries).\n\nFor these theoretical models, observational channels based on gravitational waves\nare mostly sensitive to the reflection coefficient Γ. This is due to the main difference\nwith respect to electromagnetic radiation that is typically assumed: gravitational waves\ninteract extremely weakly with standard matter. However, the lack of detailed knowl-\nedge of both the matter forming these objects and the possible nonlinear interactions\nof their gravitational fields with gravitational waves makes it impossible to assume at\nthe moment that these objects will display an appreciable reflection coefficient. In any\ncase, gravitational wave observations are starting to place constraints on this coefficient.\nThese constraints will improve in the near future, thus providing valuable feedback for\ntheoretical research. It is worth stressing that observational channels involving gravita-\ntional and electromagnetic waves are therefore complementary, thus providing a strong\nmotivation for a multi-messenger approach to the problem.\n\n\n\n108\n\n\n\nGeneral conclusions and outlook\n\nIn this thesis, we have investigated possible deviations from general relativity using dif-\nferent methods. In chapter 1, we have performed a systematic analysis of a specific class\nof minimally modified theories of gravity, which have the peculiarity of propagating the\nsame degrees of freedom as general relativity. Our analysis required the interplay of\nmany different techniques. In fact, both the Hamiltonian and the Lagrangian formula-\ntion of the theories were necessary in order to apply the spinor helicity formalism and\nshow that the theories under consideration are actually general relativity in disguise.\nThis does not mean that this class of theories is not interesting, as the equivalence holds\nin vacuum but can be broken by the matter content. In fact, as shown in [72], these\ntheories can have interesting phenomenological aspects in cosmological scenarios.\n\nThe second part of the thesis approaches the problem of black hole singularity in\na model independent way. In chapter 2, we have studied which type of constraint we\nneed to impose on the spacetime in order to have a well posed notion of causality.\nWe have extended the hierarchy of causality condition of general relativity to generic\nmodified theories of gravity. In particular, for all the scenarios we have discussed, global\nhyperbolicity is always a necessary condition, even if in some cases it has to be replaced\nby some stronger condition (for instance we have seen that in the presence on a mode\npropagating at infinite speed, we have to assume the much stronger requirement of\nglobal parabolicity).\n\nThis knowledge was very important for the analysis of chapter 3, where we provide\na complete classification of non-singular spacetime with trapping horizon. In fact, the\nkey assumption of the analysis is that the spacetime has an effective description in\nterms of pseudo–Riemannian geometries. Once that we accept this property, in light\nof the results of the previous chapter, we know that the spacetime has to be global\nhyperbolic. With these assumptions and with the request of geodesic completeness\nand the absence of curvature singularities, we were able to introduce and study the\nproperties of four classes of spacetimes: evanescent horizon, everlasting horizon, one-\nway hidden wormhole and asymptotic hidden wormhole. We have then proved that\nthe most generic spacetime compatible with our hypothesis has to be a combination\nof these four classes. While the analysis was performed in spherical symmetry, most\nof the results can be immediately generalized to a less symmetric configuration. We\nhave seen that some classes of geometries can mimic exactly a classical black hole from\nthe point of view of an external observer while other classes are forced to have some\n\n109\n\n\n\n110\n\nmodification outside the trapping horizon. The geometrical analysis cannot provide\ninsight on which of these two scenarios is more plausible nor on the timescale after\nwhich the modification leaks outside the trapping horizon in the second scenario.\n\nTherefore, in chapter 4, we have added extra ingredients so to study the viability\nof the various solutions. We obtained the remarkable results that it is very difficult to\nobtain a well defined geometry without allowing for deviation with respect to classical\nblack hole to arise in a short (typically Plankian) timescale.\n\nThe one way hidden wormhole and the asymptotic hidden wormhole geometries have\nproblems due to the required topology change and their consistency with semiclassical\nphysics, while the long lived evanescent horizon and the everlasting horizon geometries\nare generically unstable due to the presence of mass inflation instability. Therefore, the\nonly model which is free from self consistency issue is the short lived evanescent black\nhole.\n\nAmong the various self consistency issues, mass inflation deserves special attention\nas it is a very general argument but it also present many subtleties that have to be\ninterpreted correctly. It may appear counter intuitive that it is possible to prove the\npresence of an instability without specifying the dynamics of the theory. The reason\nwhy it was possible to use purely kinematical arguments is that we have only proved\nthe existence of a linear instability, i.e., we have shown that small perturbation has a\nhuge impact on the geometry and the dynamical evolution is going to be highly non\ntrivial, but it is not possible to predict what the outcome of this evolution would be.\nIn general relativity, the instability of the inner horizon usually produces a singularity.\nHowever, in a full theory of quantum gravity, we expect that this will no longer be\ntrue and the backreaction will drive the time evolution to one of the other classes of\ngeometry (maybe it will lead to a short lived evanescent horizon as that one is the only\nclass free from pathologies).\n\nSome possible frameworks for this analysis are given by asymptotic safety and loop\nquantum gravity as there are examples in which the theories regularize the singularity\nintroducing an (unstable) inner horizon (see, e.g., [97, 134]). These results are perfectly\nconsistent as the works consider vacuum spacetimes without studying the interplay\nwith perturbations. It is very interesting to note that these quantum theories of gravity\ntame the black hole singularity even if in idealized situations. The results in this thesis\nsuggest that these analyses are actually incomplete, and the study of the backreaction\nof the perturbation in these frameworks will definitely be a non trivial but essential\ncalculation.\n\nThe fact that it is not easy to write down a self consistent geometry without long\nrange effect gives us strong motivation to look for phenomenological signatures of non\nsingular black holes. In chapter 5, we parametrize the deviations from classical black\nholes with a set of phenomenological parameters and we analyze the possible observa-\ntional channels that can be used to constrain them. Our geometrical analysis gives us\nstrong motivations to believe that these phenomenological parameters differ from the\none corresponding to classical black holes, but it cannot provide any inside on the scale\nof the differences. We have discussed that if such deviations arise at the Planck length\n(as expected by several models), than it is very difficult to observe them experimentally\nwith the current technology due to the highly non linear behavior of the gravitational\nfield close to the trapping horizon. We have also seen that different channels can probe\n\n\n\n111\n\ndifferent parameters, thus underlying the need for a multi-messenger approach to the\nproblem.\n\nLet us finally stress that it is very interesting to analyze the interplay between our\nresults and the logic behind the cosmic censorship conjecture. The cosmic censorship\nconjecture formalizes the intuition that whatever happens at the singularity does not\ninfluence the physics outside the event horizon. In this thesis, we have shown that, if\na notion of spacetime in terms of pseudo–Riemannian manifold survives the regular-\nization of the singularity, it is very difficult for this intuition to be correct, and that\nmodifications are expected to percolate outside the horizon, regardless the fact that\nprobing any deviation from classical black holes is very challenging from an experimen-\ntal point of view. Of course, it is impossible to prove that singularity regularization will\nhave long range effects as any analysis, including ours, has to make some assumptions.\nAnyway, we have shown that the geometries that do not have modifications outside the\ntrapping horizon are very difficult to make self consistent. Therefore the main message\nof this thesis depends on the personal belief of the person reading it. If one strongly\nbelieves that quantum gravity will regularize the spacetime only deep inside the black\nhole, our analysis highlights some highly non trivial self consistency issues that a full\ntheory of quantum gravity has to address. On the other hand, if one is open to the\npossibility that black hole spacetime can be modified by quantum effect also outside\nthe trapped region, then our analysis constitutes a further motivation to look for such\ndeviations.\n\nWhatever is the reader opinion, the crucial point about this field is that we live in\na new era of multi-messanger astronomy and very exiting times lie ahead towards our\nunderstanding of black holes and what they have to teach us about the final theory of\ngravity.\n\n\n\n112\n\n\n\nAppendix A\n\nExtracting the Poincaré algebra\n\nIn this appendix we detail the calculations that permit to extract the Poincaré algebra\nfrom the non-linear algebra of Poisson brackets discussed in Sec. 1.1. The function (D.23) has a global minimum\nfor r? =\n\n√\n3` and M? = 3\n\n√\n3`/4, which corresponds to the extremal mass. The surface\n\ngravity of the outer horizon is\n\nκ+ =\n3\n\n4M\n− 1\n\nr+\n\n. (D.24)\n\nFig. D.1 shows the dependence of κ+/2π on the mass M : We see that there is only one\nmaximum at M = Mpeak. In order to find the exact value of Mpeak it is sufficient to\nminimize the function\n\nF̃ (r,M) =\n∂F (r,M)\n\n∂r\n+ λ̃F (r,M) (D.25)\n\nwith respect to r, M and λ̃, finding rpeak = 3` and Mpeak = 27`/16. The corresponding\nheight of the temperature peak is\n\nTpeak =\nκpeak\n\n2π\n=\n\n1\n\n18π`\n≈ 10−2\n\n`\n. (D.26)\n\nTherefore, if we identify ` with the Planck length, the peak temperature is two orders\nof magnitude smaller than the Planck temperature. In order to assess the extent to\nwhich this is consistent with the quasi-static condition, let us point that at Mpeak the\nsystem is dominated only by the scale `. Therefore we can roughly estimate the mass\nloss at the peak by multiplying the peak luminosity\n\ndM\n\ndt\n\n∣∣∣∣\npeak\n\n= −σSB T\n4\npeak4πr4\n\npeak (D.27)\n\n\n\n133\n\nby the characteristic timescale at the peak, tpeak ≈ `. Identifying ` = Lplanck we find\nthat the emitted mass is about 10−6Mpeak. We interpret this result as an indication that\nthe system is not much perturbed even at the peak point, implying that the adiabatic\napproximation is reasonable.\n\nWe have numerically computed rpeak and Mpeak for the “Bardeen black hole” [103,\n108] and the “Dymnikova black hole” [107], finding that the mass emitted at the peak\nis 10−7Mpeak in the former case and 10−5Mpeak in the latter one. A similar conclusion\nwas reached in [330] in the context of asymptotic safety.\n\nBeyond the quasi-static or adiabatic regimes\n\nComparing Eqs. (D.14) and (D.21) it is evident that it is not possible to satisfy the\nadiabatic condition and also have a finite evaporation time (this follows from σ > 0).\nTherefore, the only way to build a model with finite evaporation time is going outside\neither the quasi-static or the adiabatic regimes.\n\nIt is possible to go outside the quasi-static approximation by simply picking a\nφ(r,M) 6= 0 that is very large at the peak mass. In this case the system would enter\nin a regime that requires beyond semiclassical physics to be addressed (in other words,\nthe effective description in terms of the regular black hole geometry breaks down).\n\nEvading the adiabatic condition is less trivial. One would need to pick a function\nφ(r,M) such that it diverges at r+ = r? whenM = M?. Indeed, returning to Eqs. (D.16)\nand (D.21), it is sufficient for σ − 3γ to be positive that\n\ne−φ(r?+∆r,M?+∆M) ∝ ε−δ, (D.28)\n\nwhere\n\n(n− 1)− σ\n\n3\n≤ δ ≤ n− 1. (D.29)\n\nIn particular, the lower bound of δ in Eq. (D.29) ensures that the adiabatic condition\nis violated, while the upper bound prevents κ? from diverging. Notice also that, when\nthe upper bound is saturated, δ = n− 1, we are in a special case: κ? is not zero but it\nis discontinuous, namely limr+→r? κ+ > 0 while limr−→r? κ− < 0.\n\nLet us remark that Eq. (D.29) is not the only constraint that φ(r,M) must satisfy in\norder for the scenario to be internally consistent. Obviously the metric should remain\nnon-singular. There are two places in which the metric could become singular, at r = r?\nand at r = 0. Computing the Ricci and Kretschmann scalar, one can check that, if\nEq. (D.29) holds only when M = M?, i.e., only when r? is an horizon, then the metric is\nnot singular. Additionally, it can be checked that, in order for the metric to not diverge\nat r = 0, we must have that e−φ(r,M) goes to a constant in the limit r → 0, while its\nderivative with respect to r must vanish in this limit. Furthermore, we also want the\ninstability timescale of the inner horizon to be much longer than the evaporation time,\nimplying exp [−φ(r−,M)]� 1. Strictly speaking, this condition is necessary only when\nthe black hole is macroscopic or mesoscopic (M � M?). Indeed F ′(r−) approaches\nzero in the limit M → M?, and, from Eq. (4.10), κ− might still be small for values of\nexp [−φ(r−,M)] of order unity or even greater.\n\nIf these properties are satisfied, the model can in principle be consistent from a\ngeometric perspective. However, this limits the predictability of the late stages of\n\n\n\n134 APPENDIX D. EVAPORATION TIME\n\nevaporation, because one must resort to yet unknown physics beyond the effective\ndescription provided by regular black holes. Filippo","first_name":"Francesco","recid":1718060},"control_number":1817433,"document_type":["thesis"],"texkeys":["DiFilippo:2020ooa"],"abstracts":[{"source":"INFN","value":"Einstein’s general relativity is an extremely elegant and successful theory. Recent obser- vations coming from the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration as well as from the Event Horizon Telescope give us the possibility to perform precision test of general relativity in regimes never tested before. Even though all the current observations are in perfect agreement with the predictions of general relativity, there are several reasons to study extensions of the theory. From the experimental point of view, we are forced to include a dark sector for the matter and energy content of the universe to explain the cosmological data. Whereas from a conceptual point of view, the theory is not perturbatively renormalizable, and it predicts the formation of spacetime singularities. This thesis studies possible modifications of general relativity both considering spe- cific theories of modified gravity and implementing a model independent approach. In the first part of the thesis, we study a specific class of modified theory of gravity which has the peculiarity of propagating the same number of degrees of freedom of general relativity. The existence of these theories apparently challenges the distinctive role of general relativity as the unique non-linear theory of massless spin-2 particles. However, we provide strong evidence that these theory are actually equivalent to general relativity in vacuum. In the second part of the thesis, we focus on the problem of black hole singularities which are unavoidably present in general relativity. However, it is reasonable to assume that there will be a mechanism preventing their formation in a full theory of quantum gravity. Without specifying any theory of quantum gravity or the nature of such mech- anism, simply assuming a minimal set of kinematical constraints, we classify and study the properties of non-singular spacetime with a trapping horizon. Contrary to what one might expect, the set of regular geometries that arises is remarkably limited. Further- more we show that it is very difficult to construct a self consistent geometry without any long range effect. This give us further motivation to study the phenomenology of non-singular black holes. To this end, we provide a set of parameters describing the deviations from classical black holes, and we review the possible observational channels that can measure or constrain them.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"INFN"}},{"source":"SISSA","value":"Einstein's general relativity is an extremely elegant and successful theory. Recent observations coming from the LIGO/VIRGO collaboration as well as from the Event Horizon Telescope give us the possibility to perform precision test of general relativity in regimes never tested before. Even though all the current observations are in perfect agreement with the predictions of general relativity, there are several reasons to study extensions of the theory.From the experimental point of view, we are forced to include a dark sector for the matter and energy content of the universe to explain the cosmological data. Whereas from a conceptual point of view, the theory is not perturbatively renormalizable, and it predicts the formation of spacetime singularities. This thesis studies possible modifications of general relativity both considering specific theories of modified gravity and implementing a model-independent approach. In the first part of the thesis, we study a specific class of modified theory of gravity which has the peculiarity of propagating the same number of degrees of freedom of general relativity. The existence of these theories apparently challenges the distinctive role of general relativity as the unique non-linear theory of massless spin-2 particles. However, we provide strong evidence that these theories are actually equivalent to general relativity in vacuum. In the second part of the thesis, we focus on the problem of black hole singularities which are unavoidably present in general relativity. However, it is reasonable to assume that there will be a mechanism preventing their formation in a full theory of quantum gravity. Without specifying any theory of quantum gravity or the nature of such mechanism, simply assuming a minimal set of kinematical constraints, we classify and study the properties of non-singular spacetime with a trapping horizon. Contrary to what one might expect, the set of regular geometries that arises is remarkably limited. Furthermore, we show that it is very difficult to construct a self-consistent geometry without any long range effect. This gives us further motivation to study the phenomenology of non-singular black holes. To this end, we provide a set of parameters describing the deviations from classical black holes, and we review the possible observational channels that can measure or constrain them.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"SISSA"}}],"titles":[{"source":"INFN","title":"Beyond General Relativity: Modified Theories and Non-Singular Black Holes"},{"source":"SISSA","title":"Beyond Sebastian","last_name":"Murk","first_name":"Sebastian","recid":1742414},"control_number":1955204,"dois":[{"material":"publication","source":"APS","value":"10.1103/PhysRevD.105.044051"},{"material":"publication","source":"arXiv","value":"10.1103/PhysRevD.105.044051"}],"document_type":["article"],"texkeys":["Murk:2021qiv"],"abstracts":[{"source":"APS","value":"The existence of black holes is a central prediction of general relativity and thus serves as a basic consistency test for modified theories of gravity. In spherical symmetry, only two classes of dynamic solutions are compatible with the formation of an apparent horizon in finite time of a distant observer. Moreover, the formation of black holes follows a unique scenario involving both types of solutions. To be compatible with their existence, any self-consistent theory of modified gravity must satisfy several constraints. We derive properties of the modified gravity terms of f(R) and generic fourth-order gravity theories and find that they naturally accommodate both classes of solutions. Consequently, the observation of an apparent horizon by itself may not suffice to distinguish between general relativity and modifications including up to fourth-order derivatives in the metric.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"APS"}},{"source":"arXiv","value":"The existence of black holes is a central prediction of general relativity and thus serves as a basic consistency test for modified theories of gravity. In spherical symmetry, only two classes of dynamic solutions are compatible with the formation of an apparent horizon in finite time of a distant observer. Moreover, the formation of black holes follows a unique scenario involving both types of solutions. To be compatible with their existence, any self-consistent theory of modified gravity must satisfy several constraints. We derive properties of the modified gravity terms of f(R) and generic fourth-order gravity theories and find that they naturally accommodate both classes of solutions. Consequently, the observation of an apparent horizon by itself may not suffice to distinguish between general relativity and modifications including up to fourth-order derivatives in the consequences of black holes physics beyond the domain of general relativity, mainly in effective extra dimensional models. The investigation is carried along three gravitational effects, namely the Hawking radiation, the strong deflection of gravitational lensing and the formation of quantum black holes. A cosmological thick brane solution is also investigated. Effective theories and models provide a prominent approach for testing the limits of known theories and show what would be expected beyond that. Based on such idea we have used effective models for finding deviations of general relativity associated to each of the mentioned phenomena.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"arXiv"}}],"primary_arxiv_category":["gr-qc"],"titles":[{"source":"arXiv","title":"Aspects of Black Hole Physics Beyond General Relativity: extra Mathematics, Statistics, and Operations Research, Victoria University of Wellington\nE-mail: matt.visser@msor.vuw.ac.nz\n\nWhat is going on (as of August 2008) at the interface between theoretical general relativity, string-\ninspired models, and observational astrophysics? Quite a lot. In this mini-survey I will make a\npersonal choice and focus on four specific questions: Do black holes “exist”? (For selected values\nof the word “exist”.) Is black hole formation and evaporation unitary? Can one mimic a black\nhole to arbitrary accuracy? Can one detect the presence of a horizon using local physics?\n\nBlack Holes in General Relativity and String Theory\n24–30 August, 2008\nVeli Losinj, Croatia\n\n∗Speaker.\n†This research was supported by the Marsden Fund administered by the Royal Society of New Zealand.\n\nc© Copyright owned by the author(s) under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike Licence. http://pos.sissa.it/\n\nmailto:matt.visser@msor.vuw.ac.nz\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\n1. Introduction\n\nThis workshop deals with a large number of topics:\n\n• Astrophysical Black Holes (from super-massive to stellar);\n\n• Primordial and Mini Black Holes;\n\n• Black Hole Entropy;\n\n• Information Paradox;\n\n• Asymptotic Symmetries;\n\n• Anomalies;\n\n• Attractor Mechanism;\n\n• Holography;\n\n• ADS/CFT correspondence.\n\nInstead of trying (uselessly) to address each of these topics in turn, I will use this mini-survey\nto address four specific questions, these questions representing my personal choice regarding the\ncurrently important questions of black hole physics:\n\n• Do black holes “exist”?\n\n• Is black hole formation and evaporation unitary?\n\n• Can one mimic a black hole to arbitrary accuracy?\n\n• Can one detect the presence of a horizon using local physics?\n\n2. Do black holes “exist” ?\n\nThis innocent question is more subtle than one might expect, and the answer depends very much on\nwhether one is thinking as an observational astronomer, a classical general relativist, or a theoretical\nphysicist.\n\nObservational astronomer: Astronomers have certainly seen things that are small, dark, and\nheavy. But are these small, dark, heavy objects really black holes in the sense of classical general\nrelativity? Accretion disks, and in particular their inner cutoff radius, probe the spacetime geometry\nsurrounding black hole candidates down to the innermost stable circular orbit [ISCO] 2m/r ≈\n1/3. (See, for example, [1, 2].) Furthermore, advection dominated accretion flows [ADAFs] are\ncommonly interpreted as probing the spacetime geometry down to 2m/r . 1, though there are\nstill some disagreements on this point within the community. (See, for example, [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].)\nCertainly, everything observed so far is compatible with the standard Schwarzschild and/or Kerr\nspacetimes. (See, for example, [2, 8, 9].)\n\n2\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nClassical general relativist: Eternal black holes certainly exist mathematically, as stationary\nvacuum solutions to the Einstein equations. (See, for example, [10, 11, 12, 13], or any of the\nmany standard textbooks in general relativity [14].) Furthermore classical astrophysical black holes\n(future event horizons) certainly exist mathematically as the end result of classical collapse based\non certain physically plausible equations of state. (See, for example, [15].)\n\nTheoretical physicist: But one can always argue that we have not seen direct observational ev-\nidence of the event horizon [16], and unless and until we do so one retains some freedom to pos-\ntulate new and different near-horizon physics. In fact doing so is not entirely perverse, in that a\nwell-thought-out alternative to standard near-horizon physics can give observational astronomers\nspecific ideas of what to look for.\n\nMore radically one could just pick one’s favourite “problem” or “oddity” related to black hole\nphysics, and use it as an excuse to speculate. One of the most abused issues in this regard (which\nstill has a nugget of physics hiding at its core) is the relationship between unitarity, information,\nentropy, and black hole physics.\n\n3. Is black hole formation and evaporation unitary?\n\nThe most important thing to realise is that information “loss” is (in and of itself) not a prob-\nlem, it is merely a “feature”. Information loss is just one of those things you have to live with\nif you accept the standard Carter–Penrose diagram for the causal structure of stellar collapse, see\nfigure 1. For all practical purposes: Information loss ⇔ non-unitary evolution in the domain of\nouter communication⇔ existence of an event horizon.\n\nFigure 1: Strict event horizon (absolute horizon).\n\n3\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nAs soon as one has an event horizon, one has an inaccessible region, and an external observer\nmust then “trace over” the states hidden in that inaccessible region, and for that observer pure\nstates become density matrices. Thus an event horizon (absolute horizon) automatically leads to\nnon-unitary evolution — at least as seen from the outside.\n\nBut is “event horizon” the right concept to be using? There are many other possible definitions\nof horizon: apparent [14, 17, 18], dynamical [19], and/or trapping [20] horizons, that may make\nmore physical sense. Even classically, event horizons are seriously diseased in numerical general\nrelativity, simply because they are so difficult to find with any certainty — local or quasi-local\ndefinitions of horizon are often preferable from a purely pragmatic point of view [21, 22].\n\n+\n\nJ\n\nJ\n\n!\n\nFIG. 1: The standard space-time diagram depicting black hole formation and evaporation.\n\nevent horizon should steadily decrease. This then leads to black hole evaporation depicted\n\nin figure 1 [11].\n\nIf one does not examine space-time geometry but uses instead intuition derived from\n\nMinkowskian physics, one may be surprised that although there is no black hole at the\n\nend, the initial pure state has evolved in to a mixed state. Note however that while space-\n\ntime is now dynamical even after the collapse, there is still a final singularity, i.e., a final\n\nboundary in addition to I+. Therefore, it is not at all surprising that, in this approximation,\n\ninformation is lost —it is still swallowed by the final singularity [10]. Thus, provided figure\n\n1 is a reasonable approximation of black hole evaporation and one does not add new input\n\n‘by hand’, then pure states must evolve in to mixed states.\n\nThe question then is to what extent this diagram is a good representation of the physical\n\nsituation. The general argument in the relativity community has been the following (see\n\ne.g. [12]). Figure 1 should be an excellent representation of the actual physical situation\n\nas long as the black hole is much larger than the Planck scale. Therefore, problems, if any,\n\nare associated only with the end point of the evaporation process. It is only here that the\n\nsemi-classical approximation fails and one needs full quantum gravity. Whatever these ‘end\n\neffects’ are, they deal only with the Planck scale objects and would be too small to recover\n\nthe correlations that have been steadily lost as the large black hole evaporated down to the\n\nPlanck scale. Hence pure states must evolve to mixed states and information is lost.\n\nTight as this argument seems, it overlooks two important considerations. First, one would\n\nhope that quantum theory is free of infinities whence figure 1 can not be a good depiction\n\nof physics near the entire singularity —not just near the end point of the evaporation\n\n3\n\nFigure 2: Standard Carter–Penrose diagram for an evaporating black hole.\n\nFurthermore, once you add semiclassical quantum physics, specifically Hawking evaporation,\nthe issues again become more complicated, leading to the so called “information paradox” — what\n(quantitatively) happens to the information you thought you had lost once the evolving black hole\nreaches its final state? (Whatever that final state happens to be.) If you believe that Hawking\nevaporation is unitary (as seen from our own asymptotically flat domain of outer communication),\nthen there had better not be any any event horizon in the spacetime. To quote Stephen Hawking in\nthe abstract to his talk delivered at GR17:\n\n“The way the information gets out seems to be that a true event horizon never\nforms, just an apparent horizon.”\n\n(The actual talk given at GR17 has never been published, even informally, though transcripts can\nbe found on the web. The scientific publication closest in content to that talk is [23].) Largely\nindependent of one’s favourite model for the “quantum theory that would be gravity”, whether\nloop-based, string-based, or something else, the last few years has seen a consensus shift to where\nmany if not most physicists now seem to think that Hawking evaporation is unitary. Thus the\nevent/ absolute/ apparent/ trapping/ dynamical horizon distinction may be more than just a matter\n\n4\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nof mathematical convenience — it may be critically important to the underlying physics of black\nhole formation and evaporation. (For earlier somewhat related ideas, see, for instance, [24].)\n\nConsider the standard Carter–Penrose diagram for an evaporating black hole, figure 2. In this\nstandard picture there is always a region of “don’t ask because we certainly cannot tell” associated\nwith the (vertical) timelike line emerging from the endpoint of the evaporation process. This is the\nsource of the famous tri-chotomy: Is the endpoint of Hawking evaporation\n\n• complete evaporation?\n\n• a timelike (naked) singularity?\n\n• a stable remnant?\n\nAs long as one insists on the black hole being defined by an event horizon (absolute horizon),\nthen the standard diagram of figure 2 is unavoidable — as is the associated information loss and\nnon-unitary evolution.\n\nAs an counterpoint to the standard Carter–Penrose diagram, Ashtekar and Bojowald [25] have\nsuggested replacing the spacelike singularity by a region of Planckian curvature — leading to\nan alternative Carter–Penrose diagram for the causal structure of black hole evaporation. While\nAshtekar and Bojowald were working within the framework of loop quantum gravity when they\ndrew their version of the Carter–Penrose diagram, figure 3, it is critically important to realize\nthat qualitatively the same sort of causal diagram might be compatible with a unitarily evolving\nstring-based model of black hole evaporation. Depending on one’s favourite model for “quantum\ngravity” the shaded region of Planckian curvature might be viewed as a “loop network”, “strongly\ninteracting string muck”, or more prosaically as a region of violently fluctuating spacetime.\n\nJ\n\nJ\n\n!\n\ni\n\n+\n\n0\n\nH\n\nI\n\nFIG. 2: Space-time diagram of black hole evaporation where the classical singularity is resolved\n\nby quantum geometry effects. The shaded region lies in the ‘deep Planck regime’ where geome-\n\ntry is genuinely quantum mechanical. H is the trapping horizon which is first space-like (i.e., a\n\ndynamical horizon) and grows because of infalling matter and then becomes time-like (i.e., a time-\n\nlike membrane) and shrinks because of Hawking evaporation. In region I, there is a well-defined\n\nsemi-classical geometry.\n\ntwo considerations: i) the situation in the CGHS model where detailed calculations are\n\npossible and show that the quantum space-time has this property; and ii) experience with\n\nthe action of the Hamiltonian constraint in the spherically symmetric midi-superspace in\n\nfour dimensions. However, only detailed calculations can decide whether this assumption\n\nis borne out. Since our goal in this paper is only to point out the existence of a possible\n\nspace-time description in which information can be recovered at future null infinity, for our\n\npurposes it suffices to note only that none of the existing arguments rule out this mechanism.\n\nWe will refer to figure 2 as a ‘Penrose diagram’ where the inverted commas will serve\n\nas a reminder that we are not dealing with a purely classical space-time. Throughout the\n\nquantum evolution, the pure state remains pure and so we again have a pure state on I+.\n\nIn this sense there is no information loss. Noteworthy features of this ‘Penrose diagram’ are\n\nthe following.\n\ni) Effect of the resolution of the classical singularity: Region marked I is well-\n\n10\n\nFigure 3: Ashtekar–Bojowald version of the Carter–Penrose diagram for an evaporating black hole.\n\n5\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nWhile there is no event horizon in the Ashtekar–Bojowald diagram, there typically is an appar-\nent or dynamical horizon. There definitely is a “Planck horizon” or “reliability horizon”. Once one\ncrosses the lower-left dashed line, (which replaces the notion of event horizon), one is guaranteed a\npersonal encounter with Planck scale physics. While this is likely to be just as fatal as running into\na spacelike singularity, the highly curved (highly fluctuating, highly discrete) shaded region is now\nno longer an absolute barrier to unitary evolution. (Related ideas have also arisen in the study of\nchronology horizons and the “chronology protection conjecture” [26, 27, 28, 29]. It seems that the effective cosmological constant\nprotects the core.\n\nThe ingoing energy flux is positive if m is increasing\nand negative if m is decreasing. Then one can apply the previous analysis to\nlocate the trapping horizons in (v, r) coordinates param-\neterized by m, given by m(r±) in (6) and a mass profile\nm(v); qualitatively, by inspecting Figs. 3 and 4.\n\nIngoing radiation.
