Outgoing Hawking radiation will\nnow be modelled by adapting an idea of Hiscock [13]:\nselect a certain radius r0 > 2m0 outside the black hole,\nand adopt the above negative-energy radiation only in-\nside that radius, balanced by outgoing positive-energy\nradiation outside that radius, with the same mass pro-\nfile (Fig. 5). This is an idealized model of pair creation\nof ingoing particles with negative energy and outgoing\nparticles with positive energy, locally conserving energy.\n\nIn more detail, consider an outgoing Vaidya-like region\n\nds2 = r2dS2 − 2dudr − Fdu2 (20)\n\nwith F (r, u) as before (5), with m replaced by a mass\nfunction n(u). Fix the zero point of the retarded time\nu so that r = r0 corresponds to u = v. Now take the\nabove model only for v < vd (13)–(15). For v > vd, keep\nthe profiles (16)–(17) for r < r0, but for r > r0, take an\noutgoing Vaidya-like region with\n\n∀u < vd : n(u) = m0 (21)\n\nFigure 4: Hayward version of the Carter–Penrose diagram for an evaporating black hole.\n\nYet another causal diagram for an evaporating black hole is that due to Hayward [31]. At a\ntechnical level the main difference is that Hayward prefers to work with trapping horizons [20],\nwhile Ashtekar and Bojowald prefer to work with dynamical horizons [19]. While the diagram in\nfigure 4 at first glance looks rather different from that in figure 3, remember that all these causal di-\nagrams are conformal diagrams — they depend to some extent on one’s choice of coordinates, and\nadditionally are specified only up to a conformal factor that can be used to expand or contract parts\nof the diagram depending on what aspect of the physics one is most interested in. In particular, the\npurple line in figure 4 labelled “regular centre” is timelike, and with a suitable choice of coordinates\ncan be “straightened out” so that it looks like the vertical line in figure 3. Furthermore, in figure 4\n\n6\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nno attempt has been made to identify the region of Planck-scale curvature. Despite appearances,\nthe two causal diagrams of figures 3 and 4 are to a large extent compatible with each other, and both\nare compatible with the unitary evolution and evaporation of black holes. This qualitative result\ndoes not depend on whether you choose to believe in loops or strings, or indeed any other candidate\ntheory of “quantum gravity” that has Einstein gravity as an approximate low-energy limit.\n\nFigure 5: Roman–Bergmann double-null causal diagram for a regular collapsing star.\n\nThere is also some very nice considerably older work by Roman and Bergmann [32], where\nthey considered the possibility of obtaining apparent horizons without an event horizon. While\nthey were not specifically interested in Hawking radiation, being more interested in ideas of stellar\ncollapse with a regular centre, many of the qualitative features of that article now resonate in the\nHayward and Ashtekar–Bojowald causal diagrams. In particular, the curve labelled r = 0 on the\nleft of figure 5 is timelike, and with a suitable choice of coordinates can be “straightened out” so\nthat it looks like the vertical line in figure 3. Furthermore, although Roman and Bergmann adopted\ndouble null coordinates to clarify the causal structure, they did not perform the singular conformal\ntransformation that is needed to pull asymptotic infinity in to a finite “distance” and so produce\na Carter–Penrose diagram. Not performing this singular conformal transformation is sometimes\nan advantage; it can make the diagram a little more realistic when it comes to studying the metric\nfeatures, (as opposed to causal features).\n\nThese ideas have now mutated and spread throughout the theoretical relativity community, and\nvariants of these ideas can be seen, for instance, in recent work by Nielsen [33]. I should caution the\nreader that just sketching a suitable causal diagram is only the first step, since by definition Carter–\nPenrose diagrams only capture the conformal structure of the spacetime. One should in addition\nthink very carefully about the metrical structure — and one should fix the conformal factor so\nthat the spacetime geometry is close to Schwarzschild and/or Kerr over a suitably large portion of\n\n7\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nFigure 6: Null geodesic expansion/contraction for a Roman–Bergmann regular collapsing star.\n\nthe manifold. Furthermore, one should really then patch the resulting spacetime geometry onto a\nself-consistent quantum calculation leading to a Hawking-like flux near spatial infinity. Only then\nwould one have a really compelling picture of black hole collapse and evaporation.\n\nA key aspect of all these discussions is this critical point: You do not need an event horizon to\nget Hawking radiation. A long-lived apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizon is more than sufficient.\nThis is (or should be) a well-known result, dating back (at least) to Hajicek [34], and many other\nworkers of that period. This is one of those elementary and utterly important results that has been\nrepeatedly forgotten, and repeatedly rediscovered, over the last 30 years [35].\n\nMore recently it has been realised that you do not even need apparent/ dynamical/ trapping\nhorizons to get a Hawking-like flux — asymptotic approach to trapping horizon formation is quite\nsufficient [36, 37]. This naturally leads one to ask: Do we actually need “black holes” to do “black\nhole physics”?\n\n4. Black hole mimics?\n\nEven if we do not actually need “black holes” to do “black hole physics”, can we at least be sure\nthat we have something very similar to a black hole, a “black hole mimic”?\n\n• Can one avoid black hole formation with a suitably weird equation of state?\n\n• Can one avoid black hole formation with semi-classical quantum effects?\n\n• Can one avoid black hole formation with “quantum gravity”?\n\nThe possibilities are rather tightly constrained. (There is of course the utter gibbering crackpot\nfringe, but names will be suppressed to protect the guilty.) The “physically reasonable” alterna-\ntives to black hole formation can be counted on the fingers of one hand. (For selected values of\n“physically reasonable”.) This limited set of alternatives includes:\n\n8\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\n• Quark stars [38], Q-balls [39], strange stars [40].\n\n• Boson-stars [41].\n\n• Gravastars: Mazur–Mottola variant [42], and Laughlin et al. variant [43].\n\n• Fuzz-balls: Mathur et al. variant [44], and Amati variant [45].\n\n• Dark stars/ Quasi-black holes [46], and other proposals similar in spirit [47, 48].\n\nQuark stars, Q-balls, strange stars: The idea here is to change the equation of state of nuclear\nmatter under extreme conditions [38, 39, 40]:\n\nOrdinary star→ white dwarf→ neutron star→ (something unexpected?) (4.1)\n\nThe justification for the hypothesised equation of state is somewhat questionable. Note that one\nstill has the Buchdahl–Bondi bound: 2m/r ≤ 8/9 for any isotropic pressure profile. So you cannot\nget “close” to 2m/r . 1, which is a signal that you are “close” to forming an apparent/ dynamical/\ntrapping horizon, unless you are at the very least willing to adopt anisotropic stresses [49].\n\nBoson stars: The idea here is to have a (classical or possibly semiclassical) scalar field con-\nfiguration corresponding to a heavy compact object [41]. Anisotropic pressures then ariase from\nthe fact that the scalar Lagrangian, combined with spherical symmetry, automatically leads to an\nanisotropic classical stress-energy tensor. (And in view of the Buchdahl–Bondi bound, you will\ncertainly need the anisotropies if you want to get “close” to 2m/r . 1.)\n\nGravastars: These are hypothetical objects where the core is de Sitter like, and the exterior is\nSchwarzschild like, and something odd has to happen in the region 2m/r . 1 where the horizon\nwould otherwise have formed [42, 43]. See also [50, 51, 52]. In the region 2m/r . 1 various\nauthors have argued for:\n\n• Guaranteed anisotropies [49];\n\n• Breakdown of the spacetime manifold [43] ?\n\n• Quantum effects from the one-loop action [53] ?\n\nFuzz balls: Explicit calculations appear to be limited to the extremal/ near-extremal regime. The\nblack hole “interior” is replaced by “strongly interacting string muck”. The black hole “interior” is\nnot a spacetime, rather it is taken to be a superposition of “spacetimes”. (And none of the individual\n“spacetimes” in the superposition has a horizon [44, 45, 54]. See [55] for a survey.)\n\nDark stars/ Quasi-black holes: Here the idea is to have some nonsingular configuration that\nmimics a black hole [46], see also [47, 48]. Typically the configuration is continually and asymp-\ntotically collapsing, but never quite developing a horizon. Typically the authors appeal to quantum\neffects as an intrinsic part of the picture. (See the accompanying article [56], and reference [46],\nfor more details on the specific proposal by the current author and his collaborators.)\n\n9\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\ncurvature scales at the horizon are much larger than this length for large black holes.\nThus it would appear that the precise theory of quantum gravity is irrelevant to the\nprocess of Hawking radiation and thus for the resolution of the paradox.\n\nString theory is a consistent theory of quantum gravity; further, it is a theory with\nno free parameters. We should therefore ask how this theory deals with black holes.\nThe past decade has shown dramatic progress in our understanding of black holes in\nstring theory. We have understood how to count microstates of black holes. Recent\ncomputations suggest that the resolution of the information paradox lies in the fact that\nquantum gravity effects do not stay confined to microscopic distances, and the black\nhole interior is quite different from the naive picture suggested by classical gravity. This\nreview gives an elementary introduction to these ideas and conjectures.\n\n1(a) 1(b)\n\nFigure 1: (a) The conventional picture of a black hole (b) the proposed picture – state\ninformation is distributed throughout the ‘fuzzball’.\n\n2 Making black holes in string theory\n\nSusskind et. al [3] proposed an interesting approach to studying black holes in string\ntheory. Consider a highly excited state of a string. Thus the state has a mass M !\nα′−1/2. Assume that the string coupling is small (g \" 1) so the string is essentially\nfree. The left and right oscillator levels are NL, NR ∼\n\n√\nα′M ! 1, so there is a large\n\ndegeneracy N of states with this mass. This count of microscopic states gives an entropy\nSmicro = ln[N ] ∼\n\n√\nα′M . (The exact proportionality constant depends on how many\n\ndirections are compactified; such compact directions provide winding modes that also\ncontribute to the entropy.)\n\nNow imagine increasing the string coupling g; this brings in gravity since the Newton\ngravitational constant is G ∼ g2. If M was sufficiently large then we expect to get a black\nhole of mass M . We can compute the Bekenstein entropy of this hole SBek = A/4G. For\na Schwarzschild hole in 3+1 noncompact dimensions we get SBek ∼M2. More generally,\n\nif we had D noncompact spacetime directions we get SBek ∼ M\nD−2\nD−3 .\n\n3\n\nFigure 7: Fuzzball picture.\n\nFor all of these black hole mimics, there are substantial issues to address:\n\n• Calculations are often somewhat less explicit than one would like, simply because computa-\ntions are technically difficult.\n\n• There are a number of observational issues to address. For instance, rotating black hole\nmimics typically exhibit an ergoregion instability [57]. There are also constraints coming\nfrom accretion observations [58].\n\nIn short, one does not have complete freedom to speculate, any model for a black hole mimic\nalong any one of the lines described above should at some stage be carefully confronted with the\nobservational constraints.\n\n5. Detecting horizons?\n\nA common statement that one often encounters in the literature is this:\n\n• “Horizons are not detectable with local physics”.\n\nThe above statement is, of course, false. Note however, that it is almost true. Two closely related,\nbut true, statements are:\n\n• “Event horizons are sometimes not detectable with local physics”;\n\n• “Apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizons are not detectable with ultra-local physics”.\n\nNote the very careful and precise phrasing of these two statements.\n\nRegarding the first point, it is an elementary exercise to verify that event horizons can form\nin locally flat portions of Minkowski spacetime. Just let a dust shell collapse (classical dust, zero\npressure). Apply Birkhoff’s theorem. The region outside the shell is a portion of the Schwarzschild\nspacetime. The region inside the shell is a portion of Minkowski spacetime. The event horizon\n(and I really do mean event horizon, this statement is not true for apparent/ dynamical/ trapping\nhorizons) first forms at r = 0 in flat Minkowski space where the Riemann tensor is zero, and\nthen sweeps out to encounter the infalling dust shell just as it crosses r = 2m. (If one insists on an\n\n10\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nexplicit calculation, then it is advisable to use nonsingular coordinates, such as Painlevé–Gullstrand\ncoordinates.) The key point is this:\n\nEvent horizon 6= strong (local) gravity.\n\nEvent horizons are statements about the global geometry, even if the global geometry is sufficiently\ndistorted to prevent light escaping to infinity, this does not tell you anything about the local strength\nof the gravitational field at the event horizon itself. In particular, this class of event horizons,\nbecause they occur in flat Minkowski space, are certainly not detectable (even in principle) by any\nlocal physics. (If one has additional “metadata” this situation can change. For instance, if one\nknows a priori that the spacetime is static, then event horizons are also Killing horizons and are\nalso apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizons — as we shall soon see, this additional structure may\nthen make them detectable using local (though not ultra-local) physics.)\n\nRegarding the second point, spherically symmetric apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizons in\nspherically symmetric spacetimes are typically associated with 2m(r)/r ≈ 1. Furthermore, at least\nin spherical symmetry, the quantity 2m(r)/r is measurable using local (though not ultra-local)\nphysics. To see this, recall that in any finite-size laboratory you can measure the Riemann tensor.\n(Equivalently, physics with finite-range interactions is sensitive to the Riemann tensor.) But in\nspherical symmetry the orthonormal components of the Riemann tensor are linear combinations of\ndensity, radial and transverse pressures, and the quantity 2m(r)/r3 (which is related to the average\ndensity inside radius r). In fact, it is an easy exercise to check [18] (see especially pages 27–28,\nand page 110, exercise 1):\n\nRt̂\nr̂t̂ r̂ =\n\n2m(r)\nr3 −4π(ρ− pr +2pt); (5.1)\n\nRt̂\nθ̂ t̂θ̂ = Rt̂\n\nφ̂ t̂φ̂ = −m(r)\nr3 −4π pr; (5.2)\n\nRr̂\nθ̂ r̂θ̂\n\n= Rr̂\nφ̂ r̂φ̂\n\n= −m(r)\nr3 +4πρ; (5.3)\n\nRθ̂\n\nφ̂ θ̂ φ̂\n=\n\n2m(r)\nr3 . (5.4)\n\nHere pr is the radial pressure, pt the transverse pressure, and ρ the density. Now the stress-energy\ntensor is certainly measurable using local physics, therefore 2m(r)/r3 is measurable using local\n(though not ultra-local) physics. Finally, r itself is just the radius of curvature of the surface\nof spherical symmetry passing through the point of interest, and is again measurable using local\n(though not ultra-local) physics.\n\nCombining these observations: In spherically symmetric spacetimes 2m(r)/r is measurable\nusing local (though not ultra-local) physics, and so the presence of spherically symmetric apparent/\ndynamical/ trapping horizons are detectable using local (though not ultra-local) physics. At the\nrisk of initiating tribal warfare:\n\n• In spherically symmetric spacetimes, restricting attention to spherically symmetric horizons:\nThe most physically interesting horizons, the apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizons, are\ndetectable using local (though not ultra-local) physics.\n\n11\n\n\n\nP\no\nS\n(\nB\nH\ns\n,\n \nG\nR\n \na\nn\nd\n \nS\nt\nr\ni\nn\ng\ns\n)\n0\n0\n1\n\nBlack holes in general relativity Matt Visser\n\nWhen one moves beyond spherical symmetry, either of the spacetime itself or of the trapped sur-\nfaces and/or world tubes used to define apparent/ dynamical/ trapping horizons, then the situation\nbecomes considerably more complex [59].\n\n6. Discussion\n\nThe message that I hope readers take from this micro-survey is that there are still many subtle\nand interesting things going on in black hole physics. Many deep issues of principle remain, despite\nat least 50 years, and by some measure 90 years, work on the subject. Note also that in many cases\nit is worthwhile to carefully re-analyze and re-assess work from several decades ago. Sometimes,\nin my more cynical moments, I feel that each step forward involves 99% of a step backwards:\n\n“Take the red pill to remain in denial. L.","recid":989138},"control_number":616801,"earliest_date":"2003-04","document_type":["article"],"texkeys":["Shapiro:2003xe"],"abstracts":[{"source":"arXiv","value":"There is compelling evidence that supermassive black holes exist. Yet the origin of these objects, or their seeds, is still unknown. We discuss several plausible scenarios for forming the seeds of supermassive black holes. These include the catastrophic collapse of supermassive stars, the collapse of relativistic clusters of collisionless particles or stars, the gravothermal evolution of dense clusters of ordinary stars or stellar-mass compact objects, and the gravothermal evolution of self-interacting dark matter halos. Einstein's equations of general relativity are required to describe key facets of these scenarios, and large-scale numerical simulations are performed to solve them.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"arXiv"}}],"primary_arxiv_category":["astro-ph"],"titles":[{"title":"Formation of supermassive black holes: simulations in general relativity"},{"source":"arXiv","title":"Formation of Supermassive Black Holes: Simulations in General Relativity"}],"external_system_identifiers":[{"schema":"ADS","value":"2004cbhg.symp..103S"},{"schema":"SPIRES","value":"SPIRES-5523176"}],"facet_author_name":["989138_Stuart L. Once the matter shrinks inside the inner horizon for the exterior geometry, an untrapped region is formed and eventually the singularity becomes timelike. Part of the matter forming the black hole collapses into the singularity while the rest can bounce and cross the Cauchy horizon. All the matter can bounce inside the trapping horizon without forming a singularity inside the matter distribution. In this Letter we challenge this view by analyzing a charged spherically symmetric black hole formed through gravitational collapse and evaporating via Hawking radiation. We show that the electromagnetic repulsion and the violation of energy conditions due to the presence of Hawking radiation can be sufficient to avoid the formation of both a singularity and a Cauchy horizon. We argue that a similar mechanism may apply to astrophysical black holes in which the role of the electric charge is replaced by the angular momentum.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"APS"}},{"source":"arXiv","value":"It is common knowledge that black holes necessarily contain a region where general relativity breaks down, due to the inevitable formation of either a curvature singularity or a Cauchy horizon. In this work we challenge this view by analyzing a charged spherically symmetric black hole formed through gravitational collapse and evaporating via Hawking radiation. We show that the electromagnetic repulsion and the violation of energy conditions due to the presence of Hawking radiation are be sufficient to avoid the formation of both a singularity and a Cauchy horizon. We argue that a similar mechanism may apply to astrophysical black holes in which the role of the electric charge is replaced by the angular momentum.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"arXiv"}}],"primary_arxiv_category":["gr-qc"],"titles":[{"source":"APS","title":"Radiating Black Holes in General Relativity Need Not Be to general relativity, black holes are incomplete, which prevents developing a complete physical description of their dynamical formation and evolution once quantum effects are taken into account. Theories beyond general relativity may provide a more complete description of black hole interiors. In this work, the most general form of the field equations for spherically symmetric gravitational fields, in which the Einstein tensor is deformed into a conserved tensor constructed from up to second-order derivatives of the metric, is described. These equations set up the stage for the study of the dynamics of spherically symmetric spacetimes beyond general relativity, providing tools for the theoretical exploration of a paradigm of black hole physics free of the incompleteness characteristic of Einstein’s theory. A general proof of the Birkhoff–Jebsen theorem for vacuum solutions, and the construction of field equations describing the effective geometrodynamics of regular black holes interacting with matter, are discussed.","abstract_source_suggest":{"input":"Springer"}},{"source":"arXiv","value":"According to general relativity, black holes are incomplete, which prevents developing a complete physical description of their dynamical formation and evolution once quantum effects are taken into account. Theories beyond general relativity may provide a more complete description of black hole interiors. In this work, the most general form of the field equations for spherically symmetric gravitational fields, in which the Einstein tensor is deformed into a conserved tensor constructed from up to second-order derivatives of the metric, is described. These equations set up the stage for the study of the dynamics of spherically symmetric spacetimes beyond general relativity, providing tools for the theoretical exploration of a paradigm of black hole physics free of the incompleteness characteristic of Einstein's theory. A general proof of the Birkhoff--Jebsen theorem for vacuum solutions, and the construction of field equations describing the effective geometrodynamics of regular black holes interacting with matter, gravitational collapse of the Brans-Dicke scalar field and formation of black holes in 2+1 Gravity is examined. In contrast to general relativity, there are two conformally related frames in the Brans-Dicke theory: the Jordan frame and the Einstein frame. All the self-similar solutions are first re-derived in three dimensional Brans-Dicke theory, and then their local and global properties are studied by paying particular attention to the formation of black holes due to the gravitational collapse of the scalar field."}],"titles":[{"title":"Gravitational collapse and formation of black holes in the Brans-Dicke theory of gravity with (2+1)
